text:
I declare open this hearing of the Education and Employment Legislation Committee into the 2026-27 supplementary budget estimates. I begin by acknowledging the traditional custodians of the land on which we meet today and pay my respects to elders past and present, and I extend that respect to any Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander people joining us here today.

The committee has fixed Thursday 17 December 2026 as the date for the return of answers to questions taken on notice. The committee's proceedings today will begin with corporate and enabling services, cross-portfolio and general matters of the Employment and Workplace Relations portfolio.

Under standing order 26, the committee must take all evidence in public session, and this includes answers to questions on notice. I remind all witnesses that in giving evidence to the committee they are protected by parliamentary privilege. It is unlawful for anyone to threaten or disadvantage a witness on account of evidence given to a committee, and such action may be treated by the Senate as a contempt. It is also a contempt to give false or misleading evidence.

The Senate has endorsed the following test of relevance of questions at estimates hearings: any questions going to the operations or financial positions of the departments and agencies which are seeking funds in estimates are relevant questions for the purpose of estimates hearings. I remind officers that the Senate has resolved that there are no areas in connection with the expenditure of public funds where any person has a discretion to withhold details or explanations from the parliament or its committees unless the parliament has expressly provided otherwise.

The Senate has resolved also that an officer of a department of the Commonwealth shall not be asked to give opinions on matters of policy and shall be given reasonable opportunity to refer questions asked of the officer to superior officers or to a minister. This resolution does not preclude questions asking for explanations of policies or factual questions about when and how policies were adopted. Witnesses are reminded of the Senate order specifying the process by which a claim of public interest immunity should be raised, and I incorporate the public immunity statement into the Hansard.

The extract read as follows—

Public interest immunity claims

That the Senate—

(a) notes that ministers and officers have continued to refuse to provide information to Senate committees without properly raising claims of public interest immunity as required by past resolutions of the Senate;

(b) reaffirms the principles of past resolutions of the Senate by this order, to provide ministers and officers with guidance as to the proper process for raising public interest immunity claims and to consolidate those past resolutions of the Senate;

(c) orders that the following operate as an order of continuing effect:

(1) If:

(a) a Senate committee, or a senator in the course of proceedings of a committee, requests information or a document from a Commonwealth department or agency; and

(b) an officer of the department or agency to whom the request is directed believes that it may not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, the officer shall state to the committee the ground on which the officer believes that it may not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, and specify the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document.

(2) If, after receiving the officer's statement under paragraph (1), the committee or the senator requests the officer to refer the question of the disclosure of the information or document to a responsible minister, the officer shall refer that question to the minister.

(3) If a minister, on a reference by an officer under paragraph (2), concludes that it would not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, the minister shall provide to the committee a statement of the ground for that conclusion, specifying the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document.

(4) A minister, in a statement under paragraph (3), shall indicate whether the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document to the committee could result only from the publication of the information or document by the committee, or could result, equally or in part, from the disclosure of the information or document to the committee as in camera evidence.

(5) If, after considering a statement by a minister provided under paragraph (3), the committee concludes that the statement does not sufficiently justify the withholding of the information or document from the committee, the committee shall report the matter to the Senate.

(6) A decision by a committee not to report a matter to the Senate under paragraph (5) does not prevent a senator from raising the matter in the Senate in accordance with other procedures of the Senate.

(7) A statement that information or a document is not published, or is confidential, or consists of advice to, or internal deliberations of, government, in the absence of specification of the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document, is not a statement that meets the requirements of paragraph (1) or (4).

(8) If a minister concludes that a statement under paragraph (3) should more appropriately be made by the head of an agency, by reason of the independence of that agency from ministerial direction or control, the minister shall inform the committee of that conclusion and the reason for that conclusion, and shall refer the matter to the head of the agency, who shall then be required to provide a statement in accordance with paragraph (3).

(d) requires the Procedure Committee to review the operation of this order and report to the Senate by 20 August 2009.

(13 May 2009 J.1941)

(Extract, Senate Standing Orders)

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text:
Thank you. Chair, before I begin, I'd like to add my voice to those who've expressed their shock at the horrific attack on the member for Indi, Dr Helen Haines. On behalf of the department, I extend our thoughts and best wishes to Dr Haines, her family, her staff and her community.

I'll briefly update the committee on senior staffing arrangements in two matters central to the department's responsibilities: the Targeted Compliance Framework and our internal workforce strategy. Starting with senior staffing arrangements, there has been a temporary change to the leadership of Employment and Workforce Group, with Ms Lisa Schofield acting as deputy secretary while Ms Tania Rishniw leads employment services reform through to the May budget. There have been no other changes at the deputy secretary level since the last estimates.

Moving now to the Targeted Compliance Framework, or TCF, on 19 October I issued a public statement detailing progress on returning elements of the TCF to lawful administration, providing compensation to those adversely affected by unlawful administration in the past, and developing a digital protections framework. In that statement, I indicated that on 26 October decision-making would resume under two of the six paused elements of the TCF. The first element that resumed on that date is decisions made under section 42AG of the Social Security (Administration) Act, which allows a person's social security participation payment to be suspended for a work refusal failure. The second element is decisions made under section 42AM, which allows a person's participation payment to be cancelled if they do not meet a reconnection requirement within four weeks. Before recommencing these provisions, the department worked with Services Australia to complete comprehensive assurance activities and system testing, made necessary ICT changes and improved our guidance and training for decision-makers. This included requiring all relevant provider staff to complete updated training.

On the days leading up to 26 October, we also removed all existing mutual obligation failures in the system and lifted active payment suspensions for participants in Workforce Australia, Inclusive Employment Australia and Transition to Work. This means that participants receive the full benefit of the applicable resolution period and four-week reconnection period before a payment cancellation may occur.

We're actively monitoring the resumed provisions in partnership with colleagues at Services Australia and the Department of Social Services to ensure that the system operates as intended. This active monitoring of system performance and work-refusal decisions will continue beyond when the first payment cancellations may start to occur, in early December.

The remaining four paused elements of the TCF, all of which relate to ensuring that legally required human discretion is supported in decision-making, will remain paused until further safeguards and assurance arrangements are in place. At this stage, those elements are expected to resume in the first quarter of 2027, subject to completion of comprehensive system, decision-making and assurance work.

In my statement on 19 October, I also indicated the department has commenced the compensation process for people who may be eligible because of unlawful payment cancellation decisions made under sections 42AM, 42AG and 42AH. We are taking a proactive invitation-to-claim approach using data held in DEWR and Services Australia systems to identify people most likely to be eligible for compensation under the Compensation for Detriment caused by Defective Administration Scheme. At the same time, we have made it clear in all of our communication that anyone who believes they may have suffered detriment can apply for compensation under this scheme at any time.

The first stage of this process focuses on those affected by cancellation decisions under 42AM. The department will be proactively inviting 50,652 people to apply for compensation, who have been identified through data analysis as most likely to be eligible for compensation under the requirements of the CDDA Scheme. This process commenced on Monday 19 October, and, by the end of yesterday, we had sent 1,430 invitations.

Receipt of an invitation or making a claim does not determine eligibility. Each claim will be assessed individually, having regard to the person's circumstances and any detriment experienced. Clear information and support are available online through providers via Economic Justice Australia, the community legal sector and Services Australia. Our focus is on ensuring affected people understand their options, are supported to make a claim and can seek a review where appropriate.

The department has also completed public consultation on the draft digital protections framework and the associated section 40Y guidelines. We are considering the feedback and expect to finalise the framework soon. Compensation, the resumption of compliance decisions and finalisation of the digital protections framework are separate processes. The department will continue progressing compensation while continuing to bring the Targeted Compliance Framework into lawful administration and ensuring that appropriate safeguards remain in place. Chair, the officials working on these matters will be here to provide evidence under outcome 1, scheduled for this afternoon.

The final topic that I wanted to cover in my opening statement is the department's workforce strategy. A significant focus in recent months has been ensuring that our workforce and resources remain aligned to the government's priorities and the department's broader accountabilities. In the May budget, the government made an additional investment in frontline employment services, driving an overall increase in the department's affordable staffing level for 2026-27. Outside frontline employment services, though, the department's affordable staffing numbers are lower this financial year. There's also a mismatch between the capabilities and APS levels of the staff that we need in frontline employment services and staff in other parts of the department.

Therefore, while the focus of our workforce strategy is to build the capability of our staff and allocate them to the areas of greatest need within the department, we've also been actively recruiting into frontline employment services at a time when we've been seeking expressions of interest for voluntary redundancies and incentives to retire. As of 23 October, the department has made formal voluntary redundancy offers to 101 employees this financial year, of which 91 have been accepted. We also had two of our senior executives accept an incentive to retire. Importantly, there have not been any involuntary redundancies, and I don't expect any will be required.

In making these decisions, our objectives have been to direct the department's resources to the highest priorities, retain and build the capability of our workforce and keep the department financially sustainable over the medium to long term. Thank you, Chair. My colleagues and I look forward to assisting the committee with its questions.

text: This is my first estimates on this committee, so excuse me if it takes a bit of time to get familiar with who's who. Mr Duggan, I understand you told this committee on 2 June that the department 'remains on track to stay within its approved operating deficit'. What was the actual outcome?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text:
Just to provide a little bit of context, 2025-26 was the department's fourth financial year of operations since its establishment on 1 July 2022. The department had recorded operating losses in three of those four financial years. One of my priorities since commencing as secretary has been to get the department back onto a sustainable financial footing. The answer to your question is that, for the last financial year, DEWR's annual report recorded an operating loss of $25 million, which is larger than the operating loss of $15 million previously approved by the finance minister—and that was disclosed in our portfolio budget statements.

On my commencement as secretary, I put in place a number of initiatives that were intended to bring our operating expenditure down. Those were largely successful. On an operating cash basis, we actually recorded a small surplus last financial year. The reason we ran an operating deficit, and one that was larger than the one that was approved by the finance minister, is, at the end of the financial year, we needed to record a number of accounting adjustments to account for the impairment of some assets. The economic value of property and of software was assessed by the accountants as being lower, which meant that those accounting adjustments more than offset what was an improved operating position on a cash basis to drive our accrual position to a larger operating deficit at the end of the financial year. It didn't impact our cash balance—our cash balance remains broadly what it was at the start of the financial year and at the end of the financial year—but, as I noted, it meant we recorded a larger operating deficit than I'd been predicting.

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Good morning. I was wondering if I could ask you about the department's work on Closing the Gap. As you know, it's always a topic that this committee likes to discuss. Could you share with us any updates you have for the department in progressing these priority reforms and any outcomes that you are seeing.

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text:
I'll start, and then I'll hand to my colleague to provide more detail. The department, as you know, plays a very significant role in closing the gap on Indigenous disadvantage. A new development is that in the past six months we have articulated a new strategic framework for the department. Within that strategic framework, we identify embedding Closing the Gap as being a core cross-cutting priority. So it's important for all of the work of the department, not just some of the work of the department.

As you'd be aware, we administer policies and programs that directly impact four of the 17 socioeconomic outcome areas. At the Commonwealth level, we share responsibility with the Department of Education for outcome 5, around student learning potential; outcome 6, further education pathways; and outcome 7, around youth engagement in employment or education. We also share outcome 8, on strong economic participation and development of people and communities, with the National Indigenous Australians Agency. We are making progress against each of those outcome areas. Target 8, around strong economic participation and development of people and communities, is on track to be met by 2031. Targets 5, 6 and 7 are improving but at this stage not on track. I'll turn to Mr Castro to see if there's anything he wants to add.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text:
Our department's implementation of the priority reforms really starts with priority reform 3, the internal transformation. In the past few years we've done a number of things to improve the governance and accountability around Closing the Gap within the department. One of the first things that we did under the previous secretary was establish a central Closing the Gap function to oversee and drive our Closing the Gap efforts. Shortly after that, we developed a Closing the Gap strategy that really gave authority for the rest of the department to understand the Closing the Gap priority reforms and make those changes. That quickly resulted in some big change for the department.

Our governance framework for the department was modified to ensure that everybody in the department took accountability for Closing the Gap and that our internal governance forums had First Nations voices on them as well. That was a clear transformation. Shortly after that, we also changed our internal audit framework to make sure that every internal audit that's conducted considers whether our business units are considering the department's commitments to First Nations people. They're really key transformational pieces, which were soon followed by a launch of a departmental Reconciliation Action Plan, which lays the foundation for developing those foundation skills to build better relationships with First Nations people, which is really important for the way that we engage, consult and listen to people.

Those internal transformations are starting to have a demonstrable effect on our externally facing policies and programs. We've seen in employment services, probably starting with the Parent Pathways program, a lot of engagement with First Nations people that effectively resulted in First Nations providers delivering services on our behalf to all parents under that program. We've seen growth in the ACCHO, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander community controlled, sector through programs like the SEE First Nations grant, which deliberately recognises that First Nations people have a different experience, and we wanted to get communities involved to make sure that the projects we were delivering were meeting their needs as well. I can keep going if you'd like.

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations

When we talk about the targets, as Mr Duggan stated, we do share responsibility for those targets not just with other Commonwealth agencies but with states and territories as well. In our employment services space, I've talked about the Parent Pathways program. The Reconnection, Employment and Learning program, as well, which this committee has heard a lot about, took deliberate actions to make sure that that program was designed in consultation with First Nations people not just in the way that the program's set up to operate but also in the indicators of what success looks like in that program. What we saw there was 15 out of 16 organisations engaged to deliver that program being First Nations owned or Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander controlled organisations, which is a really great outcome as well.

In our skills space, the National Skills Agreement was one of the first agreements that embedded Closing the Gap as a foundation. What we've seen through the National Skills Agreement is work to develop a new VET policy partnership and other actions to build the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander community controlled sector and their engagement. Some of the examples of what's been done in that space are: there's a new Indigenous Centre of Vocational Excellence set up. That's designed to identify best practice and share and grow that best practice across the vocational education and training sector. There's also a First Nations RTO community of practice, which, again, is about supporting First Nations providers to work together to share their experiences and to advocate for First Nations impacts throughout the skills and training sector as well. All states and territories have a bilateral implementation plan with the Commonwealth to deliver on Closing the Gap commitments, as well, which is really focused at getting more First Nations people through the skills and training sector.

text: Does Ms Tuckwell report to you?

She does; therefore I take accountability for this issue as much as anybody else. I think our evidence, both in the answer to the question on notice and at the previous hearing, is that the media release was published in error by a junior staff member who didn't correctly apply the guidance around which material should be published to which websites. We've acknowledged that error. As soon as we became aware of the error, we corrected it. I think we have been very clear and focused on making sure that we strengthen the systems to try to prevent those kinds of errors happening in the future, but also in detecting whether things are published in error so that we can act more quickly and not need to rely on somebody else to bring it to our attention.

So I think there have been a series of things that Ms Tuckwell and her team have focused on—including strengthening those procedures, lifting the level at which people have the authority to authorise things to be published on websites, and reinforcing guidelines with the staff in the communications branch—just to ensure that we're not in this position again. This was, as I think I said at the last hearing, a human error, and we need to make sure that we strengthen our systems and processes to try and prevent those things in the future.

witness_position: Chief Operating Officer, Corporate and Enabling Services

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: It's a fair comment. As I said, we've elevated the level at which people have the authority to publish those things, and we've strengthened the oversight of those matters to ensure that we're not inadvertently publishing things in the wrong places.

One of the things that has also been made very clear through the framework is that value for money really is central to spending decisions. The framework itself sits alongside price, quality, relevant experience and performance history as key factors in that assessment.

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Yes, certainly. As Mr Manning said, I think you are referring to part 9 of the building cooperative workplaces No. 1 bill, which was passed by the parliament earlier this year. That part amended part 3.1 of the Fair Work Act. What it did was create targeted exceptions to specify general protections provisions for certain Commonwealth financial and contractual arrangements—so, really, grants and procurement. That allowed preference to be given to employers based on specified enterprise agreement coverage. I would note that it didn't require the Commonwealth to give a preference or require an employer to have an enterprise agreement, though; it was a facilitative sort of change.

witness_position: Acting First Assistant Secretary, Chief Counsel

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: The provision Mr Kerr's referring to was a provision that was made to change the operation of the Fair Work Act, which prohibited any distinction being made between different types of legislative instruments. So, for example, if the government was funding an area of public life and had a preference for there to be enterprise agreements in there to ensure that the conditions were above the minimum standards and could be passed through to the employers, then that provision could facilitate that and remove the prohibition that had existed before that. It doesn't require that to occur. It's purely a facility provision. It doesn't necessarily apply in any specific context. For example, it doesn't necessarily apply to the Secure Australian Jobs code, which we were talking about earlier. It was changing a restriction that was in the Fair Work Act up until that time.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations

In relation to the standards, the minister has said on a number of occasions, for example, that the standards 'will not require employees to enter an enterprise agreement covered by a union' as a condition of receiving Commonwealth government funding, and 'nor will the government preference union covered enterprise agreements when considering tenders for federally funded building and construction work'. That's the intention of them—how to lift up the standard of safety, productivity et cetera in construction where there's federal government funding.

Separately to that, there's the Secure Australian Jobs Framework, which, the intention is, won't apply to construction and also won't require an EA either. text:
I think we probably have the people I need for this question, but I'll be in your hands if we need somebody else. I want to go back to the CFMEU administrator and also, obviously, the importance of the NCIF, the National Construction Industry Forum, and that code that's been built. It does reflect a little bit about the importance of governments' doing procurement policy. There are numerous companies that can be used as examples, but I have used this one before and I think it's appropriate: last year, the CFMEU administrator's interim report outlined shocking allegations in regard to Future Form. And I noted that Future Form was in a number of state and partially federally funded projects as well through supply chains, so there is a direct link on the money trail of responsibility. But I also note that companies like Multiplex are also, separately, where there isn't federal or state government money, engaging Future Form—have been, to my knowledge, at least up until a few months ago.

That company—in that administrator's report and a number of subsequent media reports, there were allegations of mafia-style intimidation, threats and violence designed to terrorise a union official into silence, from the administrator: masked men turning up at his family home, spray painting vile abuse across the property while his wife and young children slept inside; his car and boat being doused in petrol and set alight while he and his wife and his kids were asleep inside their home; his relative being ambushed in a car park by several men claiming to represent Future Form. These men told him that they knew where he worked, where his family was and even that they were at the dentist at the very moment that these men were confronting him. We could all imagine how devastating that would be, because it would be sheer terror that you would feel, and even just repeating it brings up some of the terrible scenes that we've seen in the construction industry. The message, of course, from Future Form was simply to stop investigating that company. The NSW government has subsequently made a ministerial direction to not use them—and I made my comments before about Future Form.

This goes to a very important thing. One of the recurring complaints that I hear and have seen reports on is that workers that work for good companies are being undercut by contractors who willingly cut corners on wages, conditions, job security, sham contracting. And these are big projects; these aren't some fly-by-night small operators. These are big projects with big money—tens of millions and hundreds of millions of dollars involved. So, with the discussions and the aim of the discussions of the NCIF—how's that supposed to tackle not only what we've seen previously from the construction union but also, more generally, what happens in the construction industry, combating this sort of behaviour that Future Form illustrates?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text:
The potential Commonwealth standards for the construction industry could establish clear minimum expectations for the industry in terms of addressing structural and systemic issues that may require government oversight, regulation and enforcement. They would be designed to address existing gaps without duplicating existing arrangements. The potential construction standards represent an opportunity for government to support the industry in the reform work that's being undertaken, largely through the National Construction Industry Forum but also otherwise. Both the draft charter—which is an industry led voluntary framework that was intended to support industry participants to align decisions and behaviours with agreed expectations and demonstrate a commitment to acting in good faith—and the potential construction standards are intended to support improved productivity, lawfulness, sustainability and worker outcomes. They're both consistent with the work of the National Construction Industry Forum as it's reflected in its blueprint, in particular some of the priority recommendations under that blueprint, particularly priority recommendation 3.1, which is about procurement frameworks and settings. That is not the only work that is underway in relation to priority recommendation 3.1. We're also working closely with the Department of Finance, who have engaged the Australian Procurement and Construction Council. They've been commissioned to also do work to support this recommendation.

So there is a considerable body of work underway to tackle this problem that reflects the severity of the concerns that you have outlined and that are shared by quite a few members of the National Construction Industry Forum—the blueprint sets out their agreed pathway for addressing challenges in the industry.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Safety and Industry Policy

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text:
The ATO estimates it is losing $1.4 billion in unpaid taxes each year from dodgy companies who are ripping off taxpayers. That has an effect on everyone as a community. It affects our defence spending and our education spending—the list of important things goes on. One contractor told the AFR in an article on 28 February 2024 that they were 'sick of what is happening' to the industry. Referring to Sydney Metro, they said that subcontractors 'undercut everyone on price and leverage the ATO to make a living' and continued:

The tier-one builders turn a blind eye because it all comes down to price. The true cost of the Sydney Metro developments, the new hospitals and schools should factor in the unpaid taxes. The taxpayer is being screwed.

Again, part of the purpose of the code is to look at these sorts of things—which, I would argue, are still running rife in elements of the industry.

Of course, then we can go to illegal phoenixing as well. On 14 March 25, there was a prime example, involving construction company City Scape and the $3.8 billion Burswood Point urban housing, where the company owed $10 million to the ATO and it was written off at 10c in the dollar. Bryce, a CFMEU member and construction worker, said, 'Our family was destroyed by the Phoenix model of collapse of GN construction, and I hope no worker ever goes through that again.' Tax avoidance and phoenixing companies not paying workers have, unfortunately, been seen too often—and, of course, as I mentioned in the previous question, violence occurs.

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text:
To add another dimension to that, it impacts this portfolio because we administer the Fair Entitlement Guarantee program, where people whose entitlements aren't paid can go and get them from government and then government seeks to recover them. Construction has for a long time been, and remains, one of the largest sectors in that, so that's another way it impacts the taxpayer.

The issue you touch on is an issue that the NCIF has been very focused on since its inception in the sense that, in addition to the race to the bottom on price, it also means that it impacts on the employment models in the industry. It stops people building careers through the industry et cetera and creates lots of disincentives. That's why the charter that Ms Godden referred is an important foundational bit of work, because it sets out those shared goals and expectations of behaviour that the industry agrees we should see not only generally but on individual projects. Then there are a range of other bits of work in the blueprint that Ms Godden spoke about that go to trying to overturn that impact of just competing on price and then getting into everything from sharp to outright illegal behaviour and violence, for example. It's an important first step, and then the standards are meant to complement that by saying that the NCIF is a tripartite body.

One thing government can do is use its investment in construction to drive the types of behaviour it wants to see around secure work, diversity of workforce, safety and productivity. To go to some of those examples you've used that we touched on earlier in relation to Senator O'Sullivan's questions—things like, should there be a 'fit and proper person' test for certain contractors of a certain level on projects of a certain size so that people who are either proven to be engaging in or there are allegations that can be substantiated, could be excluded, potentially. That's the type of work the government's got under consideration at the moment. As I said earlier, we're looking at all of those submissions and then giving advice to government in relation to how it can use its purchasing power to be part of that industry drive for change.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Sorry to say this, but this part leads to the same point. Evidence can be drawn from lots of places: from the worker who's been ripped off is probably not a bad starting point, as are companies that are being unfairly competed with. My experience has been that good companies are reluctant to speak out. It's a club. They are fearful of repercussions from other contractors, let alone the nature of business, so it does go to this important question about putting those guidelines in place to try to give that opportunity for people to speak out. The union and the administrator obviously play an important role in giving whistleblower protections as well. Is it the whole industry's responsibility? When I say industry, I mean union, employers and government.

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations

For example, they want to ensure that workers have access to the same terms and conditions regardless of who their employer is, but they can't control who their employer is. It goes to broader issues around the culture of the industry and who is able to be involved in the industry. The NCIF is very much meant to be unions and employers coming together to represent the whole industry to try and lift those standards and behaviours that have been seen in the industry.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: There's been a whole series of reports from successive governments, including the previous government, and reports of state governments of different political persuasions, that have outlined this: phoenixing, tax avoidance, wage theft, superannuation theft—again, that superannuation theft goes into many billions of dollars. It's not that we haven't got enough reports. It's a question about how we get the industry to change culture. Would that be a fair analysis?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations

agency: Fair Work Commission
text:
The CFMEU has previously successfully opposed attempts by employer bodies to insert casual mineworker roles into the Black Coal Mining Industry Award. I have a copy of a CFMEU publication titled 'Employers push for casualisation in black coal award defeated', which is no longer readily available online, so that's why I'm sharing it with you. The CFMEU, as the black coal mining union, opposed casuals. As a mine manager in the 1980s, I know that they were adamant about not allowing casuals or even contractors. However, it started the first labour hire firm that was used in the coal industry. I've forgotten the name of it, but it retrenched mineworkers. It had a labour hire firm that it owned. It then sold that and was involved with other labour hire firms in various stages of ownership. It was well and truly opposed to it in a public stance, but it was supporting it and being a labour hire firm in private.

The purpose of an enterprise agreement is to provide terms that, subject to the statutory requirements, operate against the relevant minimum standards. Where an enterprise agreement permits mineworkers to be employed as casuals when the relevant award does not provide for that classification, the agreement appears to introduce employment arrangements materially less secure than the full-time or part-time arrangements contemplated by the award. Is that correct?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: The evidence that I provided previously is that a modern award will apply unless it is ultimately displaced by an enterprise agreement. The enterprise agreement will apply to the workers that are covered, the employees that are covered, by that enterprise agreement. The application of the minimum rate of pay is applicable not to penalties but the minimum rate in that enterprise agreement.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Yes.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: That is the better off overall test?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: That's right.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: It must at least match the provisions of the award?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: That's right.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Since 2019, I raised concerns that black coal mining industry enterprise agreements made from 2010 onwards have, in some cases, delivered terms and conditions below those available under the relevant award, including lower rates of pay, and that a large number of those agreements were negotiated, recommended or endorsed by the CFMEU. Minister, given that an individual Fair Work commissioner cannot vary or revoke a modern award, do you agree that approving a black coal mining industry enterprise agreement that permits casual mineworker employment where the relevant award does not permit that classification raises a question as to whether the commissioner acted beyond their statutory authority or jurisdiction?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: I am not sure that I can accept all of the premises that are in your question. Obviously, the government supports fair pay and good job security for workers, which is why, for example, we passed our same job, same pay provisions, which have been very important in the mining industry. The Fair Work Commission is independent. We respect the independence of decisions of the commission.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Will the government investigate and then acknowledge and address the historical underpayments, subject to that investigation, that may have resulted from such agreements, irrespective of which employee or employer organisation negotiated or endorsed them?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Again, I don't have all the information to accept all the premises of your question, but we do respect the independence of the Fair Work Commission.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: If you could get the evidence, you would investigate?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: That's a hypothetical question.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Senator, do you mind if I just clarify a piece of evidence I gave? In terms of varying a modern award, a single member of the commission can, but custom and practice, in the normal course of things, is that they are dealt with by full benches of the commission.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Let me ask you a question back: that is because it is a very significant thing to do?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: It is. It can impact on many hundreds of thousands, if not—
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: I have been in the CFMEU as a member. Sometimes the person running the meeting can manipulate that. Heaven forbid, but it happened. I've seen it. When the union membership endorses something at a mine—I'm not talking about nationally but at a mine—it can be as a result of manipulation. Thank you, Mr Furlong.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: No response required?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: No.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Senator Kovacic.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Mr Furlong, at the last estimates you told the committee—my questions relate to the CFMEU—that you work on a trust-but-verify basis and meet weekly with senior officials from the administration. Is that still the case?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Yes, I meet very regularly with senior officials from the administration.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Does Mr Crosby attend those meetings?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: I deal with Mr Crosby on a needs-to-know basis. My scheduled fortnightly meetings are with the chief of staff.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: With Mr Crosby's chief of staff?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Chief of staff, yes.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Would you mind detailing how the commission keeps track of the administration's progress? Is there a progress tracker or a similar document the commission uses for this?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: The administrator is independent of me and is independent of government. For all intents and purposes, he has all the powers of all officers under the rules of the organisation vested in himself. He conducts the operation of the union in accordance with the rules of the organisation, in line with the scheme of administration and, obviously, the obligations under the amended RO Act and section 323 of the RO Act. My interactions and the commission's interactions with the administration, the office of the administration and the CFMEU Construction and General Division are many times each week. They have two purposes. One is to clean up that union, and the second is to advocate on behalf of the members of that union with enterprise bargaining, and with ensuring the work health and safety of members on site.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: But the original purpose of the union is maintained—not what it has become.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Absolutely. In terms of the meetings the interactions include right-of-entry permits, enterprise bargaining, other interactions around annual returns and other obligations under the Registered Organisations Act. The CFMEU still has to meet all of its obligations under the Registered Organisations Act that apply to all registered organisations, and so we ensure it is complying with all of its obligations under the RO Act. In addition, I obviously have a significant interest in ensuring the scheme of administration is being effectively applied. When I appointed Mr Crosby, I gave him, attached with his instrument of appointment, a list of matters that I would like him to consider focusing on over the next 12 months. Yesterday I received correspondence from the chief of staff and from the administrator that outlined some of the areas they are focusing on. Having spent decades in and around regulation and industrial relations, I remain satisfied by the operations of the administration and the work they are undertaking. My assessment is that they are essentially doing more than every other industry participant combined. I can talk to some of the areas of the work that they're focusing on at the moment, some very significant, impactful work that I believe will significantly improve workplace relations in the building and construction industry.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: There is nothing that you specifically track? If I reframe it: in your report on Mr Crosby's appointment as administrator, you said that he explained what success for the administration would look like at the end of the three years. I take your answer to my question, but I assume that there is no tracker or similar document, because you believe there is no need for one. Are there any benchmarks or milestones that the commission has set down that we can mark progress against so that we have an understanding of how the administration is progressing? I note your comments that you are satisfied but, beyond that, is there any documented process to substantiate that?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: To hopefully provide you with some comfort, the administrator is intending shortly to circulate a discussion paper relating to the conditions under which he would eventually recommend to the government that part of the CFMEU be released from administration. The administrator, in relation to this piece of work, intends to consult widely on this matter and will engage stakeholders at every level.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: I have two questions. I can understand there is no document or process by which progress is measured. It is purely a matter of satisfaction of both you and the administrator. Is that correct?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: In terms of the formal process, there are ongoing conversations and consultations. They have outlined a program of work. They have a strategic plan in place.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: I get that. If you were on a board, you would have a risk tracker. If you were having a changeover, an organisational changeover or anything such as that, you would check off each of those to ensure they are completed. Is there any such document?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: That document is being prepared at the moment.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: It does not yet exist in that format?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: In that format? No.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: When did the preparation of that document begin?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: As I just indicated, in my conversations with the CFMEU it has been contemplating the development of—your word—a 'tracker' for a number of months. It has been on its work program. Obviously, it has a lot of competing priorities, but it is something that, from my understanding and from my conversations with them and questions that I have asked, it is intending to prepare. The basis of that will be that the administrator will have to be satisfied before approaching the minister about whether or not any of the branches of the division should be released from administration.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Respectfully, I'm mindful that we are two years into the administration. If it goes for the full five years, we are almost halfway. To suggest that a process to track progress is being considered and was perhaps not yet high on the list of priorities is a concern to me, because I am very much of the view that you can't track or improve what you don't measure.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: I agree with that premise. I am possibly in a unique position to observe the activities of the administration. With my knowledge and experience, I am satisfied with the activities they have taken to date and what they have proposed to do over the next six to 12 months. I think it was brought into evidence earlier today that over half the employees of that organisation are no longer working for that organisation. There will be very few organisations in Australia that have undergone such significant reform change as the CFMEU Construction and General Division. No-one is saying that the work is done. If you read Mr Crosby's biannual report to parliament closely, you will see that he indicates that there is significant work to be done, particularly in the Victorian-Tasmanian branch. No-one is resiling from that assessment.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: I accept your comments in relation to that—and you are the expert—but I would also suggest that no other organisation has caused the damage both to its members and to the taxpayer that the CFMEU has in recent years. I think that is an equal parallel. Your report also lists areas of focus you discussed with Mr Crosby, including resolving longstanding demarcation disputes, particularly with the AWU, and preventing delegates or organisers misusing WHS and enterprise agreement levers to drive industrial outcomes. Has the commission recorded any progress on these two issues in particular since Mr Crosby's appointment?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text:
I will deal with the demarcation matter first. I'm very pleased to report that significant progress has been made in relation to the resolution of longstanding demarcation disputes between the AWU and the CFMEU. Geoffrey Watson SC's report that related to conduct in Queensland in particular talked about the menacing conduct and intimidation associated with demarcation, particularly in relation to the AWU. On the back of that, I understood that there was a very significant issue. Associated with my letter of appointment to Mr Crosby, I asked him to focus on this particular element, and he has absolutely done that.

There is a signed agreement between the AWU and the CFMEU to work together with a former Fair Work Commission member, a very highly respected and esteemed Fair Work Commission member in former commissioner Julius Roe, through their eligibility rules and determine where the eligibility sits for each of those unions—and not only to determine a standing agreement between the organisations. They have done a lot of work together already, and other stakeholders have been involved.

I understand that Mr Roe has also met with employer associations and those who represent the interests of employers as well. In terms of an initial draft decision for certain elements of the demarcation, he has made preliminary findings. Part of the agreement is that the AWU and CFMEU have agreed to comply with and to observe what Mr Roe identifies as the demarcation between the two unions. To improve things for the future, it's not just about people understanding where the demarcation between the unions rests. In the normal course of matters, there will be disputation because there will be areas where it's not particularly clear where the eligibility sits. One matter that has been considered by Mr Roe and the unions at the moment is: when these issues arise, what is the best mechanism for resolving them? It's not through industrial fixes. It's not through other means. It's to identify a mechanism that they both agree to such that, when a dispute arises, this is how it will be dealt with.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: At the last estimates you told the committee in a letter which you sent Mr Crosby that you asked him to focus on reform work in Victoria, because a significant amount of work still needed to be done in that branch. I note the matters upon which you have just commented that I have just asked you about, but are you able to point to anything specifically that has changed or has been improved in the Victorian branch since that letter? Again, is that progress recorded anywhere? If so, are you able to table that for us?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: I can. There are a number of matters. I neglected to respond to your question about the weaponisation of WHS matters. I received correspondence and communications from employer interests in the industry. On receiving that information, I wrote to HWSA, the work health and safety agencies. That is made up of the CEOs of the regulators across the country, including the Commonwealth regulator. I asked them to meet with the most senior leaders of the employer interests to discuss elements of weaponisation in the WHS. I've also discussed this in quite significant detail with Mr Crosby. In terms of Victoria, there is information in the biennial report that was recently tabled in parliament. In addition, I'm aware of operational activities that are underway in Victoria about which I do not want to disclose too much information, because I may disturb the operation.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: I did read the report, but is there anything more specific than what was contained in that report?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: There is. There's a memorandum that has been issued by the administrator to staff, former staff, former officers and other relevant persons from the Victoria-Tasmania branch in relation to the Victorian royal commission.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Are you able to table that for us?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: I can table it for you. It sets out very clearly who the union will assist if it's called to give evidence and who they will not assist. Category 1 are people they will not provide representation for. It is outlined in this document as former senior office holders who exercised substantial leadership responsibility, including persons occupying positions such as divisional branch secretary, assistant secretary, president, vice-president or other positions that involved substantial governance and industrial leadership responsibilities. There is a presumption against representation. In relation to that, there will be a presumption against providing representation where there is credible information to the administrator that a person engaged in misconduct, facilitated or enabled misconduct, or obstructed reform efforts of the administration. That relates to officials in Victoria and other people associated with the union.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Senator Payman.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text:
The June statement of Commissioner Hunt and Vice President Asbury stated

Protocols will now be put in place to ensure a mutually safe and respectful workplace for Commissioner Hunt and Vice President Asbury.

What protocols have been put in place?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: There's a significant amount of public information available about this matter between Commissioner Hunt and Vice President Asbury. They issued a media release on 5 June and asked for privacy going forward. Both of the commission members are working and have a full caseload at the commission.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission
witness_position: Executive Director, Legal Performance and Engagement

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: You can't discuss protocols that have been put in place?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: I understand that there are protocols in place so that the commission members don't attend the office at the same time, but that's all I'm aware of.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission
witness_position: Executive Director, Legal Performance and Engagement

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Ms Hunt had approval from public servants for her email setting to be changed, so any emails from Ms Asbury went straight to her junk folder and not to her inbox. Is that still the case?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: I would have to confirm on notice, but I think that might still be in place, yes.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission
witness_position: Executive Director, Legal Performance and Engagement

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Commission staff also agreed that Ms Hunt would be given advance notice of when Ms Asbury was travelling away from the office for work as Ms Hunt was only prepared to go into the office when Ms Asbury was not present. Is that still occurring?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: I understand that is part of the 'they don't attend the office at the same time' protocol.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission
witness_position: Executive Director, Legal Performance and Engagement

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: The President, Mr Hatcher, gave permission for Ms Hunt, who earns more than $400,000 a year, to work from home whenever she wanted. Is that still the case, and how often is she working from home?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: I don't have that information, but working from home is a flexibility that a lot of commission staff and members take up. It would not be unusual that there are working-from-home arrangements in place across the commission.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission
witness_position: Executive Director, Legal Performance and Engagement

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: I am just curious to know how many days or how often she is working from home. Are these officials, Commissioner Hunt and another official, who are on more than a $400,000 a year salary fit and proper people to be making decisions on workplace disputes of Australian workers?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: In the normal course of things, in any workplace issues sometimes arise. The Fair Work Commission is a very respectful, kind and safe work environment. In the very rare times that these situations do arise, we deal with them like any workplace does. These members have sworn an oath of office and are discharging their functions in accordance with the requirements of the Fair Work Act.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: I may have missed this earlier, but Ms Bright said that their workload has not changed?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: That's right.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission
witness_position: Executive Director, Legal Performance and Engagement

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: It remains the same. Thank you.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: I note that we're overdue in moving to the Ombudsman but, notwithstanding, the opposition has the call.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Mr Furlong, on 21 May, you wrote to the AFP commander warning of limited tangible progress on their pursuit of the CFMEU and called for a well resourced response. I would like to ask you some questions about your engagement with the AFP on this. Before that letter, had you raised these concerns with the AFP at all, formally or informally?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Mr Coyle will be able to give you some information on the quantity of referrals and allegations but also information and reports that were provided to the AFP. What prompted that letter is that I attended a meeting—there were several meetings with AFP officers—of the Joint Agency Working Group. From that meeting, I wanted to ask further questions around the progress. I wanted to be satisfied, from my perspective as the regulator of registered organisations, that there had been operational activity undertaken to deal with these issues of alleged noncompliance.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Had any industry participants told you that they had tried to report matters to the AFP and been turned away?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: None is coming to mind. I can take that on notice.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: The letter was sent 12 days before the commission last appeared before the committee. Did you consider speaking to the committee about those concerns?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: At that point in time, I didn't receive any questions in relation to it.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: That was not my question. My question was whether you considered proactively telling the committee that this was something that you had done.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: I hadn't received information, a response from the AFP, I believe, at that point in time. Obviously, I wanted to give them the opportunity to consider my request and to respond.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: They did reply on 10 June. Can you confirm to this committee that the reply informed you that the agency would not brief beyond what is shared in the Joint Agency Working Group and Taskforce Hawk meetings?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: That's accurate, yes.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Were you satisfied with that response?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Satisfied? Probably not, but I understand, from an operational, regulatory and a law enforcement perspective, that the information that they could disclose they would reasonably disclose. I maintain a strong working relationship with the officers at the AFP who are responsible for these operations. I continue to engage with them, and so do my officers from the organisation.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: You say that you continue to engage. Have you written to them again or have you met with them again on this particular issue?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: I've met with them about these particular operations, yes, and I received a verbal update within the constraints of what could be provided about sensitive operational matters that are active before the AFP.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Do you feel that you've seen the tangible progress in operations that you were looking for in the letter?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: As a very proactive regulator, I don't think I'm ever going to be satisfied with the amount of activity. I understand that there still are active matters and complex matters that they're dealing with—corrupting benefits and things of that nature. I'm certainly not in a position to comment on AFP operations.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Your letter formally restated the commission's offer for assistance to the AFP. When was the first offer to assist made?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: The corrupting benefits legislation was first enacted in 2017, and there has been an ongoing engagement with the AFP across the period of time. As subject matter experts in relation to registered organisations, we have provided previous assistance to the AFP in relation to those types of matters and to New South Wales police in relation to Michael and Darren Greenfield, who were convicted of corrupting benefits legislation contraventions. We have provided that level of subject matter expertise. We have provided educational materials about corrupting benefits to registered organisations so that they can understand those provisions better. From that perspective, the standing offer has been there in relation to law enforcement agencies for a number of years, and we've had engagements from time to time over that period. It would probably now be difficult for us even to identify the number of engagements over that period, but there has been in respect of a range of corrupting benefits matters that have been alleged over the last nearly 10 years.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission
witness_position: Acting Executive Director, Registered Organisations Services

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: It has been reported since that in July the AFP declined a request from Victoria police to investigate alleged Commonwealth corrupting benefits offences. Is that something that you were aware of, that the commission was aware of?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Through our participation in the Joint Agency Working Group, we will have had some vision of those matters, but obviously that's a matter as between two law enforcement agencies. We have only a tangential role in that regard.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission
witness_position: Acting Executive Director, Registered Organisations Services

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: You were aware of it?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Yes.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission
witness_position: Acting Executive Director, Registered Organisations Services

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: That led to Victorian and Queensland police running their own probe and conducting raids in September. The government has since said that it had full confidence in the AFP and that operational decisions are independent, but I think the frustration of the commission is clear. When did you become aware of that issue, or was it raised in the Joint Agency Working Group?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: I'm sorry, can you clarify the question, please?
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission
witness_position: Acting Executive Director, Registered Organisations Services

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: You have a Joint Agency Working Group, yes?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Yes.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission
witness_position: Acting Executive Director, Registered Organisations Services

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Was the fact that the AFP had declined a request from Victoria Police to investigate alleged Commonwealth corrupting benefits offences raised in that group?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: I would have to take it on notice specifically, but the Joint Agency Working Group is an opportunity for agencies to come together to deconflict possible matters. There are discussions generally about reports of information that come through and which agency may or may not accept it. I think it would be fair to say it remains, however, under the Joint Agency Working Group, a matter for each agency as to whether they will or will not accept or investigate a referral that might be made.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission
witness_position: Acting Executive Director, Registered Organisations Services

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Yes, I can understand that. Was it an issue that was raised in that group, though?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: I gave evidence before that my recollection was that, through the Joint Agency Working Group, there were some discussions about whether matters would be referred to the AFP in that case.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission
witness_position: Acting Executive Director, Registered Organisations Services

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: If you wish, Senator, we can take it on notice, provide some further information on that and other referrals that were made to the AFP insofar as they've occurred, and provide you with the documentation around those.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: That would be good. I don't need you to breach any confidences about what those instances were, but, if there have been instances, I would really be interested in the number, the dates that they were referred and whether the AFP has since pursued them.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: If it's appropriate, the substance of those referrals as well?
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission
witness_position: Acting Executive Director, Registered Organisations Services

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: That would be terrific, if appropriate, but I don't want to put at jeopardy the rest of the information if you can't share the specifics. Did you inform the minister or the department that you had written to the AFP on this issue?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Not that I can recall, but in the normal course of things, I wouldn't. I am an independent statutory officer, an independent regulator. I may have had a conversation with a senior official at the department, but the decision would have been made before, and the letter would have been sent before, any conversation occurred.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: In that letter you specifically stated that the CFMEU administration cannot by itself resolve those issues. Is that a statement that you stand by?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Yes, I do.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: What more do you believe is needed from law enforcement if the administration on its own cannot resolve these issues?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: I think it requires the best efforts of everyone involved. I was listening to the evidence earlier this afternoon and contemplating the contribution that other industry participants have made. Late last year, I gave a presentation to CEOs, very senior people, tier 1 builders in Victoria, and I'm happy to table that presentation. I concluded that presentation by saying that it requires conspicuous leadership from everyone and that the CFMEU itself can't resolve all of the issues, because all of the issues don't just rest with the CFMEU. It is the activities of other very senior people in the industry that need to contribute to the solution. Given that I significantly—and rightly so—focus on the CFMEU, what I asked for last year in this presentation to these very senior officials from tier 1s was that they need to contribute to the solution and that they need to start showing conspicuous leadership. I said, 'If we were to meet again in 12 months, what would you like to be able to say?' I think I might have said, 'What would you like to be able to say to your children that you were able to achieve over the past 12 months?' We now are coming up to that 12 months.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: The concern of the commission, and, indeed, of the opposition, is that, unless there is law enforcement attached to the good work of the administrator, any good work of the administrator will be for naught if there is not subsequent law enforcement action.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: That is absolutely accurate. It is consistent with what Mr Crosby has indicated as well.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Minister, can you tell us or give us some comfort that the government will insist that law enforcement respond to the work that the administration is doing in order to make sure the work that the administration is doing is significant and has its intended effects?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text:
Of course, we're in the situation that we're in today where we have Mr Furlong giving evidence that the administrator of the CFMEU is doing more than any other participant to clean up the industry because of decisions of this minister and previous ministers of this government to take the unprecedented step of passing legislation to allow the administration of the CFMEU. We've heard evidence today about the effects of the administration, including that, on commencement of the scheme, there were 200 officers of the union who were removed at that time. Since then, an additional 150 people were removed, constituting about half of the workforce of the CFMEU.

I note that the progress that has been made on cleaning up the industry under this government far outweighs and outstrips progress made in the previous decade. I don't think a single person was removed from the CFMEU by the ABCC, let alone around 350 officers and people removed. If this government had not taken the decision to pass legislation allowing the administration of this union, we would not be in the position that we're in today where we're getting this evidence from officials and where Mr Furlong is saying that it is in fact the administrator of the CFMEU who is doing more work than any other participant to clean up this industry, including employers in the industry as well. We are extremely focused on delivering a clean union and a clean industry, and that is exactly what we are doing.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: With Senator Hume's permission, if I could interject, given what we've heard today from the commission—and, perhaps more importantly, what we haven't heard—and your comments about cleaning up construction more broadly, why has the government voted three times this year against establishing a Senate select committee into corruption? It's not just the CFMEU specifically but corruption in construction? You're saying that the administrator has done more than anyone else, including organisations involved. Why not allow every crossbench senator who voted in support of the inquiry, and only Labor and the Greens opposed it? That's actually counter to the statement that you just made. Perhaps you can answer why the government is so determined to avoid proper scrutiny of corruption in the whole construction industry?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: There is more scrutiny on corruption in the construction industry because of the decisions that this government has taken that coalition governments never took. We have taken the strongest action available to us by placing the CFMEU into administration, a step never taken by the coalition. Indeed, under the coalition and under the ABCC, corruption flourished in the construction industry. Of course, we are doing the hard work of cleaning up the construction industry. The evidence today has been that it is the administrator of the CFMEU that is doing more than any other participant to clean up the industry. Mr Crosby, the administrator, provides a biannual report to parliament. That has been available. Indeed, Senator Kovacic just said that you've been reading that report. There is transparency and scrutiny. Of course, Mr Furlong is answering all of your questions today here in Senate estimates again. I repeat that this government has done more than any other government on record to clean up corruption in the construction industry, including in the construction union.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: It's your government's view that a national inquiry isn't necessary to investigate potentially billions of dollars lost to corruption in construction particularly as they relate to Commonwealth construction and infrastructure projects? It's not necessary?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: We have taken the strongest action possible at the Commonwealth level.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: No, you haven't. This is the point. The strongest action possible would be having a concurrent administrator and an inquiry here. In fact, the government has resisted the strongest action possible, because the administrator's responsibilities only surround the CFMEU, not the industry more broadly. We know that there are senators even around this table from your own side who suggest that corruption runs far deeper than just the union. Why would the government resist an inquiry into corruption in the construction industry more broadly, particularly when we now hear evidence that, potentially, law enforcement agencies aren't pursuing the work that the administrator is doing?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: I shall repeat again that we've passed legislation to allow the administration of the union. There has been evidence today that 200 officers of the union were removed at the time that the scheme was implemented and that around half of the workforce has been removed from the CFMEU. Respectfully, there is no inquiry of this parliament or of the Senate that could achieve that. Indeed, no previous government could achieve that. The ABCC did not achieve that. That is just, of course, part of the work that the government is doing. The government has also sought to bring together the industry to work on a code and a framework for the industry going forward. We are a government that believes we need unions and employers in the room together to make progress. That is exactly what we are doing.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: The government has repeatedly opposed a dedicated Senate inquiry that could fill the gaps of the royal commission in Victoria and the Queensland commission of inquiry that would perhaps enable the AFP to do the things it's currently saying it can't do. The CFMEU administrator has declined to appear at estimates. How do you, Minister, expect the parliament to actually scrutinise the work that the administrator is doing? That is our job. Are you saying that we actually don't have the capacity to scrutinise it effectively and that only your government by instruction of the administrator can do that? Clearly, the AFP is saying that's not adequate.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: I just want to check, Chair, whether the correspondence that Senator Kovacic has referred to was tabled?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: I believe all of the correspondence we've now received in today's distribution has been tabled.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Senator Kovacic, you referred to your invitation to Mr Crosby to appear—

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: That's correct. My question, effectively, is that the government has repeatedly opposed a dedicated Senate inquiry. The administrator has declined to appear at estimates. How on earth are we meant or how is the parliament meant to properly scrutinise the work of the administrator if we cannot have an inquiry and we cannot ask the administrator questions?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Letters have been tabled. I note the letter from Mr Crosby to Senators Hume and Kovacic and would just like to put this on the record: that he respectfully declined the invitation to appear at estimates doesn't deem it to be appropriate in all of the circumstances. However, he offers to meet with you at a time of your convenience to brief you—

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: A private meeting is not transparent—

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: In addition, of course, under the scheme of administration, which our government delivered, which you never did, the administrator is required to report to parliament, as he has recently done. The administrator works closely with Mr Furlong, and the Fair Work Commissioner, Mr Furlong, has answered all of your questions today.

agency: Fair Work Commission
