text: Minister, to finish this off, do you believe that the parliament should be able to scrutinise the performance of the administrator?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: I think the results of the administration are clear. Again, there were 200—

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: That's not evidence.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: There were 150—

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: We will allow Minister Walsh to finish.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: I have a point of order.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: If you have a point of order after you've heard her answer, I'm happy to hear it.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: There were 150 officials removed from the union. Evidence has been given today that that was about half of the people who have worked at this union. Evidence has been given today that the administrator appointed by Mr Furlong under the scheme introduced by the government is doing more than any other participant in the industry to clean up the industry. That is the evidence that has been given today. The administrator has offered you a briefing, and, in addition, the administrator reports transparently to the parliament.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: How does the administrator report transparently to the parliament?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: In the report that is tabled in the parliament that you referred to earlier.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: That doesn't allow for any discussion. It doesn't allow for any scrutiny. It doesn't allow for any questions. That's a statement.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Sure.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Okay. Trust us; we're the government! Okay.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: I hope I'm not the only person that the irony does not elude for you wishing to understand more about a scheme of administration that you had 10 years to do and that you never did. Under your government, corruption in this union and in this industry flourished. It was a very good time for corruption in the construction industry under the government that you led. On our watch, we have taken the strongest action possible.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: You haven't. That is a lie.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: This union is in administration. We've heard evidence today from the officials that the administrator is doing more than any other participant to clean up the industry and we've heard evidence about the progress of that work today.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Point of order!

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Senator Dolega, on a point of order.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Senator Dolega, I know where you're going with this. I withdraw the comment. However, I would say that the minister saying that the government has taken the strongest action possible is clearly not true.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: If you're making the withdrawal, the courtesy to the committee is to just simply—

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: I'll make a point of order: it's misleading.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: No, Senator O'Sullivan, you don't have the call. We're dealing with a point of order. I'm asking Senator Hume simply to withdraw.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: I withdraw the comment.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Thank you, Senator Hume.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: I would like to make a comment as well.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: If it's a point of order, I'm happy to come to you, but, if it's not, I'm confirming that the minister has finished her response. Are you finished? Who is seeking the call for a question or a point of order? They are the options that are available.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: If it's not a point of order, I hope you'll forgive me, but it's in relation to relevance. I'm trying to be mindful of time and that we are behind. I've received three answers that contain the same information about the number of people who have been let go. Clearly, it's a written statement. It's not relevant. I would not like us to continue to be behind, but I am going to ask all of my questions. If I keep getting the same answer, I'm still going to keep asking all of my questions.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: I remind all senators of the importance of relevance, but, from what I can observe, I believe it is. It's a very broad test when it comes to estimates hearings. Senator Kovacic, you do have the call, though. We have five minutes before we go to the break.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: I will need time after the break as well.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: That's fine. No-one is seeking the call other than you, so this is your time to manage.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Mr Furlong, at estimates on 3 December, I raised concerns about CFMEU officials being allowed to resign rather than being dismissed, potentially allowing them to avoid being classified as removed persons under the act. I want to return to that issue in light of recent allegations, but, before I go to that, I want to ask: do you keep a register—I asked the department and they said that they didn't—of the number of removed persons, or tracking of those individuals, who now are back as officials in any union?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Mr Coyle will be able to assist you.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: In terms of a register, no, but we do have some insights from a range of different sources. There's a complex matrix of different elements to this that need to be taken into account. The scheme of administration, when it commenced, resulted in about 214 unique individuals being removed from offices across the CFMEU—
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission
witness_position: Acting Executive Director, Registered Organisations Services

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: I've heard from Senator Walsh multiple times this afternoon.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: That is one of the mechanisms by which a person could become a removed person, but a person could also become a removed person by activity of the administrator during the administration. We are not, on a day-to-day basis, privy to the actions of the administrator.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission
witness_position: Acting Executive Director, Registered Organisations Services

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: The administrator doesn't report any of this data to you? That's what I am trying to understand. The administrator may hold it; they may know it. Does the department not know it, and does the commission not know it either?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: The administrator independently runs the CFMEU. He will take such action as he deems necessary. His opinion as to the steps that he has taken may be a relevant consideration as to whether a person falls under one of the relevant removed persons categories. He has, however, from time to time, reported to us a list of persons who are removed persons. Most recently, on 1 June this year, he provided us a list of 27 names of persons who he considers have been removed under the scheme by the activities of the administration.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission
witness_position: Acting Executive Director, Registered Organisations Services

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: What would make it different for him to provide you those 27 as opposed to any others prior or since? I want to understand why you get that list and not any other list?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text:
Perhaps I can approach this in two different ways. The first is that we have recently published a guidance note in relation to removed persons to provide information to other registered organisations about what their responsibilities are, about the potential risks associated with engaging persons who formerly worked at the CFMEU or were officers of the CFMEU without undertaking due diligence, such as making inquiries about whether they are a removed person or whether they have received the necessary certificates to enable them to be employed or to act as a bargaining representative or become an officer of a different organisation.

Information exists in respect of any person to be able to identify, through engagement with the administrator, whether or not that person is a removed person. We at the commission do not have an up-to-date, updated-daily list of names of people. But, to the extent that matters come before the commission, we engage in respect of individuals with the administrator and with the Fair Work Ombudsman about information that they may have about a person if they were to apply for a right-of-entry permit, for example. In those circumstances we can obtain the information necessary to satisfy ourselves as to whether or not a person falls within a category of removed person.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission
witness_position: Acting Executive Director, Registered Organisations Services

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: If you're approached for a right-of-entry permit, do you cross-check to see if they are a removed person?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: We do.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission
witness_position: Acting Executive Director, Registered Organisations Services

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Do you need to go to the administrator to get that information, and will they confirm that with you?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: We already have a list of quite a number of names of people.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission
witness_position: Acting Executive Director, Registered Organisations Services

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: You don't have all of them, so you will not know. Do you cross-check with the administrator or your own list?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: We have a standing arrangement where we would look at engaging with the administrator about whether they have information about a person that is relevant to a right-of-entry permit application if they were previously a permit holder for the CFMEU.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission
witness_position: Acting Executive Director, Registered Organisations Services

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: There's also a similar regime associated with removed persons. There are reactive regulatory powers that we have in relation to this. I will ask Mr Corcoran to give you a minute update on one of our investigations that relates to these provisions around a removed person.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: As a regulator, we receive information from a range of sources. If any stakeholder is concerned that a person who is a removed person has been employed contrary to the removed persons provisions, we can receive information about that and we can investigate those matters. To the point in question, we currently have a current investigation in relation to the UFUA and whether the UFUA may have engaged a person who was a removed person—that being Michael Ravbar, the former secretary of the Queensland divisional branch.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: We are due to suspend. I understand that we still require these witnesses after the break.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: The committee will now resume. We're returning with questions to the Fair Work Commission. Senator Kovacic.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: I asked some questions earlier regarding CFMEU officials being allowed to resign rather than being dismissed, potentially allowing them to avoid being classified as 'removed persons' under the act. Are you aware of a current investigation or of a most recent past investigation into a CFMEU New South Wales organiser concerning his dealings with a labour hire company called Unite Recruit?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: I'm not personally aware, no, not on the basis of that information.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: I understand that the organiser concerned is a Mr Ozluk from the New South Wales branch of the CFMEU. You have no knowledge of that?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: No.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: I'm told that the administrator engaged an independent barrister from Victoria to conduct the investigation. That information hasn't been provided to you by the administrator?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: The administrator and his senior officers provide significant information. I want to check my records, because it may have come up in a conversation. It may have come up in an update that I have personally received. I just want to caution as we go forward that I haven't prepared briefings to answer questions on this. It will take me a couple of minutes.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: If there is anyone else in the room who might have that information, I'm happy to wait a moment.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: O-s-l-a—is that the gentleman's surname?
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: O-z-l-u-k.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: I don't have any record, just on the basis of that very quick search.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: For some context—and obviously not referencing this particular scenario—my understanding is that the allegation suggests that the individual was engaging in conduct where he was taking around someone from Unite Recruit, suggesting to organisations that the union had a relationship with Unite Recruit and that he was recommending that Unite Recruit be hired on particular sites. Would that constitute behaviour that would or would not be acceptable?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Talking hypothetically—that is the limitation?
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Yes, correct.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Depending on the nature of the conduct associated with that recommendation, if Mr Ozluk were to receive a benefit—
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Any individual.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: If any individual were to receive a benefit from that labour hire for recommending or applying coercion, duress, influence—
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: This suggests influence, at the very least.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Then it could be perceived as a corrupting benefit. Further, if it relates to enterprise bargaining as well, which is a different scheme, there are obviously obligations and requirements around that. I might just hand it to Mr Coyle to see if there's anything that he would to add here.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: I can table it. There's a page from the website of that organisation which notes specifically that Unite Recruit describes itself as CFMEU aligned and EBA compliant. I will just circulate that now; I'll get it right, Chair. If there were a circumstance where you had an organiser from the CFMEU taking an individual from this organisation around with them and suggesting to contractors that they should be hiring somebody from here, would that constitute a problem under the current circumstances in terms of undue influence?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: It goes to the circumstances. It could be a recommendation from an organiser to, say, a head contractor without any corrupting benefit and without them receiving any benefit. But, if there is an employer or labour hire company out there that is absolutely meeting all of their obligations under an enterprise agreement and the union is satisfied that they are EBA compliant from the perspective of paying their workers what they're entitled to and they're not engaging in sham contracting, other unlawful phoenixing activity or other conduct that's associated with some labour hire or other entities in and around the construction industry, in and of itself a recommendation would not pose—
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: The recommendation on its own is not a problem. What about if that organiser drove in their car a representative from that organisation, took them from site to site and went to head contractors and said, 'These are our best guys; it would be really good if you used their services'? Would that be considered to be—

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: I think it would certainly warrant investigation or inquiries. I'm not too sure if you—
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: I am a supporter of the administration—I've spoken on it many times in parliament in supporting it—but I'm concerned about hypotheticals. That's quite hypothetical.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: There is no standing order which prevents hypothetical questions being asked in estimates. It's up to the officials how they respond.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: What I am trying to understand, particularly given the current circumstances with what we're seeing in Victoria, what we've seen in Queensland and what is now beginning to unfold in New South Wales and WA, is: if you have an organiser from the CFMEU taking somebody from an organisation around to sites and saying to those head contractors, 'These are our best guys; it would be really good if you could throw some work their way', how would that be perceived by yourselves and the administrator? If I were one of those head contractors, I would be worried about saying 'no' to that. More generally, what distinguishes that line between recommending someone and making someone feel like they do not have a lot of choice but to comply?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: I am trying my best to assist you with this line of questioning. It gets more difficult the more we extend the example. I feel like I could possibly be moving to a place where I would be misleading the Senate if I were asked to answer further on the abstract. One of the things that I can say which might provide some assistance is that there is a code of practice for organisers of the CFMEU. It has been reviewed by the administration, but there is also a review of the delegates code of conduct. The CFMEU has over 1,000 delegates across the country. Each branch is developing a detailed delegate development strategy implementation. Organisers and delegates are being retrained. Everyone acknowledges that there's further work to be done, but Mr Crosby and his team are in the process of retraining their delegates and their organisers across a whole raft of matters, including about behavioural change and respect at work.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Is there a requirement for the administrator to notify the commission where an investigation substantiates serious misconduct by a CFMEU official? What happens if that CFMEU official is terminated?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: The CFMEU administrator—and he has exercised this power previously—has the power to refer matters to me for investigation. We have initiated investigations and have prescribed certain thresholds for the commission to satisfy in relation to those interactions. Those powers have been exercised by the administrator, and we have acted in accordance with our obligations under the RO act as well.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Some of the difficulty that we are having in answering some of these questions belongs to the limited jurisdiction that we have. The general manager is the financial regulator of the registered organisation. We are responsible for investigating civil penalties, including officers' duties, which apply to those elected officials. From the information you've provided, we here are talking about an organiser in New South Wales. There are some limited cases where an organiser may be an officer, but in most cases they are not; they are an employee of the union. Some of what you're talking about could, in theoretical sense, step into some of those corrupting benefits issues. They may be simple conflict-of-interest issues as between that person and their employer, but, at its most simple, these are then issues as between the employer and the employee about whether the employee is conducting their employment in accordance with their duties.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission
witness_position: Acting Executive Director, Registered Organisations Services

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: For transparency, I am not being difficult with the detail. Given that you do not have awareness, I don't want to share further detail; I don't think that's appropriate given that you don't have that level of awareness. I have articulated my concern a number of times today. I understand the parameters from within which you are trying to operate. Without having the administrator here, we have this entire black hole of information that we cannot get. I'm really concerned about my ability to do my job to scrutinise when I cannot get the information. This is why we are picking around at the edges to try and understand what we can. What I am trying to get at is: if there has been a serious misconduct issue with an employee who is not an official, the administrator does not necessarily have to notify you, because they are not officials as they are just employees; is that correct?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Strictly speaking, possibly.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Possibly?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: It depends on the circumstances.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Senator, if I may, for the purposes of the removed persons elements, a person who is an employee of the union can become a removed person by the activity of the administrator. If a question were to come to us at some point in time about an individual, we may find out through engagement with the administrator that a person has become a removed person through the conduct of the administrator.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission
witness_position: Acting Executive Director, Registered Organisations Services

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: That's where my total confusion in this whole thing is. How can you properly do your job and identify matters that warrant regulatory action and intervention if you do not know all of the instances of when this is happening in terms of what these people are doing?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Just like most regulators, we respond to information that we receive.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission
witness_position: Acting Executive Director, Registered Organisations Services

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: That's right. If you're not getting it, you don't know. If the administrator is not telling you, you can't respond?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: The point at which the administrator takes action in relation to employees is perhaps not the relevant point of engagement for us. The point of engagement for us would be if someone who may be a removed person shows up in a different organisation without having obtained the certificate and someone makes a complaint to us about that, we can then investigate. There are significant civil penalties attached to that behaviour.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission
witness_position: Acting Executive Director, Registered Organisations Services

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: I'll put the balance of the questions on notice that relate to the specifics.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: I just have a couple of follow-up questions on that particular issue. Of the people to whom you are referring as removed persons, do you have a count of how many are officials, how many are organisers and how many are delegates?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Probably not broken down in that way, but we're talking about not a particularly long list. There were 214 officers removed on day one by the scheme itself. There is a list of some 27 names that have been shared with us to date as being removed by the activities of the administrator since. Anecdotally, we know the roles of most of those people.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission
witness_position: Acting Executive Director, Registered Organisations Services

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Anecdotally, you do not know whether they fall into any one of those categories?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: It's a matter that we would be able to identify if we needed to, but it is not something that we have proactively done.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission
witness_position: Acting Executive Director, Registered Organisations Services

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: How many people who have left the union were not considered removed by the union or removed by the administrator?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: I think you have heard from the bar table a few times that there has been significant turnover of staff across the organisation. A lot of those people have left under their own volition. Many of them have left in various circumstances. There may be some, as you have identified, where the administrator has foreshadowed some disciplinary action and they resign. It remains an open question, from my perspective, as to whether those people may qualify as being 'removed people' under this scheme, and that would be a matter of the facts in each particular case that we then would need to investigate.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission
witness_position: Acting Executive Director, Registered Organisations Services

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: As the registered organisations administering body, how do you deal with that?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: If credible information comes to us about a particular circumstance, we will take interest in it, make the inquiries and will investigate it if necessary.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission
witness_position: Acting Executive Director, Registered Organisations Services

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Isn't it the intention of the administrator to report, in his report to government—considering the government has appointed this administrator—not just the number of people who have been removed from the union but the positions from which they have been removed?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: I think the administrator's approach with us has been to respect the privacy of these individuals who are employees, and has shared with us such information as is necessary. Generally, we have a view of the circumstances or the names and the positions that people held who have been removed. Again, to the extent that a complaint were to come to us about an individual, we could make those inquiries.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission
witness_position: Acting Executive Director, Registered Organisations Services

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Without knowing the names of all of those people who have been removed, how do you, as my colleague has said, know that they are not phoenixing themselves in other organisations?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: We do not have a proactive approach to trying to track the movements of the 150 staff who have departed from the CFMEU. We do not see that as our regulatory role, but we will act if we receive credible information that someone who may be a removed person is operating contrary to the legislation.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission
witness_position: Acting Executive Director, Registered Organisations Services

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Is the objective of putting the CFMEU into administration to clean up the CFMEU or to remove corruption from the construction industry?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: The objective of the administration is for there to be a clean union, to remove corruption from the union.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: To remove corruption from the union?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Yes. It is also, as Mr Furlong gave evidence to before, to ensure there is a strong and effective union to represent workers in what is a dangerous occupation, what can be an insecure occupation and in what can be a poorly paid occupation in some parts of the sector.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: They're doing all right now. Is it the government's position that corruption in the construction industry is limited to the CFMEU?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: I think there's evidence that there is corruption in the industry as a whole or in parts of the industry. I note again the evidence that was given earlier by Mr Furlong in that the administrator is driving reform not just in the union but across the industry. Of course, the administration itself is one part of the government's agenda in relation to building a stronger and cleaner construction industry. Some of the other measures that the government has been taking have been referenced here, including the Joint Agency Working Group. There was some evidence given earlier today about the National Construction Industry Forum as well, which has released a blueprint about how to work together as an industry—unions, employers and government in a tripartite way—to build an industry today and for the future that is productive, safe, has a good culture and is sustainable. That group is doing a considerable body of work as well in order to drive a better, cleaner construction industry.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Minister, you said earlier in your testimony that your government was doing more than any previous government to clean up corruption in the construction industry. Can I just ask you: in the past 15 years, legislation that has been brought to this parliament to do exactly that has been rejected over and again by the Labor opposition. I shall ask you about various pieces of legislation and perhaps you can tell me which way your party in opposition has voted. The Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment Bill 2013 was voted on in 2014. I understand it is before your time, but surely you know how your side of parliament voted?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: I can tell you that I will not have that information. I'm sure it's on the public record.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: I can help you. I just didn't want to teach you how to suck eggs; I can tell you. The Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment Bill voted on in 2014 was rejected by Labor. The Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment Bill voted on in March 2015 was also rejected by Labor. The Building and Construction Industry (Improving Productivity) Bill 2013 was voted on in August 2015. That was also rejected by Labor. The Building and Construction Industry (Consequential and Transitional Provisions) Bill was voted on in August 2015. That was also voted against by Labor. In 2015, the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment Bill [No. 2] was again rejected by Labor. The Building and Construction Industry (Improving Productivity) Bill 2013 [No. 2] was voted on on 18 April 2016, and rejected by Labor. The Building and Construction Industry (Consequential and Transitional Provisions) Bill 2013 was voted on on 18 April 2016, and that too was voted against by your party. Are you telling me that this Labor government, by putting the CFMEU into administration, is doing everything it can, everything in its power, to clean up corruption in the construction industry? That was your testimony.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Yes. What I have said is that we are taking the strongest action available to clean up the construction union and the construction industry. We have your government's record on display. I understand your effort to attempt to clean up your government's record with that statement that you just made, but it remains the case that, on your watch, corruption in this industry flourished. On our watch, this union is in administration. As the general manager of the Fair Work Commission has said, the administration of this union is doing more than any other participant in the industry to clean up this industry. That is the result of the actions that this government has taken.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: What does success look like for the government in its efforts to clean up this industry? What are your KPIs?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Mr Furlong gave evidence before about the objects of the act that set up the administration. We want to see a clean union and we want to see a union that is effective in advancing the interests of safe and secure jobs in the construction industry. This administration is a significant part of the government's agenda. Another significant part of the government's agenda is working together in a tripartite way across the whole industry through the National Construction Industry Forum, which we created because we believe that the solutions for this industry need to be found with the industry as a whole. That is why we have brought NCIF together. It's why the minister is participating in that forum with industry, and of course we welcome the blueprint for the future of the sector that NCIF has worked together to deliver. That is a blueprint supported by more work, including a charter for the sector to set shared goals and expectations, as well as the procurement frameworks that we were talking about before to make sure that, when public dollars are going to construction projects, the work being done is conducted in a way that is lawful, productive, safe and sustainable.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Noting the minister's comments, the government's discussion paper on its proposed Commonwealth construction standards specifically identifies the need to prevent employee bargaining representatives from dictating the choice of subcontractors on construction sites. As I articulated in my previous questions, does that concern extend to union officials pressuring contractors to engage particular labour hire companies? I am happy for the general manager to answer that or for a brief answer from the minister.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: From my perspective, that's a matter of policy and something that I cannot provide you with any guidance on.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Is it not a matter of setting the same standard? If a standard applies to subcontractors, surely that standard applies to union officials?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: My understanding is that the standards have not been made yet, and there is ongoing consultation with the Department of Employment and Workplace Relations into the substance of those standards. I am only aware of that because, as the regulator of registered organisations, I have been consulted, but my understanding is that the consultations continue—and Mr Manning might want to add to this—and that the standards have not been set.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Is it your view or your hope, or would it be your advice, that the proposed standards prohibit union officials from pressuring contractors on Commonwealth-funded projects to engage preferred labour hire providers, particularly where those officials have personal or financial connections to those providers? Surely that would be a given?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: It is very difficult to talk in the abstract in those circumstances.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: No, it's not abstract.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: The premise is not offensive.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: It may be okay for union officials to pressure contractors on Commonwealth projects to take up—

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: I just want to return to the evidence that was provided earlier. In terms of my role as a governance regulator for each of the organisations and the financial management accountability of those organisations, I'm not best placed to answer that question.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: The minister mentioned the proposed standards in the discussion paper, so that is why I asked the question. Surely there would be something in those standards that would preclude a union official from coercing or forcing someone to use a labour hire company in which they have a personal or financial interest. I would assume that is a given.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Mr Furlong indicated that it is a matter for government. As you said, I raised the standards for the construction industry. You talked about the discussion paper, which sets out the areas for feedback: integrity and lawful conduct, productivity for industry and industrial practices.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Would you consider that to be unlawful conduct, Minister: to coerce someone to use a labour hire company in which they have a personal interest?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: You are asking a lot of hypothetical questions about work that is underway. What is real is the work that is underway. I was just in the process of giving a broad overview of where we are at in the work that we are doing before going to Mr Manning to articulate further where we are at. Essentially, we are doing this important work through the National Construction Industry Forum, setting up standards. There is a discussion paper that is out. It talks about integrity, lawful conduct and coercion. You use the word 'coercion'. I would not consider coercion to be an act of integrity or lawful conduct. This is a paper that is out. It is under consultation at the moment. It is part of the NCIF's ongoing work program. I believe Mr Manning has some further information.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: I was just simply going to say that the issue you are raising was an issue on which views were expressly sought in the standards discussion paper. It is question 9 in relation to that: what safeguards, if any, are needed to complement existing laws and commercial practices to ensure decisions about subcontractor engagement are transparent, merit-based, commercially appropriate and free from coercion or inappropriate influence?
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: That is the purpose of my question, because it references subcontractor behaviour. I wanted to get an understanding of whether the same applies to union officials.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: The views sought of course relate to the entire system, so all parties in the system. One of themes in the discussion paper was what, if anything else, is needed to ensure the bargaining system arrangements could be strengthened to ensure there is genuine, good faith bargaining, for example, and that goes to that issue as well.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: We spoke earlier about the building cooperative workplaces bill and how that was introduced the day after Senate estimates rose. We did not get a chance to speak to the Fair Work Commission about that bill and how it would affect your work. There was an element of that bill that we have spoken about additionally today, section 9, which integrity experts have specifically said opens the door to corruption and it has done when it has been replicated in state legislation. This is why we need an opportunity to scrutinise this legislation. This is why we reject it when the government says it is as transparent 'as we can be and we want to see corruption in construction eliminated and we're doing more than any other government could do'. Minister, can you please give some assurance that there will be no sneaky or underhand action of government to try to slip legislation through without appropriate scrutiny, particularly in construction, where corruption is clearly rife?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: I reject the premise of your question. I will save you and Senator Kovacic in particular from going through everything that the government is doing to attempt to do the really important work of driving a safe and clean union and a safe and clean industry. That is what we are about; not about the words in your question.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: I think you said that you were the 'most transparent government'. Do you think that slipping through a piece of legislation and announcing it in a media release five minutes after the Fair Work Commission had left the building is a demonstration of your government's commitment to transparency?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: I think that the legislation was introduced in the usual way. The introduction of legislation is a matter for the government business program in the parliament. It is managed by the managers of government business. The way in which legislation passes through the parliament is a matter for the parliament.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Is your government committed to transparency?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Of course.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Can I have a copy, please, of the Fair Work Commission's most recent annual report? Why was it tabled five minutes ago and not during a time where we could have had a chance to go through it and ask questions? Did you think that perhaps the Fair Work Commission would have left the building before we had a chance to get a copy of this report? What is this? Why is there a problem with transparency?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: I think you know, Senator—

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: We do know!

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: The—

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Senator O'Sullivan, you do not have the call. If you're seeking a point of order, you can do so, but you do not have the call. Minister Walsh has the call. She can be heard in silence and then I will come back to you to put a question. Senator Walsh.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: I think the senator can see that I had no information as to whether the report had or had not been tabled. I understand from Mr Furlong and yourself that this report has been tabled. I'm sure that it has been tabled through the normal process of the parliament for tabling reports.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: The minister is not even being transparent with you, and you're representing her. You didn't know that this was going to be tabled today? You didn't know that it was going to be tabled potentially while the Fair Work Commission was sitting next to you?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: I don't see the issue that you see. Documents are tabled in the parliament. Bills are introduced into the parliament. That is the normal business of the parliament.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: The annual report of the agency that is sitting next to you at the desk was tabled in the parliament after your minister thought that this agency would have left the building.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: That's your assertion.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Why wasn't it tabled yesterday?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: I reject your assertion. You have the report. If you have any questions, both Mr Furlong and his team are here to answer those questions.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Mr Furlong, is there anything in this report that you think would be of interest to the opposition?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: I think there is a lot of operational information in there. I think that the opening statements from the President and myself go to a number of the issues that we have discussed today in relation to the disruption to our workload. How we have responded to that provides information that I have put on the record today about our performance as well, and obviously KPIs, PBS and our financial performance for the year. It is regrettable that the tabling of our report occurred today. As I understand it, in an effort of full transparency and disclosure here, our annual report is one of the last annual reports to be provided to the minister's office. As part of that process, it is regrettable. I apologise for my agency's contribution to the late tabling of that report.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Did you know that it was going to be tabled today?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: I understood that it was going to be tabled today. We received a notification either very late yesterday or earlier this morning that it was going to be tabled today.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Is that not something that perhaps you should have mentioned early on in testimony today for the sake of full disclosure and transparency?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: I am telling you now. You have asked the questions and I have responded as honestly as I can. I would also like to put on the record that in terms of every October round of Senate estimates while I have been the general manager—I think this might be my fifth or sixth annual report in this role—each of them has been tabled prior to the sitting of estimates.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Minister, this is becoming a pattern of behaviour of your government in that it's treating even its junior ministers with contempt if it's not telling you that annual reports are being tabled while you are at the desk with the agency whose report it is. It's no wonder your caucus is losing confidence in your Prime Minister. If this is the contempt in which your minister treats you, imagine what they feel for us.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: I will just remind everyone here that this process works best when statements are put as questions and then answered appropriately. Minister Walsh, if you seek to respond to that comment, you are able to, but otherwise, Senator Hume, I ask you to rephrase it as a question.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Mr Furlong has given evidence that, regrettably, the report was provided a little later than he would have liked, if I can paraphrase, and the report has been tabled in the usual way in the parliament. I reject your assertions in relation to the minister needing to tell me exactly when a report was to be tabled.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Happy to be blindsided?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: We are doing the important work that we have been talking about today, and that is what is important.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Mr Furlong, is there anything in the report—and Senator Hume asked a similar question—that is concerning to the Fair Work Commission or that is not as you would like it to be?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: The question is bordering on opinion, in my mind, but it is up to you.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Not from the commission. If I were on a board of directors where we had an annual report I had published and submitted and I was asked by a shareholder, 'Is there anything that worries you in that report?' I would say, 'I'm actually concerned about X, Y, Z or risk management,' or whatever it is.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: My view, as chair, is that borders on opinion, but I'm not preventing Mr Furlong from answering it. It's up to him if he does.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: There is one thing that I am comforted by and one thing that I am concerned about. I am comforted by the fact that, over 18 months to two years of significant disruption to the operation of the commission from the impact of AI and other changes to our users, the organisation leaned in, evolved and changed at pace, dealt with the ambiguity, implemented new systems and now has case management practices and systems in place to manage this elevated workload. We are thankful to government for allowing us to run an operational loss last financial year to support these efforts to get the commission to a point where it has the internal capabilities and systems to deal with this significant increase in work and change in the nature of the work. With change, and significant change, comes ambiguity and comes stress. Due to the tireless efforts of the members and the staff of the Fair Work Commission, we have been able to navigate this change and the ambiguity and stress that comes with it. As to the oppressive nature of the workload in addition to all of the change that we have driven through the organisation, one of our performance metrics from our annual report corporate plan about employee engagement dropped by three percentage points. That is something that, as we come out of this period of massive disruption to the organisation, I am very much looking forward to working to improve in the current financial year.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Your report records zero new investigations commenced under part 4 of chapter 11 of the Registered Organisations Act in 2025-26. Given the continuing allegations of corruption and misconduct across registered organisations, can you give us some insight as to why no new investigations commenced? That's on page 44 of the annual report. While you are at it, page 46 references no infringement notices for that same period. I would be interested in some insights on whether that reflects improved compliance or a lack of enforcement. Perhaps, as an example as we discussed earlier with the CFMEU, if you are not receiving the information from the administrator, it makes your regulatory responsibilities much more difficult to navigate.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: You correctly identify what is disclosed in the report. We have, during the relevant period, engaged in significant enforcement activity. We have commenced a couple of civil penalty litigations that arise out of investigative activities, and we continue to work on some substantial investigations that are moving forward which result from information that we have received. We also have several matters that are in the pre-investigation stage. We have commenced two investigations since this reporting period that we're talking about.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission
witness_position: Acting Executive Director, Registered Organisations Services

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Is the answer that, because you're already conducting substantive investigations, there were no new investigations during that period, but you're carrying out other investigations and have begun two new investigations since the beginning of this financial year?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Yes.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission
witness_position: Acting Executive Director, Registered Organisations Services

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: It is not only the investigations; that is just one metric, one regulatory activity, that we undertake. Since the last time we were here in June, in relation to the CFMEU—I think it is important I go through this because it will give you a sense of the scale of the operations that the commission has undertaken in relation to this particular issue—four investigations into alleged conduct of former CFMEU construction and general division officials—
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Yes, the one on page 45. I was quite interested in whether that one has concluded and what the findings were, given that it concerned alleged use of union funds for senior officials' criminal defences and conduct preventing the effective administration of the union. What happened there?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: I think the one to which you are referring is an investigation that is currently still ongoing.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission
witness_position: Acting Executive Director, Registered Organisations Services

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: So it has not been concluded?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: That one has not yet been concluded.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission
witness_position: Acting Executive Director, Registered Organisations Services

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Have you come across that anywhere else, where members' funds are being used to fund senior officials' criminal defences?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: We're aware anecdotally of a range of matters across many years where the union has paid for legal fees associated with the work involved with their officials, but this is the only matter that we are presently aware of that relates to a corrupting benefits matter.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission
witness_position: Acting Executive Director, Registered Organisations Services

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: In the past two years, has the administrator alerted you to any such instances that they have come to be aware of?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: No additional matters. This was a matter that was previously investigated by Geoffrey Watson SC.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission
witness_position: Acting Executive Director, Registered Organisations Services

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Finally, your report records at page 114—and I'm very disappointed that we have only just seen it—that there were 17 applications for certificates that could allow people subject to CFMEU administration restrictions to hold office or be employed by registered organisations. This is a concern for me, given the purpose of the administration, which is to get these people out of unions and out of the construction sector. How many were approved and how many involved former CFMEU officials?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: I have up-to-date figures in relation to that matter as of today, if you were interested in those—
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission
witness_position: Acting Executive Director, Registered Organisations Services

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: I am very interested.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: rather than what the position was as of 30 June? There have been 31 applications in relation to the various certificates, but they relate to 13 individuals. There are three different types of certificate that one is able to apply for. One relates to employment, one relates to becoming an officer in another organisation and one relates to the ability to be a bargaining representative. Those 13 individuals have applied in the two years and three months since this scheme came into effect. Those matters go before and are heard before a commission member. Twelve persons have been successful in obtaining the various certificates that they have applied for, and one matter was withdrawn.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission
witness_position: Acting Executive Director, Registered Organisations Services

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Chair, I just want to note that, according to this report, the letter of transmittal went to the minister on 6 October. It's now 28 October. That means there have been nine sitting days when this document could have been tabled.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: I would suggest, to finish—and I'm happy to have a response—that the reason this was tabled when it was expected the witnesses were no longer at the table is that the report states that 'no new registered organisation investigations, not a single infringement notice and serious CFMEU investigations still unresolved'.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Is anyone seeking to respond to that? It's not really a question.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: I think that's an inaccurate description of the operations of the organisation. I'm very happy to go through and I'm happy to sit here for as long as you wish for me to explain the extent of the operations of the organisation, the regulatory functions, what we have undertaken in relation to the CFMEU administration and playing our part in improving workplace relations but also conduct more broadly in this industry. I think that it is an untrue and an unfair assessment.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: If the minister had been honest, upfront and transparent and allowed this document to be tabled, we could have done exactly that with you, but instead we do not have the time to do that. We can only take these statistics on face value.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: To note, what I have stated is not something I have made up. Page 44 says 'zero new investigations'. Page 46 says 'zero infringement notices'. Page 45 identifies two CFMEU investigations still ongoing. That is how I have captured that information. I have not made that up. It is not a mistruth. What I have said has come from this document. Granted, I have not been able to peruse it in great detail, nor has our team, but that is the reality of it.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Well done government!

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Mr Furlong, would you like to respond to that? I remind people that it is much easier to follow this process if it's a question-and-answer-style session. Mr Furlong?

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: Yes, I would like to respond. My response is going to take probably two minutes. Since we were last here, at estimates in June, we progressed four investigations into alleged conduct of former construction and general division officials, including matters that were referred to us from the administrator. We participated in meetings with the Joint Agency Working Group, members of the Victoria police Taskforce Hawk, the Department of Infrastructure and other government departments and law enforcement bodies. I have also provided information to the Queensland commission of inquiry, and I have met with the Victorian commission of inquiry. I have met with industry participants who represent the interests of employers, employees, builders, subcontractors and government. I have met with officials from the CFMEU administration on many occasions about many matters, including current and future strategic and operational priorities. I have conducted operational activities in relation to the antiavoidance provisions of the RO Act, including commencing an investigation, the first of its kind, that goes to the conduct of Mr John Setka to determine whether Mr Setka or any other person has contravened the antiavoidance provisions of the RO Act. I have engaged former Fair Work Commissioner Julius Roe to work with the CFMEU and the AWU to resolve the long-running demarcation dispute on major civil construction works. The commission is sponsoring and providing the resources for that. I have written to the administrator, Mr Crosby, seeking copies of communications from Mr Setka about the administration to inform whether or not I should commence that investigation. We have updated our antiavoidance fact sheet to reflect that Mr Crosby is the administrator. I provided correspondence to Mr Crosby. Obviously, this was just after his appointment. We have commenced Federal Court civil penalty proceedings against former Victorian-Tasmanian branch officers following an investigation that we conducted. The proceedings seek the disqualification of, compensation from and civil penalties against those former officials. I am considering at the moment whether or not to commence an investigation into the Victoria-Tasmania branch's financial relationship with Building Industry 2000 Pty Ltd, including alleged transfers from that fund with or without proper approval. I've participated in the NCIF regulator consultation on potential Commonwealth standards for the construction industry following the release of the discussion paper on 21 August 2026. We have concluded an investigation into former New South Wales branch officers about the payment of legal expenses of two of those officers. I continue my fortnightly meetings with the administrator's chief of staff. That is since the last time we were at this table. I would have to say that for every activity I have just disclosed there are probably four or five others that I could easily add comment to.
witness_organisation: Fair Work Commission

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: I'm not challenging the work that you do and the difficulty of the work that you do. I'm simply stating that the numbers I provided were out of your report.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: To be honest, we would have loved to have asked you questions about all of those activities, but, because this was tabled so late, your minister threw you under a bus.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: I have to respond to that and say that, as I understand the process, these annual reports are provided. Mr Furlong is obviously doing a mountain of work. He's described that the report was provided later than usual. Senator Hume cited the date that the report was provided. I understand there's another process that occurs before these documents are tabled. I would also like to put on the record that, following multiple referrals from our government, there are 129 active investigations that we know of ongoing into the construction sector through the Fair Work Commission, the AFP and the Fair Work Ombudsman in addition to state and territory police investigations that are underway as well.

agency: Fair Work Commission
text: I believe that does conclude the committee's questions for the Fair Work Commission. Mr Furlong and your officers, thank you. We will suspend for a few moments whilst the Ombudsman joins us at the table.

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: I now welcome Ms Anna Booth, the Fair Work Ombudsman. Did you have an opening statement to make?

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: No, I do not.
witness_organisation: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: Senator Roberts.

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: Our first questions go to the minister, then to the Fair Work Ombudsman and then to a member of your staff. Minister, congratulations on the partial outcome of the same job, same pay laws and their application. According to the Mining and Energy Union, formerly part of the CFMEU, approximately 5,000 coalminers in the black coal mining sector have received annual pay increases of between $30,000 and $40,000 each per year, meaning an extra $200 million or so a year in workers' pockets. Over the next 10 years, that's approximately $2 billion in extra wages. Are you aware of that?

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: I am, of course, aware of our same job, same pay reforms, that they have benefited 8,000 workers and that they have benefited many workers in the mining industry. We expect workers in the mining industry on labour hire arrangements doing the same work as people directly employed to be able to receive the same pay. We said we were going to deliver that reform, and that is exactly what we have done.

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: You've partially done that. What a great partial outcome! What this demonstrates is that labour hire workers in the black coal sector have been underpaid by large amounts for a long time. Thankfully, these same job, same pay outcomes fully confirm and support our One Nation report of February 2024. That demonstrates with hard data that over at least the last 10 years the total likely underpayment of black coal miner labour hire workers has been up to $2 billion. Are you aware of that?

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: I want to clarify that we're talking about the same thing, because I am fairly sure that now you are talking in at least partially glowing terms about a piece of legislation that you opposed, being the same job, same pay legislation?

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: Correct. I'll be happy to explain that in a minute.

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: Do you now support same job, same pay?

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: Senator and Minister, that's not the way this process works. The questions are directed at the table and answered from the table.

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: It is a shame that the same job, same pay laws did not and do not address the historical underpayments now confirmed as real by the same job same, pay laws application. Would you agree that the same job, same pay outcomes have demonstrated and highlighted these historical underpayments, Australia's largest wage theft? Your legislation covered up and hid that wage theft.

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: We passed legislation. Applications need to be taken to the Fair Work Commission to apply, essentially, for coverage of the same job, same pay provisions, which then allow workers to be paid the same if they are on labour hire as direct employees. From that point, if that application is successful, there would be new pay rates that would be enforceable for that workforce. That is my understanding, and Mr Manning can assist further.

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: I think, Senator, we perhaps are talking about two different things here in the sense that, as the minister said, there is the regulated labour hire regime, which is part of those statistics, where I think over 100 orders have either been made or agreed, benefiting about 8,000 workers up to about $60,000 a year. I assume some of those figures you are quoting are about certain sectors of the mining industry specifically. That is separate from the notion of a formal underpayment in the sense that some of those workers were getting paid lawfully under other instruments, but the regime put in place arrangements whereby, if the same work was happening and there was an enterprise agreement in the host workplace, they should get paid according to that. But that is separate from the notion of not being paid lawfully pursuant to the prevailing instrument, which is what I would normally associate with an underpayment.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: I'm glad you raised that. We will get to that, and I will ask you more questions in the near future. Minister, is Labor's same job, same pay bill—I said it's a partial bill—and the cover-up of Australia's largest wage theft the reason you did not support my bill concerning same job, same pay that came out before yours? You did not support my bill because it exposed wage theft, unlike your bill, which did not mention backpay and which sought to cover up that backpay need? Was your bill intended to hide Australia's biggest wage theft?

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: Our bill, which you opposed, has delivered, on Mr Manning's evidence, pay rises of up to $60,000 per year for 8,000 workers across the country. We believe that people should be paid appropriately for the work that they do. We knew that labour hire was being used in some cases to undercut workers' pay and conditions. We believe that workers working alongside each other doing the same work who are directly employed and on labour hire should be paid the same. We have provided the architecture for workers to achieve that outcome. At the same time, the legislation also serves as a disincentive for employers to undercut existing wages and conditions by outsourcing to labour hire. We think all of those things are a good thing. That's why we introduced the legislation. The legislation is working. It's delivering pay rises of up to $60,000 a year for 8,000 workers so far, and this is legislation and outcomes that you oppose.

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: Minister, you did not answer my question. I will ask it again: was your bill designed or intended to hide Australia's largest wage theft? Why did you vote against a motion I moved in the Senate to require the government to investigate claims that casual miners working under enterprise agreements in the black coal mining industry are being and have been underpaid? That was moved on 16 May 2024 and was successfully passed in the Senate. You also opposed, I believe, 'if underpayments are found to have occurred, facilitate the reinvestment of the underpayments'. Minister, did your bill which followed my bill—I initiated this—intend to hide these underpayments that have now been proven?

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: If workers are underpaid, they have a number of avenues that they can take, including raising that with the Fair Work Ombudsman, who is here to answer questions. Our legislation was to do what it is achieving: 8,000 workers are receiving up to $60,000 a year extra because of our legislation. It was designed to do what it says on the label: same job, same pay. If you're a labour hire worker doing the same work next to someone who's a direct employee, you have the opportunity to apply to be paid the same. Some 8,000 workers have taken up that opportunity and are receiving up to $60,000 per year in pay rises—outcomes that you opposed and, it seems, continue to oppose.

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: Minister, would the Albanese government be prepared to partner with One Nation to move a bill to address and compensate casual coalminers for these historical underpayments, remedying what is a grave injustice to these hardworking Australians and a devastating failure of Australia's industrial relations framework?

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: Again, there are a number of avenues that workers can take to deal with underpayments. I do not have information about the specific underpayment that you are talking about having occurred. I am not sure whether Mr Manning or Ms Booth have information about that can assist you.

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: Let's turn to Ms Booth, then. Ms Booth, thank you for your letter of 8 October 2026 and your accompanying report exploring underpayment in the black coal sector. My focus is on what you referred to on page 5 of your report as 'the third cohort of 14 cases'. I extend my congratulations to you, too, for your media coverage in the Australian newspaper on 8 October, with the article headed 'Fair Work Ombudsman dismisses Malcolm Roberts' claim of widespread coalminer wage theft'. The PR machine appears to be well oiled. On 16 May 2024, my motion was passed in the Senate. This motion stated: '(b) requires the Government to investigate claims that casual miners working under enterprise agreements in the black coal mining industry are, and have been, underpaid.' I understand that on 6 August 2024 then Minister for Employment and Workplace Relations, Senator Murray Watt MP, wrote to your office requesting you to lead an investigation into the payment of casual coalminers under the enterprise agreements in the black coal industry. Do you believe this request by Senator Watt to your office was influenced by the Senate motion passed on 16 May 2024?

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: I do not have awareness of Senator Watt's intentions. All I know is that we were asked to conduct an investigation and did so thoroughly and extensively—56 individual investigations in total. It was the result of those investigations that I wrote to you about. In relation to the specific cohorts of workers, I would ask Mr Campbell and, if necessary, Mr Ronson to give you more detail.
witness_organisation: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: It's widely accepted that this Senate motion was in response to the February 2024 One Nation report which demonstrated factually, with backup data, widespread underpayment of labour hire workers in the black coal sector. Do you agree?

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: I'm not able to agree or disagree.
witness_organisation: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: Are you aware of the One Nation report?

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: No, I'm not.
witness_organisation: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: In the light of this, can it be inferred that your report is really a response to the One Nation report?

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: Our report is a response to the investigations that we were requested by the Senate to undertake, which we did undertake. The report, as you're aware, is extensive. If you have further questions that relate to aspects of that report, Mr Campbell and Mr Ronson are very happy to provide those details here.
witness_organisation: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: I will be asking them questions in a minute. The report produced by One Nation applied a 'better off overall' test, comparing the all-in flat hourly rates applied under the enterprise agreements to the base all-in flat hourly rates under the black coal award. Our One Nation better off overall test analysis demonstrates underpayments, but you have not seen that report, which I am surprised by, by the way, but I will come to that. Your report ignores and fails to examine the application of the 'better off overall' test, focusing exclusively on the assertion that casual labour hire employees are not subject to the black coal award. Would you agree that this is a key difference between your report and what I say is in the One Nation report?

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: Our report is founded on the legal interpretation that we take in that an enterprise agreement prevails over the content of an award. Any further detail about how that applies on a case-by-case basis, which is different, of course, depending on every case, would have to be responded to by Mr Campbell or Mr Ronson, because I do not have visibility of the individual investigations.
witness_organisation: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: The Fair Work Act, section 206, states, 'The base rate of pay under an enterprise agreement must not be less than the modern award rate.' Does the assertion in your report that the employees in question are not subject to the award remove your obligation under the act to test whether the employees are paid less than the base all-in flat hourly rates under the award?

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: My recollection of the application of that section of the act—and I here am drawing upon my past as a Fair Work Commission member—is that it acts to apply the minimum rate in the award to the minimum base rate in the enterprise agreement in circumstances where that particular base rate in the enterprise agreement is less than the minimum base rate in the award, but it does not re-enliven the scrutiny of an enterprise agreement in relation to whether it does or does not pass the 'better off overall' test. That's a different concept entirely.
witness_organisation: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: Can you understand that the everyday Australian, particularly those affected by this massive underpayment, would view your report as misleading and inadequate as it ignores the core requirement to apply the better off overall test to labour hire coalminers' wages?

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: I neither agree nor disagree on how an ordinary person might interpret the content of our investigation report.
witness_organisation: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: I have a few questions left for Mr Ronson. Ms Booth is encouraging me to ask them.

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: Sorry, Ms Booth is not managing the committee's business, I am. We normally do rotations of around 15 minutes. I am happy for you to place another question, but then I do need to keep rotating the call, as there are a number of senators here. But I can come back to you on a further rotation if you wish. Would you like me to rotate now and then come back?

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: Yes, because I have about four questions.

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: I'm coming to the opposition and then I'll come to Senator Payman and then I'll come back to you. Senator Kovacic, you have the call.

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: In July 2024, then workplace relations minister, Mr Burke, asked the Fair Work Ombudsman to undertake a targeted review of all CFMEU agreements made by the Victorian branch that apply to the Big Build projects. Can you confirm if that is correct?

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: I will ask Mr Campbell. I have a recollection around that time of such a request, but I would prefer to give you accurate information.
witness_organisation: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: Sorry, you're testing my memory a little bit, but of course I do very much recall Minister Burke's correspondence to the agency asking that we make a number of inquiries into allegations of potential breaches of the Fair Work Act as they related to Big Build projects, particularly in Victoria but also as allegations spread into other states. With respect to collective agreements, our role is to ensure they're enforced and are made in a way which is consistent with the act such that there is no coercion or unlawful influence on a person to enter into or not enter into a collective agreement. The scope of it was limited to our jurisdiction, if that makes sense. Others, like the Fair Work Commission et cetera, looked into their aspect of the process.
witness_organisation: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: How many agreements were examined? Are you able to tell me?

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: We wrote to—and I'm just going to go off my memory for now, because I do not have—
witness_organisation: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: You could provide the balance of information on notice?

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: I should be able to help, but I may not be able to give you a specific. We wrote to every employer that we could identify that had a CFMEU agreement and worked on a Victorian Big Build or government site. We asked them to provide information to us about their collective agreement and any concerns they have about how it was constructed or how and why they entered into it as a way of our trying to generate leads, if you like. Off the back of that, we received intelligence and leads then to conduct further inquiries into agreement construction issues.
witness_organisation: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: Could you provide on notice the number of agreements that were examined?

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: Yes, I will be able to provide some on notice on that.
witness_organisation: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: Did the review find any agreements that were not genuinely agreed or any evidence of coercion, adverse action or misrepresentation in the manner in which they were made?

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: We found that most of the people who had CFMEU agreements were content that they did, because that gave them access to work on government sites, as it was. That was the feedback that we got.
