witness_organisation: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: That was the price they had to pay?

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: I will not judge on the how, but that's the feedback that we got. We did identify some matters where we had some concerns about how agreements were potentially struck, as in the voting process that sat behind the collective agreements. That started to shift outside of our jurisdiction a little, so we had to be careful about how far we took that as compared to referring it to other organisations to examine, but that was the smaller proportion of it. Most of the feedback we got was that having an agreement was of benefit to their business. We got more feedback from those concerned that they didn't have access to an agreement to gain access to sites.
witness_organisation: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: Did they suggest to you why they couldn't get an agreement?

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: There were some allegations that—
witness_organisation: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: I suspect so. Could you identify for us the types of allegations they identified to you without, obviously, disclosing any specifics?

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: I'll probably do a better job on notice. If you are not happy with the answer I give you, I am happy to look at providing it.
witness_organisation: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: Let's give it a go.

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: We certainly found that, where there had been historic disagreement with the CFMEU, it was a basis on which the employer said they may not have been able to have access to an agreement, or a particular organiser or representative of the CFMEU. Equally, if they had a relationship with the AWU historically, that was a potential cause in their mind about why they may not have been able to have access.
witness_organisation: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: A barrier?

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: Potentially. As I said, this is just information we received. We didn't confirm it, but we certainly take it as intelligence that we use to help shape our investigations.
witness_organisation: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: The reason I ask these questions is that you're familiar with the reports from Geoffrey Watson and the evidence that has come out of the Queensland commission of inquiry. I asked Mr Watson questions specifically relating to this in the productivity committee inquiry. From what I have seen, it does appear that there are a number of EBAs that are illegally entered into and that it is effectively the cost of doing business, or being able to do business, on these large projects. This is a real problem for the taxpayer, because they are either state funded or state and Commonwealth funded projects. My question to you is whether the review of any of these agreements, or any of the allegations or concerns that were aired with you, has led to any formal investigations or proceedings?

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: My short answer is no, because it's outside of our jurisdiction.
witness_organisation: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: Have you referred it to anyone?

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: We have made a number of referrals to different organisations, but I suppose our coercion is the coercion for someone to enter into a collective agreement with a certain organisation. That coercive behaviour needs to be more than simply pressure; it needs to effectively deny the free will of the individual to make another decision. That's the bar we work to. 'Coercion' obviously has a range of applications as a word, but we have a legal bar that we work to. That's something we are willing to investigate, but, if a person makes a decision from a commercial perspective to enter into a collective agreement, that is not coercion for the purposes of the Fair Work Act.
witness_organisation: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: It's interesting, because you could say, 'I don't really want to do this but, if I don't do this then I don't get the work and then my business does not survive.' It is about being stood over, right?

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: I could not comment on that. I am happy to share my experience to a point with this issue.
witness_organisation: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: That's fair enough. Have you briefed the minister on the review's findings and, if so, when did that occur?

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: We did write to the minister in October 2024, I think it was, setting out some of our findings against the key subject matters that he raised in his correspondence to us.
witness_organisation: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: Can I just ask: is that letter public, or was that private correspondence?

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: I don't know. It seems like a lifetime ago already. I'm happy to take on notice if that was—
witness_organisation: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: If you could take that on notice, we would love to be able to see that letter and have that letter tabled if it was not private correspondence.

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: Yes, I will just need to check.
witness_organisation: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: In relation to the findings of your review, will that be made public, or has that been made public as yet?

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: I don't know. Again, I don't think we made a public statement, but we have made public statements about different aspects of it. The agreement part was obviously interesting, but I suppose it didn't go directly to our jurisdiction. For us, we were looking for the conduct that probably flowed from it or that was around it. We were looking for coercive practices by CFMEU officials and others with respect to employers and collective agreements in the workplace relations regime under the Fair Work Act. In terms of the construction of the agreements itself, we only had a limited role.
witness_organisation: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: Last October, the Ombudsman told this committee that it had received referrals from the Victorian Infrastructure Delivery Authority. Did those referrals form part of that review?

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: Possibly. We had to rely on a number of different organisations to identify all the employers that we wanted to write to. Obviously, the commission was a big help for us to know which employers had agreements with the building construction division of the CFMEU in Victoria and to allow us to zero in to then write to. We did draw on a number of people. I do not know whether it was VIDA or not, but VIDA is an organisation that we do receive information from, among many others, about issues occurring on government funded sites and other sites as well.
witness_organisation: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: Again, you can provide this on notice. Do you have a response rate for those letters that you wrote out? How many of those organisations responded to your letter seeking an in-confidence review of their agreement?

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: It was not a particularly big number.
witness_organisation: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: It was quite low? Is that consistent with what you expected, given the circumstances?

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: Possibly. I was not expecting a flood, because I am writing to people who have CFMEU agreements. In my history and experience—
witness_organisation: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: They're not going to say, 'I'm not happy with this', because guess what's going to happen?

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: I can't comment on that, but what I can comment on is my experience said that the individuals who had CFMEU agreements in place indicated they did not have issues to raise with us.
witness_organisation: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: Those who did respond responded and said, 'We're happy we have an agreement because it gives us the work', and you had a lot who did not respond at all?

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: Of that cohort, but we obviously receive information from others in the sector.
witness_organisation: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: Then you had others who said, 'We cannot get near it because they don't like us'?

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: Correct. We deal with them in accordance with our usual investigative processes.
witness_organisation: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: Do you have concerns around the agreements that have been entered into with the CFMEU?

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: If they have been lawfully made, I do not have a position.
witness_organisation: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: Do you have concerns that there are a number that have not been lawfully made, or can you not make that judgement?

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: I can't make that judgement. I would reflect that the administrator has indicated that he has some concerns about CFMEU agreements that have been made historically and that, now that he has been administrator, he probably would not want to enter into those arrangements into the future.
witness_organisation: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: I will ask two more questions and then we will be done. I will put the rest on notice. I have some questions relating to the administration of the CFMEU. How many referrals has the Fair Work Ombudsman received from the CFMEU administration since May of this year?

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: We have received referrals.
witness_organisation: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: We have received referrals.
witness_organisation: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: Do you have a total number? If you want to table that document and if you have a breakdown of those referrals by state and by type of offence as well, that would be useful.

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: While Mr Campbell is looking for those numbers, I can just confirm, in relation to that report that you were previously discussing, that it has not been made public at this stage.
witness_organisation: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: I'm happy for you just to table that document, Mr Campbell, to save us all time.

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: You do not want my scribbles, but I will definitely take that on notice.
witness_organisation: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: Or even to let us know before the conclusion of your session.

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: Do you mean the answer to your question about referrals from the CFMEU administrator?
witness_organisation: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: Yes, correct; the number of referrals and the detail of the number by year.

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: Sure. It is not a huge number. We have had three from the administrator. It takes away from the opportunity we have to work with the administrator to identify opportunities for us to proactively investigate issues in the sector. The administrator has been willing to engage with us on issues that we have concern about in the sector as well.
witness_organisation: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: Were they all in Victoria?

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: Definitely in New South Wales, and maybe one in Victoria, but I can confirm that for you if you wish.
witness_organisation: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: Yes, if you could, please? It is likely that there were two in New South Wales and one in Victoria.

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: There are also ones that we have on foot. They might raise a concern about a particular company, for example, and we will say, 'Noted. Thank you for that referral, but it is a matter that we are already investigating.'
witness_organisation: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: Are you able to share with me the type of offence for each of those three?

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman

witness_organisation: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: Senator Payman.

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: In an FOI request to the Fair Work Ombudsman with reference IA-2925, on page 150, there's an email dated 21 May from Ms Anna Booth. Ms Booth notes, in relation to the referral of criminal wage theft cases for prosecution, that the Fair Work Ombudsman had 'not yet referred one, although we're likely to before the end of the financial year'. Did this happen?

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: No. We have not yet referred any matters to the Commonwealth Director of Public Prosecutions.
witness_organisation: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: Is there a status or any likelihood of what we yet are to see with any cases referred?

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: Ms Carey is here, and it is within her group. As I think you are aware from the inquiry that you chaired, she is responsible for the branch that is our criminal investigation branch. Before she tells you what she wants to tell you, I will just make the point that was obviously my hope, but investigations take the time they take and need to be thorough. That's the situation we're in. Ms Carey, anything to add?
witness_organisation: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: I can give an update on the matters that are on foot. I am unable to give precise timing as to when a matter would be referred. Matters are referred to the DPP when we are satisfied that we have sufficient evidence that reaches the criminal burden of proof. I am happy to give you an update on the number of investigations and matters that we have.
witness_organisation: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: In the interests of time, is that something that you could provide to the committee on notice?

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: Absolutely.
witness_organisation: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: On unpaid super, does the Fair Work Ombudsman accept that unpaid super is unpaid remuneration and should be treated as seriously as wage theft?

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: Unpaid super is covered by the offence provision. There are some exceptions to that for some cohorts of workers that are based on the constitutional limitations of the referral powers. There are some state and local government employees, for example, excluded from the offence provision in relation to unpaid superannuation, but it is one form of a required amount that is covered by the offence provision in the act. That is by virtue of superannuation being part of the National Employment Standards.
witness_organisation: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: The National Employment Standards came into effect on 1 January 2024. What responsibility does the Ombudsman have in enforcing that entitlement?

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: The primary responsibility for enforcement of underpaid superannuation is with the Australian Taxation Office. Superannuation is obviously complicated, but it's a form of a tax to avoid the charge. Once it was introduced into the National Employment Standards, obviously we have jurisdiction in relation to underpayment of superannuation and other entitlements. Where it forms part of our investigations, holistically in relation to people's entitlements under relevant awards or the minimum wages, superannuation is a component that we do investigate and can take enforcement steps in relation to.
witness_organisation: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: Is it correct to say that you routinely check whether an employer has also failed to pay correct super when you're investigating wage theft?

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: We generally will look at super in the context of the underpayment. In calculating the underpayment, we can look at whether or not there is superannuation that is owing on the total amount of the underpayment. In relation to superannuation in terms of whether it has been remitted in the required time, primary responsibility for that sits with the ATO. We do think payday super, which obviously commenced on 1 July, would, we hope, have a significant impact on improving that.
witness_organisation: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: In 2025-26, how many Fair Work Ombudsman investigations into both wage underpayments and unpaid super have been identified? I'm curious to understand how many workers were affected and what was the total value of the super identified?

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: Senator Payman, do you mean specifically in the criminal jurisdiction or across the entire jurisdiction?
witness_organisation: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: I'm happy for you to do the entire jurisdiction.

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: I don't have those numbers. I think that might be something we would have to take on notice to see.
witness_organisation: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: Do you have the numbers for the criminal jurisdiction?

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: Not with me, but I can take that on notice.
witness_organisation: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: No worries. I would like to know in how many of those matters the Ombudsman secured payment of the outstanding super and how many were referred to the ATO? Since intentional underpayment became a criminal offence, do we know how many Ombudsman investigations have examined suspected intentional non-payment of super, or is that something you have not—

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: That is definitely a question for Ms Carey, but I suspect she may need to take it on notice.
witness_organisation: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: I would have to take on notice the subject matter. Obviously, we do not provide detailed information about ongoing investigations, but I can take on notice what information I can provide in that respect.
witness_organisation: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: No worries. Can you go through, I guess, what the formal process entails when ensuring an employer investigated for underpaying wages is also examined for unpaid super and that workers recover both entitlements? What does that process look like? Is that obviously working closely with the ATO in this instance as well?

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: Yes. I can talk from a criminal investigation perspective. Mr Campbell can speak in relation to our broader operations. We do not proactively monitor payment of the superannuation guarantee, firstly, because it is, as I said earlier, a charge to avoid tax, and the tax becomes payable; it crystallises at the particular time at which the contributions were due to be remitted. That is not information that the Fair Work Ombudsman has access to due to secrecy provisions that operate between the two jurisdictions. It's not something that we proactively, independently investigate in the criminal jurisdiction independent of the underpayment matters. We tend to focus on superannuation as part of that assessment of the underpayment that we're investigating rather than necessarily the failure to remit superannuation, which is the primary responsibility of the ATO. I do not know if Mr Campbell would like to add anything to that.
witness_organisation: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: I think you've summarised that aspect of it well, Ms Carey. Obviously, where that stewards an entitlement that we can enforce, we will build that into our investigation. It might be something that we can resolve voluntarily between the parties through a first contact, but, if it's coming down to an investigation where we see that it's likely to require a compliance and enforcement outcome, we will use our powers to gather evidence to support the allegations we say exist. Then we will make them out. If superannuation is owed, we will build that effectively into the contravention and seek recoveries. That will either be through the use of a compliance notice or, alternatively, we will litigate to the contravention.
witness_organisation: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: Some have raised criticism that this process requires workers to deal separately with the Fair Work Ombudsman for wage underpayment and the ATO for super, which obviously creates this regulatory gap and puts the burden on the worker to seek their unpaid entitlements. How do we fix that? Is that a correct characterisation of there being a regulatory gap where the burden is placed on the worker to retrieve their entitlements?

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: It's certainly not the case that we separate the wage payment from the super in either our investigations or our enforcement. For example, when we issue a compliance notice, it will include the unpaid super if that has been assessed. You will see a litigation that we take. The reporting of the court or the judgement of the court will isolate the amount that was unpaid for wages and super. In our subsequent media releases when we announce the results of our court cases, we will also indicate super separately, but that doesn't imply that the worker has to go to the ATO to recover that. As Ms Carey indicated, if the concern is around the employer's compliance with the superannuation guarantee legislation specifically, that is something that they would need to go to the ATO in relation to. As far as I am aware, when workers recover lost wages from our processes, it always includes their superannuation.
witness_organisation: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: There has not been a case where the wage has been recovered but the super has not?

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: Before it was in the NES, that might have potentially occurred, but, as part of the NES, it confirms that we have a jurisdiction there. I would like to think that, where we can exercise powers to recover super, we do. It might just be that, where it goes to SGL enforcement, there's an aspect to the conduct or the situation that means it's squarely in the ATO's jurisdiction. It's not necessarily a gap. These are overlapping jurisdictions, like we have in migration law, corporate law, discrimination law. There are overlaps, but we try to make sure we're not in any jurisdiction passing people off to others to do the work that we could have done.
witness_organisation: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: Since the NES on 1 January 2024, does it apply to cases prior to that date retrospectively?

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: I do not think it is retrospective, but, again, if you know differently, I'm happy to hear it. I can't remember our being critiqued for shifting superannuation work to the ATO when it should have otherwise been dealt with through our processes.
witness_organisation: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: I'll put the rest of my questions on notice.

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: Senator Roberts.

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: I refer to the Fair Work Ombudsman report of 8 October 2026 into underpayments of casual coalminers in the black coal sector. On page 5, the report refers to 'a third cohort of 14 cases'. My understanding is that you oversaw and directed the investigations into this third cohort of cases. Is that correct?

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: That is correct.
witness_organisation: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text:
I am aware of redacted copies of many of the preliminary assessments into those 14 cases. In each instance the preliminary assessments state:

As the FWO has determined that … the terms and conditions are governed by the relevant enterprise agreement, we do not consider that the Black Coal Mining Industry Award applied.

Further:

Consequently the wages and entitlements should not be derived from the award, but rather the relevant enterprise agreement.

Is it correct to say that these preliminary assessments by the Fair Work Ombudsman's office are based on wages and entitlements under the relevant enterprise agreements and not the award?

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: The best way to answer that question is: what you have described as appearing in those preliminary assessments is correct. What the report attempts to do is explain why that is the case. We have gone to great lengths to explain the legal technicalities, the interactions between the award and the enterprise agreements and just the situation as we determined it and we've assessed it. The way to best express my answer to you is to say it is what it is. There is not much we can do about that.
witness_organisation: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: Section 206 of the act states that 'the base rate of pay under an enterprise agreement must not be less than the modern award rate'. The assertion in the preliminary assessments is that the casual coalminers are not subject to the award. Why does this position remove the obligation, which is your obligation, under the act to assess whether or not the enterprise agreements which apply to the casual coalminers result in a base rate of pay which is less than the award?

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: I don't think it does. I think Ms Booth previously answered that particular question well. Ms Volzke has explained that, where the enterprise agreement is validly made, we had no reason to believe it was not.
witness_organisation: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: No reason?

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: We had no reason to believe it was not; therefore, the agreement applied. Picking up on your section 206 point, I refer you to the previous evidence of Ms Booth.
witness_organisation: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: I am aware that one of the 14 cases has formally disputed your preliminary assessment, provided considerable counterarguments and requested a review. I understand this was lodged at the end of July 2026. Can you please advise on the progress of that review, when you expect the review to be completed and a response supplied?

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: Yes, that's correct. What you've said is correct. It's with an independent assurance team within the Fair Work Ombudsman. I am part of the investigation branch. It's not right or appropriate for us to review our own work. It is with the assurance team. My understanding is—and I'm happy to be corrected if it's wrong—that it's quite advanced. I can't probably add more. I can take it on notice as to what its full status is.
witness_organisation: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: Senator Hume.

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: I want to follow up on some of the questions that Senator Kovacic asked around the CFMEU administration. I want to understand how many right-of-entry permit applications the Fair Work Ombudsman has opposed since the CFMEU administration began and how many of those oppositions succeeded.

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: I know that we have opposed. I will refer to Ms Volzke for the correct number.
witness_organisation: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: We commenced one Fair Work Commission right-of-entry matter in relation to Mr Edmond Margjini, seeking suspension of his permit, but we subsequently discontinued that when the criminal charges against him were discharged. We also have sought permission to be heard in relation to a number of permit application matters at the beginning, as opposed to seeking the suspension, which we did with Mr Margjini because he already had the permit. There were three of those. One of them was in relation to Mr Joel Shackleton. Another one was in relation to Mr Dean Rielly. We were heard in relation to that matter. That hearing occurred on 10 December 2025. We made submissions in relation to that, but the decision was subsequently made by the Fair Work Commission on 27 May 2026, granting him that permit. There might be one more as well relating to Mr Hassett.
witness_organisation: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: On Mr Rielly, I realise this was a conversation that occurred during the last round of Senate estimates. Has the ombudsman been monitoring Mr Rielly since June or, once the commission has approved it, are we done? How does that work?

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: Mr Campbell has already spoken about the investigation activities that we do, but it's the Fair Work Commission that's responsible for administering, I guess, the regime. But, certainly to the extent that there is any intelligence that comes our way, we would action that appropriately.
witness_organisation: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: Have there been any complaints or any intelligence about Mr Rielly since his permit was granted?

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: None that spring to mind. I am not saying that there has not been, but I also need to be careful; if it is a subject of investigation, it may not be something I will put into the public domain either way. I tend to know when concerns have been raised about a person of interest, but it's not jumping to mind straightaway.
witness_organisation: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: I want to ask about a report in the AFR in May this year that the CFMEU shut down Lendlease sites across Sydney and then, three weeks later, disrupted work at Chifley South and at three New South Wales government hospital projects. The union cited safety concerns. Has the Fair Work Ombudsman investigated whether any of those shutdowns did constitute unlawful or unprotected industrial action?

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: Yes. According to Lendlease, there were safety related concerns.
witness_organisation: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: There were safety related concerns?

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: According to Lendlease.
witness_organisation: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: In the ACT in July, the ACT Integrity Commission's Operation Kingfisher made corruption findings against two senior officials over an $18.8 million school upgrade contract. A local builder whose bid was assessed as better and cheaper did not win that contract. The commission was told that the CFMEU did not like that builder because he did not have a union agreement. Is the ombudsman aware of Operation Kingfisher and its findings?

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: No, I'm not. I don't recall an investigation into that, noting that it sounds like the matter was investigated by another organisation with respect to the title you have given.
witness_organisation: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: The Fair Work Commission has not received any other complaints about the CFMEU pressuring builders in the ACT because they do not have union agreements?

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: Do you mean the ombudsman?
witness_organisation: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: Yes.

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: Can I take that on notice? I would need to confirm whether we have had a coercion investigation in Canberra. We may have had some allegations about that, but I can't recall it.
witness_organisation: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman

agency: Office of the Fair Work Ombudsman
text: That concludes our questions for you, Ms Booth. Thank you to you and your officers.

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: I'm calling officers from the department in relation to outcome 1, Employment. Senator O'Sullivan.

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: I'd like to talk about the targeted compliance framework. I appreciate the opening statement you made earlier today, Secretary. We have covered off some of my questions, but some I now would like to explore in a bit more detail. I refer to the powers that you said would resume on 26 October—that was the evidence you gave last time—about suspending the payments of people who refuse or fail to start suitable work and cancelling payments when people do not meet a reconnection requirement within four weeks of being notified. On 19 October you confirmed that both would resume on Monday. Refresh me: what did you say in relation to when it recommenced?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: In my opening statement I noted that I made a public statement on 19 October indicating that on 26 October decision-making would resume under 42AG, which allows a person's social security participation payment to be suspended for a work refusal failure, but also section 42AM, which allows a person's participation payment to be cancelled if they do not meet a reconnection requirement within four weeks.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Did that then occur on the 26th?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Yes, that's correct; Monday the 26th.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: You said that the provisions were only resumed once you were satisfied. On what date were you satisfied?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: To preface my response, in terms of my obligations under section 7 of the Social Security Act, I have particular responsibilities under that act for the general administration of the social security law as it relates to mutual obligations. I take those responsibilities very seriously. One of those responsibilities is restoring those elements of the TCF that have been put on hold as soon as I am assured that the systems and procedures are in place to support lawful administration in accordance with the current legislation. We have established within the department a task force, and that task force now has been in operation for approximately two years. It has been providing assurance to me and my predecessor over that period about the work program to bring all the elements of the targeted compliance framework that were suspended into legal compliance. I have been briefed very frequently on this. I was briefed as recently as the Sunday prior to the commencement of the targeted compliance framework, the two sections that I referred to, to give me that final assurance that all of the systems elements were in place prior to that recommencement on the Monday. It just gives one a bit of a sense of the frequency of engagement around this, to give you that assurance.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: It was not a single moment? There was not a single date?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: There were lots of written briefings and meetings very frequently. As you could imagine, it has been a very big endeavour for the team to be able to get the system back into legal compliance over the time period. An enormous amount of work has gone into it. I can go into all of the assurance work that we did, if that is of interest to you, but it was a huge body of work. I have been very closely engaged all the way through.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: In terms of coming to that final decision to restart, when did you make that decision?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: I made that decision the week prior to making the public statement. In that public statement I was very clear that I then needed to be assured just prior to the implementation that all of the systems elements were in place as well as that the providers themselves were ready to be able to start making decisions under the resumed provisions. All the way up to the 26th, I was receiving updates on the information. On the basis of those updates, we were responding to the team, letting them know that, if there were elements that needed further work, the team would go away and do that further work. The final confirmation occurred the day before.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Are you the delegate on the decision, or does it go to the minister?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: I am actually the decision-maker under the legislation, so that's correct.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: The minister was not involved in the decision?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: This is a particular set of responsibilities that are assigned to the Secretary of Employment.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: I presume that you inform the minister ahead of the announcement?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: This is something on which I meet with the minister frequently. I have informed her all the way along about progress, and then we informed her in writing prior to the commencement.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: What date was that?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: I will just check with my colleagues to see whether they have the date of the written brief. We will have to take that on notice.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: In August, the department said that, once the work on the human decision-making is implemented, a jobseeker's circumstances will be comprehensively considered before any decision to cancel their payment. Was that in place before cancellations restarted on Monday?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Yes. If you can just give me a minute to give you a sense of the assurance processes that we went through? Essentially, there were four lines of assurance that were provided to me before I made the final decision to recommence. This is a complex system. It is a system that is shared with Services Australia but also with the private providers. We had extensive testing with Services Australia to demonstrate that the systems changes were operating as intended and, of course, in accordance with the legislative requirements. The second thing was updated training, guidance and system controls. They were put in place with providers but also the departmental staff who would be subsequently involved in decision-making. The third line of assurance was we had extensive legal review, audit and assurance processes. As part of that, I commissioned an in-flight internal audit to critically assess the work of the task force that was putting this together to bring me separate advice on whether or not the task force was delivering on the legal requirements, the system requirements, but also responding to the Ombudsman's recommendations in this regard. I was getting, if you like, a second stream of advice on this to ensure I could be absolutely assured this was all being brought into place with legal compliance.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Just so I understand, at a high level this now means mutual obligations is able to be properly assured?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: This was to bring two elements of mutual obligations that had been paused back online, but there are other elements of mutual obligations that have continued which were not in question in terms of the legality of their administration.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Yes, I know that. What were those two? You did mention that in your opening statement.

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: To remind you again: 42AG, which was allowing a person's social security participation payment to be suspended for a work refusal failure; and 42AM, which allows a person's participation to be cancelled if they do not meet a reconnection requirement within four weeks.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: On the Ombudsman's recommendation of five days to reconnect before a payment is suspended, in August the department said it accepted all the Ombudsman's recommendations. Services Australia marked that as not accepted and said it is your call. What was your call on that particular point?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: The Ombudsman provided us with two reports that are relevant: one titled Automation in the Targeted Compliance Framework: when the law is changed but the system isn't and a second one on Fairness in the Targeted Compliance Framework: when the decisions are made beyond your control. You are correct in that we issued a public response to both of those reports, accepting all of the Ombudsman's recommendations. Some of those recommendations were relevant for the provisions that have now restarted following my recent decision. Other elements are part of a longer term work program. They're not as relevant for the decisions that I just made but will be relevant to restoring the remaining elements of the targeted compliance framework, which, as I said in my opening statement, we intend to bring back into line in the first quarter of next calendar year.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Are jobseekers still able to be suspended on the spot?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: There is a number of provisions that have remained in operation. I ask you to be a little bit more specific in terms of whether there is a specific part of the targeted compliance framework that you are referring to?
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: My understanding is that with the recommendation from the Ombudsman in relation to that five days to suspend, in August you said that you accepted the Ombudsman's recommendations but Services Australia marked that as not accepted. I'm talking about the ability for, as I understand it, Services Australia to be able to suspend someone on the spot. Is that not right?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: I will ask my colleagues to jump in with further detail. To go to what I think is driving your question, there is both shared and joint responsibility between the department and Services Australia for the different parts of making the system work. Some of the recommendations from the Ombudsman Services Australia do not need to implement, because those powers sit with the department. It could be that, when you're reflecting that Services Australia has said that it's not a call for them but a call for the department, what they were referring to was that, actually, this is not a power or a function that they hold, and it would be a call from the department.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: Acting Deputy Secretary, Employment and Workforce Group

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Can you check that either now or come back to us on their reasons why?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: The recommendation to which you are referring came out of the second Ombudsman's report where he requested that DEWR and Services Australia review the automatic process to suspend jobseekers' income support in the penalty zone, ideally to provide jobseekers with five days to reconnect or provide a valid reason for any mutual obligation failure prior to suspension. The response from the department—and Ms Schofield and the Secretary are correct—
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Customer Experience and Engagement

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Is this the department or—

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: For this department, that is a piece of legislation that this department administers, which probably gets to why Services Australia responded in the way that it did. Our response is that, effectively, any change about the application of reconnection time is a matter for government. It talks to the construct of the targeted compliance framework. It's only in part of the targeted compliance framework, the penalty zone, that no resolution time is provided.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Customer Experience and Engagement

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: The committee will now suspend.

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: We have Senator Allman-Payne appearing remotely. That decision has been approved by the committee. Senator Allman-Payne, I'll come to you for a 15-minute block. You have the call.

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Mr Duggan, I note that you were answering questions asked by Senator O'Sullivan earlier about the assurance actions that the department has taken prior to restarting some of the suspensions and cancellations. Could you elaborate a little bit more on some specific areas of that. First of all, what did the testing with Services Australia look like, and how many cases were trialled in that testing?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: I'll hand over to my colleagues, who'll be able to give you all the details.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text:
I'm happy to kick off while my colleagues are getting to the right places in their folders. In terms of the IT testing piece, we had a three-phase, interagency IT testing strategy that we developed with Services Australia to undertake assurance activities just beyond the standard testing processes. This was really designed to validate critical system interactions and payment calculations delivered through that three phased approach aligned to the key decisions. Phase 1 and phase 2 testing is completed and indicated that the systems are operating in line with legislative requirements.

To strengthen assurance and traceability, business rules were mapped to the test cases, demonstrating that system functionality operates as intended. It enabled clear linkage between policy requirements and system behaviour. Testing undertaken to support the resumption of section 42AM and 42AG validated 248 business rules with over 500 test cases completed. The phase 3 testing commenced following reinstatement—that's operational now—and includes production testing with Services Australia and a hypercare period of IT system monitoring following resumption on Monday. Hypercare arrangements will be stood up again between November and December to ensure that the first work-refusal failure payment suspensions and section 42AM(3) payment cancellations are operating as intended once they start to flow through the system should any of those eventuate at that time.

In parallel with the IT changes supporting the resumption, DEWR has also modernised components of our IT platform in response to both the Deloitte and the Commonwealth Ombudsman review recommendations. This work included upgrading to contemporary design standards and migrating the code base to a modern platform, supporting enhanced version control and release management. Essentially, collectively, these really strengthened the integrity and the resilience of the TCF coding that exists in our system.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: Acting Deputy Secretary, Employment and Workforce Group

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Mr Duggan also referred to training that was provided to providers. Can you elaborate on that a little bit more. Is it possible to provide the committee with copies of documents related to that training?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: The training and guidance has been rolled out in two areas. One is to the employment services providers and the second is to the staff within the department who work within the Digital Services Contact Centre. The provider training has focused on the guidance that they need to know and the rules they need to now understand that relate to 42AG and 42AM. Those training modules were released on 2 September, and they're mandatory for provider staff who undertake compliance actions. One of the safeguards that exists within the system is that if a person, an employment services consultant, had not completed the new training prior to the recommencement of provisions on Monday, the 26th, they are unable to access the compliance system. They are unable to apply compliance against any of their participants. The training for our digital services contact centre staff and our national customer service line staff commenced on 5 October, and that training has been scheduled into their weeks. Again, any staff who did not complete the training by Monday 26 October will be required to complete it prior to undertaking any compliance action.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Customer Experience and Engagement

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Is it possible to have tabled or to take it on notice what those modules cover from the providers?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Senator, I'll have to take that on notice.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Customer Experience and Engagement

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Great, thank you. I have one more question on that, my apologies. Mr Duggan also referenced—and I don't know if this is the right term or if I heard it properly—was it an in-flight audit?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: That's correct, Senator. I referred to it as an in-flight internal audit that I commissioned to run in parallel with the work of the taskforce, which was effectively providing me with independent advice from the taskforce around both the systems changes and the implementation of the advice that we'd received from the Commonwealth Ombudsman in terms of how we should approach restoring elements of the TCF.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Is there a report of that audit?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Yes, Senator. I received two reports from that audit. It was conducted in two phases. The first report was provided to me and then informed a second phase of work by the taskforce. I received a final audit report prior to making my decision to restore those elements of the TCF.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Can you provide a copy of that audit report to the committee?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Senator, yes, on notice. I'm happy to provide a copy of that report.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Thank you. You also said that there were extensive legal reviews of the taskforce. Are any of those legal reviews able to be provided or is they in confidence?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Through our internal legal team, we received extensive AGS advice in the course of events. I am a little bit limited in what I can share about that because I don't want to cut across the legal privilege of that advice.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Well, could I maybe ask if you could provide on notice any aspects of that which are able to be provided?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Yes, Senator. I'll provide whatever we're able to on notice.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Thank you. Just going then to some of the things that have been restarted. Starting with payment suspensions under 42AG for supposed work refusal, these are typically reported by people's employment services providers. I'm really interested to understand what safeguards the department has put in place to ensure that people won't lose their payment on unfair or unreasonable grounds.

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Yes, 42AG, the payment suspensions for work refusal failures, the changes and updates that have been made in the system require that an employment services consultant must confirm that a work refusal failure has occurred, and they must record that decision and the evidence in the system prior to progressing that suspension.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Customer Experience and Engagement

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Can you just clarify for me, when you say that a work refusal has occurred, is the job service provider, under the law, required to exercise discretion in terms of whether there is a valid reason for that refusal.

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: A payment suspension under 42AG(1)(a) will occur if a provider hasn't been able to make contact with a participant to speak about a potential work refusal failure. When they make contact, that's when the conversation and the determination about a valid reason will come in. The payment suspension itself precedes that discussion and that determination of a valid reason.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Customer Experience and Engagement

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Senator, if I can just add just a couple of things in that space. One of the things that we identified, one of the changes to the decision-making process and the IT system that was required so that the payments are only suspended once a decision-maker—we've changed that so they have to be satisfied that a work refusal failure had occurred based on evidence rather than thinking it may have occurred. So we have tightened up that process in our IT systems, and that formed part of the training that has also rolled out for staff of employment service providers. The other thing I'd say just in relation to safeguards or changes for participants is that we've also done a lot of work looking at and changing the notifications that participants receive in this process to try and make all of those decisions and the points where they are in a particular process much clearer.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: Acting Deputy Secretary, Employment and Workforce Group

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: I guess one of the things that occurs to me as I'm thinking through the requirements when you talk about making contact is that right now we're in a cost-of-living crisis. People on JobSeeker are getting around $400 a week. There's not a rental in the country, I think, that anyone on that income could afford. Is it not conceivable that we may have jobseekers in situations where they don't have credit for their internet or their phone and they can't afford public transport or fuel? How does someone make contact if their financial circumstances—and for most people on income support their dire financial circumstances—mean that they may not be able to and that this is in fact placing an obligation on them to do things that they otherwise can't afford even to make contact? I don't think that's a stretch to suggest that there are people in that situation. What happens in that situation? It would seem to me then that a suspension or a cancellation is actually going to exacerbate and potentially harm that person in circumstances where the very fact that they're being kept on a poverty payment makes meeting these requirements sometimes impossible.

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: What I can talk to is, as Ms Schofield referred to, the training that has been provided and the requirements that exist with a provider. When a participant fails to attend a compulsory appointment—and I note that that may be either in person or over the phone—the provider must attempt to contact the participant on the same day as the non-attendance. The contact attempt must be recorded before any non-attendance or non-compliance result can be recorded in the system, and they must record that on the same day of the requirement. Providers should also maintain evidence that demonstrates that the appointment was scheduled, that the participant did not attend, that on the same day an attempt was made to contact the participant and that the outcome of the contact attempt was recorded. So—
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Customer Experience and Engagement

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: If I have a mutual obligation and I have an appointment, say, tomorrow and I find myself unexpectedly in hospital, which is not foreseeable, it would seem to me that if a job service provider tried to contact me, couldn't contact me on the same day and put all those things in the system, I could be potentially subject to having my payment suspended or cancelled even though I have a valid reason, but, by virtue of the fact that I can't be contacted, I'm going to suffer a penalty. Is that a fair characterisation of what could occur?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Well, there are a range of circumstances that may occur. What I'm saying is the safeguards that are put in the system are that we're requiring employment service consultants to record and provide evidence of the attempts that have been made to contact a person.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Customer Experience and Engagement

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: If I may, also—
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Customer Experience and Engagement

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Yes, go.

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: What I'm struggling with is that I don't see how that's a safeguard. That's a safeguard to say that the employment service provider—

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Senator Allman-Payne, it's difficult when it's remote. Mr Bell was seeking to provide a response. Mr Bell, you have the call.

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: My apologies.

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Sorry. A couple of additional points I'd make is there are five days of resolution time from when a work refusal failure occurs before the payment suspension, so if you're unable to make that contact immediately, there are five days before the payment is suspended. The other point I'd just make is that, importantly, following the resumption of payment suspensions for work refusal failures, the department is going to be monitoring and reviewing every single one that comes through the system to make sure (1) that decision-making from providers is accurate and reflects the changes that we've made and (2) that the quality of the information and the evidence that they're submitting to the system is correct. If it's not, we'll be reaching out to the provider and, where relevant, lifting those suspensions or lifting those failures.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Customer Experience and Engagement

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Can I ask a question of the minister?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Go ahead, Senator Allman-Payne.

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: It seems to me that we are still having a situation where it's quite possible that people can't meet these connection obligations if they don't have sufficient funds either for transport or for phone or internet communication. Has the government considered that in terms of this framework? Because, if you're on $400 a week, we're literally asking people to either pay for transport that they otherwise wouldn't need or potentially be in situations where they don't have telecommunications. I'm interested to know if the government has a view on that.

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: At a threshold level, as you know, we think that some form of mutual obligations is important. More broadly, we are looking at how mutual obligations can be reformed so that they are of greater assistance to people in finding meaningful work and realistically finding work and ensuring that those mutual obligations apply to where people are today and what their distance from the labour market is right now. So there is a reform project there in relation to mutual obligations. The government also made some changes to the current system to try to provide some extra support—for example, increasing the length of time that people have to address any missed requirements from two days to five days before that suspension process may put their payments on hold. We also introduced a grace period for new participants before there are any impacts on their payment. Those who are, for example, new to Workforce Australia don't experience any compliance action the first time that they miss a requirement. There are a couple of other reforms to assist people as well. We recognise that people can be in difficult circumstances. We do think mutual obligations are important. We've made some changes to assist people now, but we're also doing the work to reform mutual obligations for the future.

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Senator Allman-Payne, we are due to rotate, so this will need to be your last question.

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Yes. To follow on from that, Minister, you've talked about mutual obligations helping people into work. There's very little evidence that shows that it does. Does the government accept that the biggest change that they could make that would actually help people be in a position to access work would be to increase the rate of JobSeeker and other income support payments to at least the poverty line, which would be an increase of about $300 a week for someone who's currently trying to survive on $400 a week?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: As you know, the minister gave a major speech at the National Press Club earlier this year, and she talked about putting in place reforms of the employment services system. That would be the biggest change in many decades, and those changes are designed to assist people into work. The minister and the government recognise that the system needs to be better, that the support for people needs to be better and that the obligations that are placed on them as part of the mutual obligations framework need to be more realistic and more targeted to where people are in terms of their distance from the labour market. So that's the shape, the form, that the minister is pursuing, and she is very much on the record as viewing work as an absolutely critical form of providing foundational support for people in their lives. She's talked a lot about the dignity of work and wanting to have an employment services system that delivers that dignity as well.

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Senator O'Sullivan, you have the call.

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: I want to return to the issue of the compliance framework, some of which has just been covered by Senator Allman-Payne. Thinking about the suspension, I'd like to understand what happened to jobseekers while those powers were paused.

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: While 42AG and 42AM were—
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: Acting Deputy Secretary, Employment and Workforce Group

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Yes.

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Essentially, while those provisions were paused, there were no decisions that were being taken in relation to those two. There are—and the secretary talked about this a little bit earlier as well—other mutual obligations requirements that exist within the legislative framework that remained in existence while these two provisions were paused, and, while the other four provisions are still paused, there are some mutual obligations that are still in the system. So people could not be suspended for a work refusal failure, because this provision was turned off, but suspensions were still active if there were failures on other mutual obligation requirements.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: Acting Deputy Secretary, Employment and Workforce Group

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: So the mutual obligations continued?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Yes
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: Acting Deputy Secretary, Employment and Workforce Group

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: But their payment suspension was lifted. Is that right? Have I got that right?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Payment suspensions have remained in place through this period, while there were other provisions within the Social Security (Administration) Act that had been paused. For the large part, suspensions occur under section 42AF(1), and payment suspensions can occur when a person has not met their mutual obligations requirement. That might be attending an appointment; it might be completing an activity. There are other parts of the system whereby a person could find that their payment was suspended. What was paused, particularly under section 42AM, was that suspension. If a person didn't reconnect, their payment could not be cancelled.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Customer Experience and Engagement

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Has any jobseeker permanently lost any payment for failing to meet a requirement?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Not while section 42AM was turned off, no.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Customer Experience and Engagement

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Services Australia procedures say that, during the pause—and I think this sort of goes to what you're saying here—DEWR restores payment after 20 days whether the person has met their reconnection requirement or not. What happens to their payment? Is it held back?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: When a suspension is lifted, it is back-paid to the day at which it was suspended.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Customer Experience and Engagement

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Not from when it's lifted—it's backdated to when it was first suspended.

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Exactly. It's back-paid to the point at which their last payment should have been made.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Customer Experience and Engagement

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: From 5 July 2025 until Monday, all TCF suspensions and cancellations for refusing suitable work were paused. In that time, what was the consequence for a jobseeker who refused a suitable job?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: During the time when that provision was paused, no decisions could be taken under that provision.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Customer Experience and Engagement

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: So a jobseeker could just keep continuing to refuse a suitable job in that period of time—maybe, potentially, multiple times?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: It meant that a person's payment couldn't be suspended or cancelled under that provision. There are other provisions under 42AF(1) whereby a person's payment can be suspended, but using that particular provision was not—
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Customer Experience and Engagement

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: But that's not a refusal of a suitable job.

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Mutual obligations.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Customer Experience and Engagement

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: But those other measures are not—

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: They are not about the work refusal. That's correct.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: Acting Deputy Secretary, Employment and Workforce Group

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: about refusing a suitable job. So, if someone in that period of time—from 5 July until just this Monday, which is more than 12 months—repeatedly refused to take up a suitable job, nothing would happen. There would be no consequence.

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: For that particular event, that would be correct. But, as we've said, there were a range of other mutual obligations that remained in place whilst this particular provision was not in place.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: Acting Deputy Secretary, Employment and Workforce Group

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Was data still collected on the jobseeker in that way if the service provider had recorded on your system that the person had refused a job over that period of time?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Senator, I'd have to take that on notice.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Customer Experience and Engagement

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Can you take that on notice and then come back to me with the numbers, of how many, if there were any.

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: If that was data that we collected during that time, yes, we can come back with that.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: Acting Deputy Secretary, Employment and Workforce Group

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Was it data that you would have been collecting before the suspension?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: It would have been collected whilst the provision was operational, so I would have to—
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: Acting Deputy Secretary, Employment and Workforce Group

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: So you just stopped—

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: have a look and see how much data we have whilst the provision was paused.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: Acting Deputy Secretary, Employment and Workforce Group

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: I would find that concerning—if, while it was paused, you'd actually stopped recording it.

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: I think the evidence is we need to check whether or not—
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: We'll just have to take on notice how much information we have.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: Acting Deputy Secretary, Employment and Workforce Group

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: In terms of compensation, on 19 October, Secretary, you said that the department had started inviting people to claim compensation in batches over the coming months.

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Yes.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: And I spoke about that. How much is going to be repaid?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text:
We'll need to go through that, of course, once we receive any applications for compensation. The way we've approached this is to focus in the first instance on cancellation decisions under 42AM. As I said in my statement earlier, we've proactively invited 50,652 people to apply for compensation. The way we identified those people was by using our own systems and the Services Australia systems to try and identify through data analytics those who were most likely to have suffered detriment through that period. So we're proactively going out.

We've also made it clear, though, that any current or former participant in the system who feels that they may have suffered detriment can of course put in an application. We won't know precisely how much we will be compensating until we start to see the claims. Of course, making a claim in and of itself isn't enough to prove that detriment has been caused. We will need to analyse those claims and make an assessment as to whether or not they are eligible for compensation under the CDDA.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Is it a contingent liability? How have you factored in the budget?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: There was money provided at last year's MYEFO to fund the compensation that we are in the process of administering at the moment. So that was a measure.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: How much was that?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: The measure in MYEFO was $43.9 million over four years from 2025-26. That funding, that $43.9 million, included some funding for compensation as well as funding to do the system works and other IT things that we've been talking about already this evening.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
