witness_position: Acting Deputy Secretary, Employment and Workforce Group

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Of the 50,000, has any been paid at all?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: We are in the process of inviting the 50,000 people. So far, we've sent 1,430 invitations. I don't know that we've received any—
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: We have now received 50 applications for compensation, but they have not started to be considered.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Customer Experience and Engagement

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: They haven't been paid yet. The Ombudsman reported 651 people identified for back payments, of whom 604 have been repaid. In August, the department said that 47 could not be paid for a range of reasons. Have you got that data there? What were the reasons?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Of the 47 people that the department could not contact, 41 were unable to be contacted to verify their bank details. Services Australia attempted to call each customer on five separate occasions. Services Australia could not send a letter as there was no way of verifying that the customer still resided at the address held on record, so that poses a privacy risk. Five people had passed away and did not have an executor or next of kin recorded. And one person had changed payment type after the penalty was applied and was already in receipt of income support payment for that period that had been cancelled, so they were effectively not eligible for compensation.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Customer Experience and Engagement

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Okay. Are the 651, not including maybe those 47, going to be invited to claim compensation, or will their back payment be counted against it?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Those 651 were part of the 42AF(2)(d) review and compensation process which the department carried out last year. In that compensation process we reviewed the circumstances of 964 people affected by that provision. We made those recommendations for the 651, and then we sought to contact the residual. The process has finished, but, of course, anyone can make a claim at any time under the scheme for compensation for detriment caused by defective administration.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Customer Experience and Engagement

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Were those people that you couldn't contact still in the system? Were they still being serviced by a service provider?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: I don't have that information, but I know that the mix of people was both those currently still in the system at the time of the review and those that had exited.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Customer Experience and Engagement

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Okay. In trying to contact them, did you go to their previous service provider or the one that was active at the time of their suspension and ask them if they knew? To what extent did you go down the different paths to find these people?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: We can only use the information we currently hold in the system, and that's both the department's system and Services Australia system. So we went through a process to identify the most appropriate contact details or the most recent contact details for the person.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Customer Experience and Engagement

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: You can't call the service provider and say, 'Hey, we've lost contact with this person. Would you know how we can—

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Those details would be held on our system.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Customer Experience and Engagement

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: They're the same. The contact details that a service provider would have and the contact details that the department would have is the same record.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: Acting Deputy Secretary, Employment and Workforce Group

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: But is it the job of the service provider to update the contact details in your system? They may have it in their own contact management system that would be separate to yours.

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Ideally not.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Customer Experience and Engagement

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: They shouldn't be.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: Acting Deputy Secretary, Employment and Workforce Group

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: They shouldn't be, right. They're not allowed to, with privacy.

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: They shouldn't be, because, if you are on our system and then you're through to Services Australia and you're having an income support payment made to you, that data should be held across systems.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Customer Experience and Engagement

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Yes. I've finished that block.

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: If so, I will rotate the call and then I'll come back to you. Just before I do, I can advise the committee that we're in a position to release Safe Work Australia. Thank you for your service. Senator Dolega.

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Good evening. I just want to get an update on the national call centre, please.

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: What would you like an update on?
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Customer Experience and Engagement

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: At last estimates, you may recall, I was asking about the investments into the department's call centre—in particular, the national customer service line. Can you give me an update on the recruitment of additional ongoing staff?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Sure. You're right; earlier this year, in the 2026-27 budget, the government announced it would invest $26.5 million over three years into the national customer service line to increase resourcing to support jobseekers and employers. This funding largely goes to increasing our service delivery capacity. We have commenced an external recruitment process for the national customer service line. Those advertisements went out on 31 July and closed on 17 August. We're in the process of reviewing those applications and that recruitment process, and we have an intention that letters of offer will be distributed around early December with a view to commence those staff in early February 2027.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Customer Experience and Engagement

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Thank you for that. I'd asked the department about the approximately 55 non-ongoing workers whose jobs were under a cloud. I was a tad cranky at the time—you may remember. Can you tell me what happened with those? Have they been invited to reapply?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: The last time we spoke, we had a number of non-ongoing staff in the contact centre. In terms of arrangements that we have made for non-ongoing and labour hire staff in the contact centre to apply, we have held workshops internally for staff to walk them through the recruitment process. Equally, we have retained the details of non-ongoing staff whose contracts have come to an end—with their permission obviously. Where they have expressed interest in being contacted when or should a recruitment round have opened, we've also been able to contact them and make sure they are aware that the recruitment process was open.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Customer Experience and Engagement

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Sorry, Ms Dewar, was that inclusive of the labour hire staff to have those same opportunities as well?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: All staff in the contact centre were offered the same opportunity to attend those training sessions.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Customer Experience and Engagement

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: What is happening with the uplift of the capacity of the staff in the National Customer Service Line? We were talking about that in the last round of estimates, as well.

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: There are probably a couple of things. The first task we have is to increase the capacity, get more people on board. However, at the same time, the minister's speech at the National Press Club, which has been referenced earlier, set out some ambitions for what the government would like the online service to be. That necessitates an uplift in capacity and capability of our contact centre staff. So we're going through a process of enhanced role-specific learning, building structured coaching, quality feedback, knowledge management and improved leadership development to help support those staff once they come on board to not only navigate the systems that we have but provide the type and style of service that the government is expecting.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Customer Experience and Engagement

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: In addition to the staff and people having more secure jobs as part of this uplift and this process, what's going to be the benefit for people who rely on the services of the department?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Again, the minister articulated the government's ambition for much more support for people in that online service. In the recruitment process we have gone through and are going through, we have been quite specific about the customer service experience that we are seeking. But the government is also expecting us to improve the experience of people going through the online service, and that is a mix of the experience they have when they call the Digital Services Contact Centre and the online tools that are available to them and the support that is given to them. We're going through that process at the moment.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Customer Experience and Engagement

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: As a result of these measures, it sounds like the department is really focusing the labour hire workforce on more of that surge capacity that you will need for those peaks and surges of work that will occur—with the recruitment of these ongoing staff.

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Labour hire staff and APS staff work alongside each other in the same roles. While we work through this process, everyone in the contact centre—at the same levels—does the same style of job, regardless of whether they are APS permanent, not-ongoing or labour hire. The focus though, as you've articulated, is very much about a permanent APS workforce to support the participants going through that online service.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Customer Experience and Engagement

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Thank you very much for that update. That's very good to hear. I want to ask, as well—I believe this might be for you, Ms Rishniw—about the employment services reforms. Now that the public consultation process inviting submissions has closed, can you provide an overview of the level of the responses that have been achieved and some of the key themes that are coming out of the process?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: As you mentioned, we had a public discussion paper that was launched on the same day as the minister's National Press Club address of 27 May. We took submissions until 31 July. There were a few organisations that had asked for an extension, which we allowed. All up, we received 348 submissions to that public discussion paper—266 from organisations and 82 from individuals. They have now been published. Where people have allowed for them to be published, we've published those on the website. A range of themes are coming through, very much supporting what the minister outlined in her speech, particularly looking at how we make mutual obligations more fit for purpose, reflective of people's circumstances, but closer to the demand and the labour market; how we provide quality services; how we build the relationship and a stronger understanding of the needs of employers and matching the participants in provider services; and how we provide more modern ways of people seeking support—really supportive of online digital kind of transformation pieces. They were some of the common themes, but I'm happy to elaborate.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Employment and Workforce Group

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: That's good to start off with, thanks. How are you going to engage to inform the design of the reformed employment system from here on in?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Obviously, with the submissions that have come in, we've done an initial analysis and picked up the key themes, but there are a range of other consultation mechanisms in the reform space. We also have an employment services expert advisory group that is providing advice to government and looking at those submissions but also key pieces of reform in that process. There have been various community forums led by Minister Rishworth and Assistant Minister Gorman. There have been 11 different community forums where people have been able to contribute. We're doing specific focus groups with First Nations communities, but we have also met with the First Nations advisory group, looking at how we build in that First Nations voice into those reform processes. That is, as I said, going in—the expert advisory group is considering those pieces, and that will form the basis of advice to government.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Employment and Workforce Group

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Finally, on the employment services, with the budget measures, how is the implementation with the budget measures associated with the reforms?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: There were a number of budget measures announced as part of the 202627 budget in May this year. There were $312 million of initial investments in some of those foundational pieces coming through. There's $26.5 million over the next three years to uplift the National Customer Service Line and make sure that we can meet the demand there but also much stronger investment in the capability and capacity of the department's support through online digital services. We heard very strongly the need to provide modern services that are actually looking at how we can help people online to do better career mapping and planning to get them the kind of support that they need early on and connect them to the labour market sooner. That included a digital advisory service for parents, and we're in the process of finalising those arrangements with Future Women. There's the Digital Services Contact Centre foundation—that ICT build—to really build in new modern tools and help our customer support centre and online services actually be able to have all of those tools at their fingertips. There's the frontline services uplift that Ms Dewar referred to, which is really a big staffing push. We're underway with the career-mapping tool, the engagement and the building of the broader business case for reform.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Employment and Workforce Group

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: I really wish you well in getting this up and running. I know a lot of people are really excited about the reforms to employment services. I look forward to hearing through future estimates as to how it all goes. Finally, I'll touch on the complaints service, if I may. I understand that there's been a new complaint service for employment services that was established just last year and a second complaints report has been released. Can you give me an overview of how the new complaints service is different from the previous settings?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text:
Yes, of course. The new complaint service came into effect on 31 October 2024. We're almost at our second birthday of that service. Prior to this service launching, if participants or jobseekers who were in our system had concerns or wanted to complain about the service that they were provided or any issues that they were experiencing, we directed them to their providers. We did require that providers have their own complaints handling process, but there wasn't really a mechanism for the department to be engaged and come in as a slightly independent third party to those discussions. This service is the first time that that's happened. So, yes, the service has been operational now for almost two years.

As you said, we've released the second complaints report. So we're putting out two reports a year. I'm pleased to say that the third one should be out quite soon. The second report that we released in September covered the period from 1 May 2025 until 31 October 2025. It flagged that there were—let me just get the numbers for you, Senator. In that six-month period, there were 6,500 complaints received. That was up ever so slightly from the six months before. The majority of those were about Workforce Australia services, which makes sense because a lot of the interactions that people have are with their service providers. I could go on, Senator, but if there are particular questions that you have on the—
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: Acting Deputy Secretary, Employment and Workforce Group

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: I have a bit more. I also want to get an idea of what proportion of the caseload it represents—those complaints in the second round?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: I have that number here somewhere, I think. The proportion of the caseload is a relatively small proportion. I'm just looking to find the number in my system. It's about one per cent or less of the complaints that we were receiving compared to the caseload. The caseload is about 750,000. So, in that six-month period, we received about 6,500 complaints. The numbers have been relatively steady across the period.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: Acting Deputy Secretary, Employment and Workforce Group

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Were there any particular cohorts that were overrepresented? How does that compare to the Workforce Australia caseload?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: That's an interesting question, Senator. It is one that we monitor. I think it's really important to see whether or not there are particular cohorts that feel like the services aren't really delivering to them in a way that is different to their proportion on the caseload. We track that across. We look at our First Nations participants. We look at the parents in our system. We look at culturally and linguistically diverse jobseekers and also people with a disability. Across those numbers, the proportion of complainants is essentially the same as the proportions that exist in the caseload. The only cohort where there was a bit of a difference was in people with a disability. When the service first started, the proportion of complainants was about 30 per cent, and they were about 26 per cent of the caseload. Those numbers have stabilised as the service has continued. At the moment, what we're seeing, in the data at least, is that complaints and caseload are at similar proportions for all of those key cohorts.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: Acting Deputy Secretary, Employment and Workforce Group

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Thank you. Finally, how will that data be used to improve the performance of Workforce Australia providers?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: There are a few things that we're doing. Obviously, we're publishing this information every six months, which is really helpful, so that it can be out there. We know that our providers look at that. Obviously, it's available for the public and for jobseekers to be able to see all of that data as well. Information around complaints now feeds directly inside the department, to all of our policy and program teams, so that they can see the sorts of issues that are coming up in their programs. We can have a look at different program settings and see whether or not there are issues in there that we can potentially amend or revise to see whether or not we can smooth out some of those issues. We've also enabled our staff inside the department who work directly with our providers, our provider leads, to also have access to that complaints data that they can see at a provider level. They can have those conversations as part of their contract management and part of their engagement so that they can really make sure that providers are clear about what it is that's causing issues and seek to make those improvements.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: Acting Deputy Secretary, Employment and Workforce Group

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: That's it for me. Thank you for the update today.

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Senator Hume.

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: I want to follow on from some of Senator Dolega's questions about the employment services reform. At the last hearing you told us that advice on the detailed settings, on the cost of the new system—which I think you have covered off on—and most importantly on how many people will be in each stream will go to the minister towards the end of this year or early next year. agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: That still remains the case. As you know, the minister in giving her speech talked about three streams of service, depending on the participant's distance from the labour market or their specific needs. Regarding the detailed design of the reforms, we're still putting together our advice to the minister and for the minister to provide to the cabinet. witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: In response to questions on notice in July, the department said that all Workforce Australia contracts are being extended to 31 October next year, not this year; however, I note that the department's annual procurement plan on AusTender, which was updated earlier this month, doesn't list any tenders for the new system. When will that go to market?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: The government has, as you've said, said that those contracts will be extended. We have provided that advice directly to all of the providers in the system. We've written to each of them to let them know that those extensions are coming. We have some briefing that is happening inside the department and with the minister at the moment to confirm some of the minor details about how those things will work. We'd expect to be in a position to have those contract extensions offered and all resolved by the end of this calendar year.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: Acting Deputy Secretary, Employment and Workforce Group

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: That's very helpful.

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Just to clarify, Senator, I think you said that the contracts are being extended through to 31 October next year. It's actually 31 October 2028.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Oh, I'm sorry; it is too. I want to ask for some clarity around how the department is confident about knowing where jobseekers live, which obviously will be part of the way that this new system is built. Am I right in saying that the department publishes small-area labour markets, unemployment estimates, for suburb sized areas? Is that what the department does? Do you publish that?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: I might need to take that on—I can feel someone coming up behind me, Senator!
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: Acting Deputy Secretary, Employment and Workforce Group

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Whenever you need a chief economist!
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Yes, we do publish a publication called Small Area Labour Markets. It combines information from the ABS labour-force survey together with administrative data from the Department of Social Services to estimate unemployment rates and other employment statistics at small geographical regions.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Your methodology says exactly that—you take the ABS, you share it by the number of JobSeeker and Youth Allowance recipients in each area, and you average it over four quarters. Is that right? Is that how it works?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Yes, we calculate it for each region, and then we average. We do that for local government areas and I believe SA2s—Australian statistical geography standard statistical area 2 areas.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: The latest issue, which was released earlier this month, is for the June quarter. Is that what the department's going to use to decide where support for jobseekers in the new intensive stream goes?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Obviously, it's too soon to say in terms of broader reform, but it will be one of the inputs that not only goes to where are the current jobseekers, what are the labour markets, where there are thin labour markets et cetera based on the advice from the chief economist but also looks at the data that comes through from Services Australia. We've talked about a new triaging and assessment process as well which will also look at the level of complex needs and barriers. So there's geography, but there's actually assessment of jobseeker needs, particularly around that intensity of support.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Employment and Workforce Group

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Alright. That assessment of jobseeker needs, where is the data? Where do you get that data from?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: As I've said, we've been working around, and it was announced in budget, an improved triaging and assessment process for jobseekers. At the moment we use the JobSeeker classification instrument as a means of looking at someone's history, someone's complexity, the kinds of barriers that they face, their history in terms of income support and the types of services we provide. The assessment and triage process will look at how do we better elicit some of that information about a person's circumstances, situation, other features that go to their need, their distance from the labour market and the kind of support that they will need.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Employment and Workforce Group

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Obviously, you're triaging already in the current system. How do you translate the current system of triaging to the new system?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: As I've described, at the moment, that assessment is done initially through the JobSeeker classification instrument, which people fill in at the time they seek income support. They go on JobSeeker. They fill in JobSeeker classification instrument. Your scoring of that depends on whether you would currently go into online services or provider services. Then there are different checks and balances in the system as you progress. For example, if you can't meet your mutual obligations for three months in a row, the provider will do a capability assessment at that point. If you've been unable to meet your mutual obligation requirements, at the moment, Services Australia does a much more intensive assessment to see whether your mutual obligations are right for you, whether you're getting the right supports or not. So there's already those kinds of ways of triaging and assessing someone. What we're looking at is a much more comprehensive way of looking at the JobSeeker classification instrument and enhancing that to better elicit some of those early indicators and test more broadly where people need support and their distance from the labour market.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Employment and Workforce Group

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: If you're staging out, if there are certain gateways of this project, do the triaging decisions and the approach that you take to that need to happen before you then establish where the new centres need to be?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: One of the things that we're currently doing is we've put out one of the budget decisions that actually looked at: how do you build out that triaging assessment instrument and what does that look like? We've got some expert advice through Ernst & Young actually doing some of that work around that triaging and assessment instrument and what that looks like in terms of testing it with jobseekers. That will obviously inform kind of how we build out that instrument and that will inform partly where you've got the current case load and how you actually look at stream-through services. So that work is underway is what I'm saying.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Employment and Workforce Group

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: [inaudible] including geography, right—where you're placing centres.

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Yes, it will absolutely, and it looks at distance from the labour market.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Employment and Workforce Group

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: If I could just add, where this will become really relevant will be—you asked a question: will we rely on the June data to inform essentially the services that will be provided as a result of the reforms—when we get to the procurement process, which is not until midway through next year. It will be at that point.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: That was my next question. When you get to the procurement process, that will be—you said—midway through next year?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: The middle of next year will be when we have the latest data on all of these things that Mr Cowgill talked about—the processes that we go through for that data, both the administrative data and the ABS data. We'll get more data reads before that which will then inform the procurement process.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: So this year the department cut its exact monthly case load down to quarterly. The best local data that the public gets is modelled by your own guidance. Is it lagging? Is that what you're saying—that the June data is already lagging, so it's going to be inadequate for building out that model? Sorry, have I missed something here? I'm not expressing myself very well. It is getting late.

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: I think I understand what you're saying, Senator. Mr Cowgill will be able to tell us whether or not there will be updates before we get to that procurement process by the middle of next year.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Yes. That Small area labour markets publication you're referring to is released quarterly. So, between now and the procurement process that Mr Duggan has described, there will be several further updates to that publication publicly released. One additional point I would note is that the ABS is releasing labour force information at a more detailed—so more granular—geographic level. It is planning very soon to start releasing at the statistical area 3 level, which is more detailed than the SA4 level it releases currently, and it has announced plans to explore going to the SA2 level, which is what we publish in Small area labour markets.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Still quarterly or monthly, though?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: I believe that is monthly, but I will need to take that on notice to confirm. The ABS regional data—I believe it is monthly, but I'll take it on notice to confirm.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: The department already knows where every Workforce Australia participant lives. I'm wondering whether you will publish the case load each quarter by SA2 but also perhaps by federal electorate.

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: I would note that, with regard to the Small area labour markets publication that we release now, we don't calculate that by electorate, but we do provide the data to the Parliamentary Library, and they calculate—
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: They can do that.

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: the unemployment rates and so on by electorate. So that's something that the Parliamentary Library does, using the data that we provide to them.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Thank you for that. I have some more questions, but they're on a different topic. I'm not entirely sure whether you want to let me continue on, Chair.

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: We'll wait for you to get to skills.

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Yes, that's fine. I want to ask about some of the Workforce Australia low-performing providers specifically. Bear with me on this one because I might have to step it through a bit. The department rates every provider licence each quarter as high, moderate or low, and low, as I understand it, is defined as not meeting the department's expectations. In June 2026, the ratings published on 27 August put 22 providers of the 169 licences out there as low. Is that right? Does that sound right?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: I'm not sure that I have that data with me. Let me check if one of my colleagues has. I might need to take that on notice.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: Acting Deputy Secretary, Employment and Workforce Group

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Check the data and allow me to continue on. The data that I have suggests that it is 22. Of those 22, 15 are rated 'low' on sustained employment, which is the part of your framework that measures whether people not just get jobs but keep jobs, and four have been rated 'low' for five quarters in a row, which is quite significant. In July, the department said that Workforce Australia contracts are being extended to October 2028, as we've already discussed. Has every one of those 22 had their contract extended to October 2028, even the ones that haven't performed for five quarters in a row?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: I'll just go back and revisit the testimony that I gave previously. One of the things that I said was that we're just in the process of finalising some internal and other briefings around the way that we're going to do those extensions across all of the programs that are being extended out until October 2028. That's Workforce Australia services, Transition to Work—there are a range of programs that are going through that process. One of the things that we have looked at when we're looking at those extensions and that is currently being considered is provider performance. It's being considered now as to whether or not all contracts are extended as is, whether or not there are some providers who need to be put on what we refer to as performance improvement plans, or PIPs. We have used those quite successfully over the past 12 months or so to really help providers to improve their performance. At this point, I can't say whether those particular providers will have extensions for that full period of time, whether they may have a performance improvement plan put in place or whether they will be offered an extension, because, as I said, those considerations are being done almost as we speak.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: Acting Deputy Secretary, Employment and Workforce Group

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: In answer to a question on notice, the department said that 14 licences were extended last year on those performance conditions. I assume that they were PIPs?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Yes.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: Acting Deputy Secretary, Employment and Workforce Group

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: By 31 March, only two of them had improved; 12 were still on PIPs. How many of the 12 have improved since, and what happens if a provider is still rated low in a year's time?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: I might have to take on notice how many of the 12 have improved; I just don't have that detail in front of me, I'm very sorry. I also can't say how many of them, off the back of that, may then have a contract in place in 12 months time—noting that, as I said, we are working through right now how we will work with providers on the extensions beyond the end of June next year.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: Acting Deputy Secretary, Employment and Workforce Group

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Okay. If these providers are kept on, what you're saying is that poor-performing providers will potentially continue to provide services, albeit poorly, until this decision is made, or until after October 2028. Is that right? Is that what I'm hearing?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Providers are on contract right now, and those contracts run through until the end of June next year.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: Acting Deputy Secretary, Employment and Workforce Group

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: June next year?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Yes. So June 2027 is when the contracts are in place until, right now. We are then considering the extension from July 2027 through until October 2028; that's the extension period that we are talking about. There have been providers, as we have said before, as you mentioned and as I talked about, who, right now, are subject to performance improvement plans. We are, right now, looking at how those providers have responded to those performance improvement plans. That is one of the things that we are thinking about as to whether or not providers get an extension from 1 July next year through until October 2028. Does that help?
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: Acting Deputy Secretary, Employment and Workforce Group

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text:
Yes, absolutely. I think there are a lot of providers out there that are pretty sure that that extension provided to them was going to be offered to them automatically and there wasn't a deadline date at the end of June next year. But that's okay. That's for you to communicate, not for me.

I want to step through the department's headline measure for Workforce Australia, the 26-week employment outcome rate. In rough terms, this outcome rate is the share of participants who get a job and are still in that job six months later—is that correct?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: That's correct.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: Acting Deputy Secretary, Employment and Workforce Group

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: And the target is 15 per cent?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Yes.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: Acting Deputy Secretary, Employment and Workforce Group

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: That is kind of low, isn't it? The 2024-25 annual report at page 36 says that it was 13.2 per cent in 2023-24, it was 11.7 per cent in 2024-25 and it has not been achieved since it was first reported. The 2026-27 corporate plan at page 45 now calls 15 per cent a 'stretch target'. Golly! If 15 per cent is the 'stretch', what's the minimum acceptable rate?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: I should say that the current data that we have for the 12-month period to 31 May 2026 is sitting at 12.9 per cent. So it's still not meeting that 15 per cent target that has been in place for the program. I think we have put this on record at previous estimates hearings: we agree that that 12.9 per cent, as it is now, is—and the other numbers that you have mentioned were—not high enough and should be higher. The language around a 'stretch target' came as a result of us working through and looking at what the data have told us over the last few years and that obviously, as you've read out, that 15 per cent hasn't been met. I'm happy, obviously, for Ms Rishniw to chime in, but it is really one of the things that is driving the way that we're thinking about reform and thinking about: What are the types of services that need to be offered? What are the sorts of incentives that need to be in the system for both participants and providers to increase that number? The government is very clear that getting secure work—having those jobs that last for at least six months—is really what we want to be striving for in the system. We know, through other data that we have, that, if someone's in that job for six months, they're quite likely to hold that for two years or more following that. We agree that it's a really key thing for us that we want to continue to see improve, and that's really what's driving a range of decisions that are being taken around the way that we run our programs now. We've made some changes to that performance framework for providers that you were talking about before to really start to try to move them more in that direction and incentivise the sorts of behaviours that we think will help to get more jobseekers into those longer term jobs, but the minister, in her speeches, has made it clear that this is where we need to do some work.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: Acting Deputy Secretary, Employment and Workforce Group

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: I know that she said this isn't good enough, but she hasn't said what the minimum is. What's the minimum, in your mind?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: I'm not sure that I would sit here and speculate on a number that we would necessarily pick. One of the things that we need to think through in reform is what the things we want to measure are, noting that we're really keen to have—and the minister has been really clear about this—more personalised and tailored supports. What are the sorts of things that we want to incentivise, and how do we measure that progress for a person as they're on their way to get a job? That's not to say we won't measure this as one of the things that we want to keep an eye on going forward, but I think that there are other things that we need to measure and report on to see how well we're tracking with the way we want to potentially restructure the programs.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: Acting Deputy Secretary, Employment and Workforce Group

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: If I can come in there, Ms Schofield has just articulated that this is one of the big, driving pieces of reform. One of the things that we've heard consistently in the consultations and the feedback is how to strengthen the understanding and relationship with employers and how we actually look at creating a system and embedded matching of jobseekers with employers and an understanding of employer needs. We will continue to strive to meet the current targets while we reform the system.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Employment and Workforce Group

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: The current targets say that 15 per cent is a stretch target. We're just being very clear: there is no minimum and no floor at which we say, 'We've failed here.'

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: We've got a 15 per cent target that we'll continue to try and meet. We said that, as you mentioned, in our corporate plan, we'll continue to report on that through the PBS and our annual report, and we'll continue to make changes and try to get us to that or beyond it, if we can. I think that will need us to think about and make the structural changes that we're thinking about in the process of reform.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: Acting Deputy Secretary, Employment and Workforce Group

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Is the figure of 15 per cent just for that cohort or across the entire caseload of jobseekers in the system?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: It's for the caseload who are in the Workforce Australia services component—those jobseekers who are serviced by an employment services provider, that cohort.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: Acting Deputy Secretary, Employment and Workforce Group

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: On notice, can you come back to us with the retention rate across the different caseloads?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: The six-monthly employment outcomes—
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: Acting Deputy Secretary, Employment and Workforce Group

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: People in the online system.

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Happy to do that.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: Acting Deputy Secretary, Employment and Workforce Group

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: The portfolio budget statement says that you've made refinements to how that 26-week rate is calculated. Can you tell me what those refinements are?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: It was a relatively minor methodology change. We made the change to try and have a bit more confidence in the numbers. We weren't capturing all of the outcomes because of various lags in data. There were some 26-week outcomes that were just happening outside the right timeframes and weren't being captured, so we changed the methodology. We had to be able to capture a much truer sense of the 26-week outcomes that are relevant for this measurement. It did not have a significant impact on the number in the first instance.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: Acting Deputy Secretary, Employment and Workforce Group

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Can I be clear, then. Are both the 12.7 per cent in the budget papers and the 12.9 per cent figure that you provided on the newly refined method? Is that correct?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Yes, that's correct, the PBS and this number are on the same methodology, just with different end dates.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: Acting Deputy Secretary, Employment and Workforce Group

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: But 2024-25 number would have been on the old method?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: That's correct.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: Acting Deputy Secretary, Employment and Workforce Group

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Thank you.

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: I note we are breaking in seven minutes. Senator Allman-Payne.

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Is the department aware of the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare's report titled Mortality outcomes among people receiving income support?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Yes.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: Acting Deputy Secretary, Employment and Workforce Group

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Has that report been circulated amongst staff such as policy or compliance teams?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: The report is public, so it would be available for anybody that wished to look at it.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: Acting Deputy Secretary, Employment and Workforce Group

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: The department doesn't proactively share that sort of information with its teams?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: I'm aware that a number of staff in the department are aware of it because of the work that we do with the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare. I can take it on notice, but, no, I'm not aware that that was circulated more broadly to staff.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: Acting Deputy Secretary, Employment and Workforce Group

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Is the minister aware of the contents of that report?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: As the minister representing the minister, I'd have to take it on notice to provide that information.

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: I can say that we haven't briefed Minister Rishworth on this report. It's a report from the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare. If you've got questions about how that report is engaged with at the ministerial level, they may be best directed either to AIHW or to Health.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: Acting Deputy Secretary, Employment and Workforce Group

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Is the department aware that that report says that jobseekers aged between 35 and 44 years old are dying at 9.6 times the rate of people who are not on JobSeeker?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: As I said, we're aware of the content of the report. We know that this report is consistent with other literature in that, on average, people receiving income support do have poorer physical and mental health outcomes than people not receiving income support. Importantly, though, the report does make clear that the analysis does not examine, nor does it provide, evidence of a causal relationship between receiving income support payment and subsequent death.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: Acting Deputy Secretary, Employment and Workforce Group

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Minister, this is a question for you. If people living in poverty are 9.6 times more likely to die, is that of concern to the government?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: We look at the payments that are provided and increase them where we can. We know how important it is for people to be able to live an adequate, decent life on these payments. It's why we've increased JobSeeker by $4,700 a year over our time in office. It's why we've boosted rent assistance by 53 per cent. Those are really important improvements that we've made to the safety net. We know that there's always more to do to help people have better, more adequate incomes that help them lead a decent life, and we try to make those improvements where we can in the budget.

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: We've got the Reserve Bank saying that we need to have an unemployment rate of around four per cent structurally baked into our system to make our economy work. We've had evidence this evening that the success rate for mutual obligations through the Targeted Compliance Framework of getting people into work is below 15 per cent. Would it not be a better spend of this government, rather than spending hundreds of millions of dollars pumping money into the profits of big, for-profit job service providers, to abolish this system, which is not working, and give that money to people living in poverty as a significant increase in income support to lift them out of poverty, which all the evidence tells us is the best way to help people get a job, if they are able to work?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text:
The government is committed to creating jobs. One point three million jobs have been created on this government's watch. We're committed to settings in our economy where unemployment is as low as it possibly can be. Under our government, unemployment is the lowest on average that it's been in 50 years. We are committed to improving payments for jobseekers and other people who are on social security payments, where we can and where the budget gives space to do that. We've increased JobSeeker by over $4½ thousand in our two terms of government and rent assistance by 53 per cent.

We know that this system can work better to support people to find work. That's exactly what we've been talking about tonight. We're working with the department to do that on the current settings, as well as engaging in the reform that is needed for the future to give people the best chance of finding work and having the security and dignity that work provides.

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Yet we still have people dying at 9.6 times the rate of someone not on income support. I have no further questions, Chair.
