text: Sure. Yes. The committee suspends.

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: I'm able to advise with apologies that the National Centre for Vocational Education and Research are able to depart. The questions to you will be placed on notice. I hope that's good news, not disappointing news, for you. We'll continue in this outcome. Senator Nampijinpa Price?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: We spent some time during the June budget estimates hearing on Labor's $266.2 million in cuts to Australian apprenticeship incentives, whereby from January 2027 the Key Apprenticeship Program employer incentive will be reduced by $1,000 for small businesses and removed altogether for larger businesses. I'm interested to know what specific advice the department provided to the government to justify the $1,000 cut to the Key Apprenticeship Program employer incentive for small businesses.

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: The department as a first basis relied on the Strategic Review into Australian Apprenticeship Incentives, which found that particularly for larger businesses there was a greater level of capacity or less influence by the incentive in terms of influencing their hiring decisions for apprentices. The other consideration was our mapping, particularly in those priority occupations and particularly in construction. Ninety-eight per cent of the construction employers in the apprenticeship system are SMEs. That was another factor that went into the policy analysis that supported the decision-making.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Skills and Training Group

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: To reduce it then for small businesses—that was the justification behind that for small businesses. Can you point to any economic circumstances that indicate a reduction to the employer incentive that is justified from January 2027.

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: In the context of a constrained fiscal environment, the government made a decision to target and sharpen the focus of incentives to SMEs, to priority occupations and also to the Key Apprenticeship Program, which focuses on construction and net zero. That was a decision that was made in the context of a tightening fiscal environment and supported by evidence that indicated that small to medium enterprises feel the benefit of incentives. Large enterprises have more capacity. Particularly in construction, where there's such a majority, SMEs are the main employers of apprentices.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Skills and Training Group

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: I suppose, though, that any small business in this country will tell you that the cost of doing business is getting pretty tough. Having to find an extra $1,000 per apprentice is certainly going to make things harder, isn't it?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: I totally appreciate what you're saying in the context of SMEs. From 1 January, SMEs who are participating in the Key Apprenticeship Program will have access to $4,000 per apprentice and SMEs that are participating with a priority occupation will have access to $2,500 per apprentice. That's in addition to other loans and support—supports for apprentices with disability. All payments to date will be grandfathered as well, so if you've got apprentices that are currently in the system there will be a grandfathering of all of those payments.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Skills and Training Group

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: We also heard which industries will see the greatest reduction in support as a result of these apprenticeship incentive cuts, and the department's advice was that everything on the priority occupation list from manufacturing through to trades will be affected. Did the department undertake any analysis or modelling of the number of affected apprentices in each priority occupation?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: We look at our historic data, and we do use that as a proxy to do modelling of impact. So, yes, we would have done modelling to understand the projected impact based on our historic data.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Skills and Training Group

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Are you able to provide the modelling that this relies upon, that the decision is relied upon?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: What I would also say, though, is that our analysis is also underpinned by a policy discussion around the various factors that influence the apprenticeship system—the employers and the apprentices' decisions. Those factors include the macroeconomic factors such as unemployment levels. It includes terms and conditions. It includes culture within the workplace. It includes career choices and—
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Skills and Training Group

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Are you able to provide that on notice, what you've described?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: We can take that on notice.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Skills and Training Group

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Thank you. In June, the department estimated the number of affected large businesses to be 1,800. How many apprentices and trainees did those 1,800 businesses take on in 2025, and how many does the department expect them to take on in 2027?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Based on the time that the decision was made, the data showed that, of those employers that you mentioned, there were around 20,635 commencements that were related to those businesses. As Ms Faithfull has pointed out, it's difficult for us to extrapolate what that will turn into in terms of future commencements. But I would say that we did rely heavily on research that showed that, during the BAC and CAC period, large businesses were relatively unresponsive to the incentives and that a significant proportion of the incentives were being used by small and medium businesses—98 per cent and 95 per cent, respectively—to take on new workers as opposed to 29 per cent for large businesses. I guess what I'm saying is you won't see an equal reduction in employers taking on apprentices as a result of incentives, because we know they're relatively inelastic to the use of them.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: Acting First Assistant Secretary, Apprenticeships, Industry and Workforce

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: So we'll just have to wait until we get to that point in time to receive that data.

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Yes.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: Acting First Assistant Secretary, Apprenticeships, Industry and Workforce

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Can the department provide an update on the recruitment of the government's proposed skilled migration commissioner?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Certainly. The budget decision was for the government to scope and consider options on whether to establish a skills commissioner. What I would say is that the government hasn't made a decision as to whether or not it will establish a skills commissioner. It's at the beginning of a process to consult on why you might have a skills commissioner, what those options would look like, what the functions might be and what problems you're trying to solve by establishing this role.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Skills and Training Group

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: During the last estimates hearing I did raise concerns about the function of this commissioner and what it would serve, given the obvious potential for duplication in this role. You were consulting back then. You're still consulting. We were told this would be worked through. So a position description hasn't been created for the role yet or a list of duties or anything like that?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: No.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Skills and Training Group

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: When will a decision be made?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Currently, we're consulting with the states and territories. That's given the complexity of the system and, in particular, the role of the states and territories in local responses to supporting migrants into work, and also the nexus of this work with the Treasurer's link to the Council on Federal Financial Relations. Through the treasurers, we're just undertaking that consultation at the state and territory level. From there we'll work out the next phase of consultation in terms of—
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Skills and Training Group

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: So there's no firm date as yet?

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: No firm date, no.
witness_organisation: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Skills and Training Group

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Okay. I'm happy to rotate the call.

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: I think we're in a position where we can move on then.

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: Yes, we can move on.

agency: Department of Employment and Workplace Relations
text: In that case, thank you to officials from outcome 2, you're free to depart.

agency: Comcare
text: I call officers from Comcare, including its Chief Executive Officer, Mr Colin Radford. Welcome to you, and do you have an opening statement this evening?

agency: Comcare
text: No, Chair.
witness_organisation: Jobs and Skills Australia

agency: Comcare
text: Thank you. Senator Sheldon, you have the call.

agency: Comcare
text: Thanks very much. I think a document has been circulated regarding Cleanaway?

agency: Comcare
text: Yes, there has.
witness_organisation: Jobs and Skills Australia

agency: Comcare
text: I'll get to that document in a moment. I just want to ask some serious questions. Cleanaway is of course a self-insured licensee in the Comcare scheme. In my view, it has certainly become one of Australia's worst offenders when it comes to workplace safety. Are you aware that eight Cleanaway workers have been killed at work since the middle of 2022?

agency: Comcare
text: I'm aware of six in the last two years, but that could be correct so I'm not disputing that.
witness_organisation: Jobs and Skills Australia

agency: Comcare
text: Are you aware that there's been a series of serious injuries that's occurred as well?

agency: Comcare
text: Yes.
witness_organisation: Jobs and Skills Australia

agency: Comcare
text: I take it that you're aware that undertakings were given on 13 March 2025 by Cleanaway to deliver safety measures after prosecutions. I congratulate Comcare for the work in this space. The national waste management company Cleanaway has been fined a recorded $1.1 million for breaching federal work safety laws over an Adelaide truck crash that killed two motorists. It was a horrific fatality, with two lives lost. In the equation of accountability financially, that's a lot of money in a court sense, but no amount of money—and certainly that amount of money doesn't—can compensate or make people accountable when two lives are lost in the way that they were lost. But I also give credit to Comcare for getting an undertaking from Cleanaway that they would spend $900,000 on safety measures across their national operations following the incident that caused serious injuries to a Canberra worker. Are you aware of that, Mr Radford, or maybe one of your team?

agency: Comcare
text: I think that may pre-date my time at Comcare.
witness_organisation: Jobs and Skills Australia

agency: Comcare
text: Maybe one of your team could help on both the eight people killed since mid-2022—I might add that more people died at that company prior to that—and the undertaking that was given by Cleanaway on the amount of money I mentioned, $900,000, to train.

agency: Comcare
text: That's correct. Comcare accepted an undertaking on 20 February 2025 as an alternative to continuing prosecution proceedings in relation to that incident at the Cleanaway facility in the ACT where a worker sustained serious injuries when his hand came into contact with an unguarded cardboard baling machine. That undertaking remains ongoing.
witness_organisation: Jobs and Skills Australia

agency: Comcare
text: Can I just go to the document that we've circulated. There is an exhaustive list of examples. I'm aware that Comcare received these in May of this year following inspections. This document was received by Cleanaway in May this year. This document I'm giving to you is the same document that you received in May. I gave it to you prior to this hearing. I'm just going to touch on some of the contraventions. There were blood sample vials on the floor and blood samples full of coagulated blood scattered on the floor. Cleanaway, for those that aren't aware, is a waste company. It's a large national operator. It has responsibility for collecting waste from high-risk, high-biohazard areas—hospitals et cetera. So you've got blood spilled and vials broken all over the floor. There's a series of photos which you can see on page 12. You're nodding your head. I'm taking it, Mr Radford, that you're seeing those?

agency: Comcare
text: Yes.
witness_organisation: Jobs and Skills Australia

agency: Comcare
text:
There are photos of blood splatter and broken vials. There are so many pages here. I think it's appropriate that I show the gravity of what's going on. I'll just touch on some of them. There are many, many that I'm not including. On page 17, it shows pallets of used scrubs stored in the yard and undeclared biological waste in black bags in the yard. The bags are overflowing. Some of them are broken open. The scrubs are visible. The scrubs are caked in dried blood. They had a distinct, offensive and prominent odour. This was at another site. This is not the same site. On page 18, at other sites again, biological waste bins were filthy, with no adequate safe disposal. There was a distinct, offensive and prominent odour. Some bins were marked as containing toxic waste. For those that may be listening, there are pictures of bins stacked on top of each other. They're like wheelie bins at home, but these have toxic biological waste in them. They're stacked on top of each other. So someone's lifted a wheelie bin on top of another wheelie bin with toxic waste, and they're sitting in the middle of the yard. The photo certainly gives the impression that there are a considerable number of those bins scattered through quite a large area within the facility that are double-stacked.

There's another photo on page 19—scattered syringes, clinical waste photos, flammable liquid bins stacked on top of each other. There are similar photos right up until I get to page 28. There are spill test kits, out of date, on page 28. This is yet another site. The fire extinguishers—there's flammable material in there—are missing test tags. Again, I'll jump a number of pages, not because there aren't a number of horrific examples I could give but because there are so many that I'm just highlighting a few horrendous ones. The obvious thing—for those of us that have a basic understanding of safety access, on page 31, those photos show access to fire hoses blocked, and access to the fire hose in one of the warehouses is blocked by rubbish and debris on the floor. Again, this is a separate site. Going to other instances of barrels and bins, on page 32—stored in front of roller doors and emergency exit doors. The list does go on and on and on. This is a company that gave an undertaking on 13 March 2025 not only to Comcare but importantly to the courts, and we have this series of deaths that has occurred. Where are they at, and what other prosecutions either is Comcare investigating or are underway at the moment against Cleanaway from Comcare?

agency: Comcare
text: Thank you for providing the report and for taking the time to step through some of those very concerning issues that you have raised. Cleanaway is currently the subject of a national regulatory program by Comcare which involves a series of focused inspections of Cleanaway sites—primarily unannounced inspections. We have six active investigations on foot at the moment into potential contraventions of the Work Health and Safety Act. Between September of last year and 31 August this year we've commenced 113 monitoring compliance activities, which include 94 inspections and four criminal investigations. We've conducted approximately 82 site visits in that time, and we've issued 34 enforcement notices over that period. There is one current prosecution underway that's currently before the courts, which relates to a fatality at the Lucas Heights facility. Beyond that program, we also have—and I'll ask my colleague Mr Napier to provide a bit more detail—a series of regulatory programs where we target particular PCBUs or employers where we are concerned about their health and safety performance, and Cleanaway is the subject of such a regulatory program commencing this financial year.
witness_organisation: Jobs and Skills Australia

agency: Comcare
text: Before you go to Mr Napier, thank you for commenting on the seriousness of these actions. What I find particularly galling is everything that led up to the undertaking—but the fact that this investigation, where I went through that non-exhaustive but long list of examples and photographic evidence, even after the undertakings, well over 12 months afterwards, if anything, it appears to me from the evidence that I've received that it's worse than it was before, which is absolutely frightening.

agency: Comcare
text:
As Mr Radford said, we do have a dedicated regulatory program in addition to the reactive work that we undertake as and when matters are notified to us as the regulator. That program was instituted because of our concerns with safety generally across Cleanaway's operations, and that program involves a large number of unannounced site visits. We have drawn on some of the information that you've discussed earlier to inform the scope of those activities. We are concerned about Cleanaway's safety performance and we have been for some time. With that in mind, we want to engage across workplaces—Cleanaway, as I'm sure you know, has many sites across Australia. Our concern is that safety is not being consistently managed across those sites. With that in mind, we've designed a program which involves a range of unannounced visits and, where necessary, notices being issued to assess their compliance broadly across aspects of the business.

We've mentioned, for instance, the interaction of people and plant—so part of the focus is on high-risk plant, including the interaction with mobile plant and people. Vehicle interactions and traffic management planning are a concern, and that's the focus of this regulatory program. Management of hazardous chemicals—and you've made some references to some very poor behaviour and practice in that place. Contractor labour hire arrangements are in scope including consultation, supervision and coordination of activities and, importantly, engagement and consultation arrangements with workers and HSRs. We're concerned to know what officer due diligence duties Cleanaway is exercising. At the senior levels across the organisation, at board and management, are they taking account of these concerning incidents, and what steps are they putting in place to address them across the network of sites? So it's quite a comprehensive program.
witness_organisation: Jobs and Skills Australia

agency: Comcare
text:
Can I ask a follow-up question, on indulgence. I've previously spoken about Cleanaway's performance from an environmental perspective in my home state of Queensland and the issues that have been caused there, and I'm deeply shocked by the photographs which I saw in the TWU's report, especially the biological hazardous material. That's just shocking. Their chair said in their last annual report, in 2026, that they'd conducted an independent safety review. They said:

The review did not identify evidence of a systemic failure in strategy design, governance or organisational commitment to safety. The review identified opportunities to enhance consistency and feedback mechanisms closer to frontline operations.

How does that marry with what Comcare is seeing, and has anyone had engagement with the chair of the board of directors or the chief executive officer and the managing director of Cleanaway, because there seems to be an absolute disconnect between what the chair has said in their last annual report and what we've just seen in the photographs in the TWU report? I believe the shareholders would be absolutely shocked and dismayed at that disconnect.

agency: Comcare
text:
It certainly doesn't accord with our observations of Cleanaway and it certainly doesn't represent a situation where, as I mentioned earlier, we've issued 34 enforcement notices in the last 12 months alone. That does not, certainly in my view, demonstrate a clear health and safety system across the business. As I said, we've issued 34 enforcement notices. Cleanaway is the subject of a national regulatory program, and that work is continuing. In terms of the engagement with the senior officers, as Mr Napier said, part of our regulatory program is looking at officer due diligence within the company. As you would be aware, senators, officers have significant personal liabilities and duties under work health and safety laws, and we're examining Cleanaway's performance in relation to those duties.

In terms of engagement, senators may or may not be aware that self-insured licensees sit broadly within the remit of the Safety, Rehabilitation and Compensation Commission. We regulate 29 out of the 39 self-insured licensees from a work health and safety point of view. We don't regulate them all, but Cleanaway is one that we do regulate in terms of their performance and, for want of a better term, their fitness to retain their self-insurance licence that sits with the SRCC. Earlier this year—I'll correct the record if I get this wrong, but I think it was in March of this year—the chair and the CEO were called before the SRCC essentially to explain themselves. I did not attend that meeting, for the reasons that we had regulatory and a prosecution on foot. I didn't think it was appropriate as CEO and the regulator under the act to engage in that conversation when they were meeting with the SRCC.
witness_organisation: Jobs and Skills Australia

agency: Comcare
text: I'll certainly be going through the annual report and sustainability report to see if they mention that engagement. I want to commend Senator Sheldon for raising these issues and commend the TWU, actually, for the important work they've done in terms of that report.

agency: Comcare
text: Thank you. I'll pass it on. I think your question highlights the fact that, at 26 February 2026, as reported in the AFR from an external review, they said there was no systemic failures in the area of occupational safety and the eight deaths and more generally. I'm going to take this because it raises serious questions about a participating member of this committee, and I'll certainly be participating until the end of this subject matter over the coming months and year—and years if it takes them. One of the things I'll be putting very strongly to the committee is that there should be consideration given to the Safety, Rehabilitation and Compensation Commissioner appearing here. They are the ones that consider—correct me if I've got this wrong, Mr Radford. It says it will generally consider suspending or revoking a self-insurance licence only where there are serious or systemic failures or where a licensee has resisted or failed to achieve compliance. Since 2021, eight workers have lost their lives, as we've said. The penalty, of course, is $1.1 million. The undertakings, certainly from the evidence before you—as I understand, the charges that have been pursued by Comcare since the breaches of the undertakings in 2025. At some point there will be repeated fatalities or a serious, horrific injury. Has Comcare raised Cleanaway's safety record with the Safety, Rehabilitation and Compensation Commission for consideration as a self-insurance licence issue? I foreshadow that they're going to have to be here.

agency: Comcare
text: Thank you. I don't want to speak on behalf of the SRCC, but the SRCC does receive regular reports on the licensees on a range of issues, including their health and safety performance. As I said, I don't want to speak on behalf of the SRCC, but certainly, when I have been present at SRCC meetings, they have raised concerns about Cleanaway's work, health and safety performance.
witness_organisation: Jobs and Skills Australia

agency: Comcare
text: Thank you. We've got eight workplace deaths and what I understand is the largest penalty in history of the act, at $1.1 million.

agency: Comcare
text: That's correct.
witness_organisation: Jobs and Skills Australia

agency: Comcare
text: Is that not enough to trigger the consideration of a licence suspension or revocation? Is there a role that Comcare plays regarding raising consideration by them? Obviously, they have to make the decision, but is it part of the remit of Comcare—you might explain this to the committee—to make recommendations for serious consideration whilst it's being dealt with by that commission?

agency: Comcare
text: Comcare provides secretarial support to the commission. We're required to do that under the legislation. We also provide information that is asked for from the commission. I'm going to turn to my deputy down the end, who's more familiar with the interaction between the legislation and the role of the SRCC, but I don't believe we've ever made a licence recommendation, because it is not our role under the act to do that.
witness_organisation: Jobs and Skills Australia

agency: Comcare
text: I take it that you've also flagged to the commission the concerns of Cleanaway, as you said in your earlier evidence?

agency: Comcare
text: Yes. And the commission has also raised those concerns directly with Cleanaway.
witness_organisation: Jobs and Skills Australia

agency: Comcare
text: The role of Comcare, as the CEO described, is one where we provide administrative support and secretarial support. The commission itself has set out a broad framework of licence-compliant performance, a whole range of things. A lot of that's on their website. Comcare's role is to gather information related to those various areas of interest for the commission and pull together information. Against every licensee, a report is produced every meeting of the commission, and it will delve into a range of issues, including work health and safety performance, claims performance and rehabilitation performance. The commission itself has set various performance KPIs for those things. At various times the commission also will direct, which Comcare will then facilitate, prevention audits, work health and safety audits—those sorts of things. So Comcare's role is really to gather that information.
witness_organisation: Jobs and Skills Australia
witness_position: General Manager, Strategy and Performance Group

agency: Comcare
text:
I think you've given a thorough description. Thank you for that. I'll just move on to talk about what I appreciate is a specific case. A lot of this has been reported in the media, and I appreciate there's some limitation to your speaking about a specific individual. Just for the record, I've spoken to that individual directly myself, and she's comfortable about me raising this question. But I also understand the capacity for you to answer detail on specific cases.

It goes to Hine Murphy, a working mother of seven and a grandmother, who's been left with permanent vision loss due to Cleanaway's disregard for safety. Hine is a truck driver. She was carrying out a shift when concentrated methanol from a hospital waste bin poured over her. She contacted management to seek urgent safety advice. Crickets. No response. In the coming weeks she was hospitalised, before finding out she would have permanent vision loss. I'm just appalled about how this company is operating. They have photographs, they have medical evidence, and yet, as she was a self-insured operator, they've now discontinued her compensation payments. She is 85 per cent blind in both eyes. She's a single mother and grandmother who raises her kids and grandkids. She is very tough and strong. Her kids are very supportive of her. I've met them on a number of occasions now.

I might just say—just bear with me, and I apologise to the committee and the chair—I don't think it's surprising to see that an equity firm was in negotiations to purchase Cleanaway, when, as you know, one of the things you want to do is decrease costs. I put this directly on Cleanaway, and I'll say this on the record here. I'm not asking for Comcare to comment—unless you wish to for some reason—but I'm putting to the committee and to the public that this is a calculated attempt to falsely imply they had fixed their problems up. They threw her to the wolves—and her kids and her grandkids—after blinding her. They failed to respond to contacts and they failed to respond when she was speaking to them about coming to visit. They did some horrendous and inappropriate investigations, without witnesses, into her medical condition. It is just the lowest of the low.

But I want to go to this point. The private equity firm that has now purchased it is EQT Infrastructure. Has there been contact with EQT to find out what they are doing? I'm going to say this again: equity firms buy a company and either split it up or shove it off to somebody else. They paid well above—20 per cent above—the price for the shares. Here's capital sweated already; it's going to be sweated again, in an operation that's killing people, maiming grandmothers and then denying responsibility because they're a self-insurer. They deserve to be in the gallows, as far as I'm concerned, and held to account for what's going on.

agency: Comcare
text: We've not had any engagement with the private equity firm.
witness_organisation: Jobs and Skills Australia

agency: Comcare
text: Can I, then, ask you to take into full consideration contacting the private equity firm through the appropriate channels?

agency: Comcare
text: I think that would be a matter for the SRCC. Again, I don't want to create obligations for the SRCC, but I'd be more than happy to pass that message to the SRCC on the committee's behalf, Senator.
witness_organisation: Jobs and Skills Australia

agency: Comcare
text: Mr Radford, the key question is: are they actually aware of everything that is happening with respect to Cleanaway? That's one of the issues that immediately comes to my mind. I dearly hope that the chair and the board of directors each personally watches Senator Sheldon's presentation this evening, because it is shocking.

agency: Comcare
text: Thank you, Senator. There's a lot more to be said on this. I'm mindful of time, but there's a lot more to be done on prosecuting this matter. Back to the chair.

agency: Comcare
text: Can I just say one thing. Mr Radford, last time we were in Senate estimates, I asked you about the record fine that Cleanaway had received. It appears, again—after Senator Sheldon's evidence tonight—that, to these jokers, this is just the cost of doing business. It is an absolute disgrace. We need a strong regulator. We need you, and workers need you, to be out there and to have these companies fear you when they are acting like this. The whole premise behind industrial manslaughter laws is that, if you kill a worker, you go to jail. We need to see something happen with these guys. It's an absolute disgrace.

agency: Comcare
text: Are you aware that, if a successful takeover is consummated, all the senior executive team's long-term and short-term incentives will typically immediately vest and they will walk away with millions and millions? Are you aware of that dynamic in the context of a takeover?

agency: Comcare
text: Not from a regulatory point of view—but I'm aware of what generally happens when private equity buys out an existing listed company.
witness_organisation: Jobs and Skills Australia

agency: Comcare
text: Thank you.

agency: Comcare
text: Mr Radford, I think you can see the depth of passion and alarm on this committee, so I'm sure we will be returning to these issues. Thank you, Senator Sheldon, for raising it. At this point, Mr Radford, we need to let you go. Thank you.

agency: Australian Skills Quality Authority
text: I now welcome officials from the Australian Skills Quality Authority, including its chief executive officer, Ms Saxon Rice. Welcome to you; do you have an opening statement?

agency: Australian Skills Quality Authority
text: No, thank you, Chair.
witness_organisation: Australian Skills Quality Authority

agency: Australian Skills Quality Authority
text: Senator Nampijinpa Price.

agency: Australian Skills Quality Authority
text: Thank you very much. Can you please walk me through the consultation process ASQA undertook with registered training organisations, particularly smaller providers, for the most recent changes to ASQA's annual registration charge?

agency: Australian Skills Quality Authority
text:
Certainly. The whole of the process was a complete review of ASQA's cost recovery implementation statement. We are a fully cost recovered agency. We have been since 2022, so for four years now. We have progressively moved to a full cost recovery model. We undertook a full review of all of our charging because, in the period since we last consulted with the sector and set our fees and charges, which was in 2022, we have had considerable changes to the way in which we regulate the activities that we need to charge for as well as the composition of what forms the annual registration charge.

Our fees and charges are made up of two key areas. We have an annual registration charge, and that's a charge that cannot be attributed to any individual. The activities that form the cost of that total charge are attributed to the sector as a whole, so then we need to work out a methodology for the apportionment of the annual registration charge to individual providers. The second part of our fees relates to entity directed charges. So that's for, for example, an individual provider who lodges a renewal of registration application or an individual provider for whom we are undertaking a performance assessment. There's an individual charge directly to that provider.

The process that we undertook as part of the full review of all of our cost recovery was in line with the Commonwealth charging framework and the Commonwealth charging policy. We worked together with the Department of Finance. We worked together in terms of a consultation paper that we put out to the sector. I can check the exact dates, but I believe it was around the end of January or beginning of February this year. We consulted over a period of at least one month. That included a webinar—
witness_organisation: Australian Skills Quality Authority

agency: Australian Skills Quality Authority
text: Are you able to provide a briefer response? In the interest of time, I want to make sure we can get through these.

agency: Australian Skills Quality Authority
text: It was a comprehensive consultation process which included all of the states and territories.
witness_organisation: Australian Skills Quality Authority

agency: Australian Skills Quality Authority
text: I've been contacted by numerous small training organisations who are extremely concerned by these fee increases. What factors were considered in this change, which, for example, sees an organisation moving from 999 students to 1,000 students hit with an increase of more than 50 per cent in their annual registration charge?

agency: Australian Skills Quality Authority
text: The annual registration charge and its apportionment to the sector has always been undertaken through an attribution of the size and scope of a provider—the size being the number of students and the scope of their registration being the number of qualifications that they have on scope.
witness_organisation: Australian Skills Quality Authority

agency: Australian Skills Quality Authority
text: Can I understand what modelling was done by ASQA on the disproportionate effect of these changes on small providers and short course providers, given the model fails to distinguish between single units of competency or short courses and full certificates or diplomas for the purposes of the reported number of students within the fee calculation.

agency: Australian Skills Quality Authority
text: Until this most recent change, for providers who only had units of competency on scope, the number of students had not been factored as part of the calculation of where in the matrix of the annual registration charge they fell. What we have observed though over recent years is an increase in the number of providers who have significant numbers of units of competency on scope. So the change in methodology as part of this review was to consider—the average number of units that make up any qualification is approximately 10 units. In order to ensure that we had the right apportionment of providers in terms of where they fall in the matrix, part of our consultation with the sector was that we changed the methodology so that every 10 units of competency that a provider had on their scope would be equivalent to one qualification in terms of the way in which the size and scope was considered for the annual registration charge.
witness_organisation: Australian Skills Quality Authority

agency: Australian Skills Quality Authority
text: Why does the annual registration charge not include additional fee tiers beyond 1,000 students to better reflect the regulatory effort required for larger providers?

agency: Australian Skills Quality Authority
text: There are two aspects to that. One is that the annual registration charge itself is not reflective of the regulatory effort attached to any individual provider, because what makes up that particular charge under the charging framework and also the legislation is ASQA's functions that are relevant to the sector as a whole. Then we have to look at a methodology for the apportionment of that. When we look at the number, we've had, for quite some time—
witness_organisation: Australian Skills Quality Authority

agency: Australian Skills Quality Authority
text: Can I just ask you: did ASQA consider an alternative fee schedule to help smaller training providers or short course providers at all?

agency: Australian Skills Quality Authority
text: Within the context of the consideration of where all of the providers fall—we regulate around about 3,800 providers in total, and it's a very diverse sector—we know that about 83 per cent of all providers fall within the bottom 50 per cent of all annual registration charge tiers, so 83 per cent actually sit in the bottom 50 per cent of the annual registration charge tiers. We certainly considered that there may be some impact in specific circumstances, and, for that, there is provision within the legislation to consider a partial waiver of fees or charges. There's a specific legal test for that. So far we have received, I think, eight requests for partial waiver of the annual registration charge.
witness_organisation: Australian Skills Quality Authority

agency: Australian Skills Quality Authority
text: Is that due to lack of awareness of that availability? You said there are eight. I imagine that, if there were more providers out there who understood that was available to them, they'd probably take that up. Can I just ask you, quickly—and you might have to take this on notice—how many complaints have been received to date from small or short course providers about the changes to the fee charges.

agency: Australian Skills Quality Authority
text: I'm happy to take that on notice.
witness_organisation: Australian Skills Quality Authority

agency: Australian Skills Quality Authority
text: Senator O'Sullivan, take us home!

agency: Australian Skills Quality Authority
text: You want me to take us home? Okay. These will be speedy questions with speedy answers, if I can. I won't press you too much, though. I'd like to start by understanding how ASQA handles tip-offs about fraudulent qualifications.

agency: Australian Skills Quality Authority
text: All tip-offs are received, assessed and considered as part of the overall intelligence that we receive more broadly. We, as you know, established the tip-off line, I believe, in October 2023. We have received considerable thousands of tip-offs since that time and assessed all of those. We're not a complaints-handling body, though, and that's very deliberately the case within our established legislation, but we certainly receive all of that information, assess it, consider it against everything else that we know in relation to where that information has come from and take appropriate action.
witness_organisation: Australian Skills Quality Authority

agency: Australian Skills Quality Authority
text: At some point, do you triage? Is there a point in that process chain that you triage? How do you determine if something is maybe a higher priority? Is safety, for example, taken into consideration?

agency: Australian Skills Quality Authority
text: Absolutely. As part of all of the consideration that we have, we assess our regulatory risk priorities at least on an annual basis but often more regularly than that, depending on the nature of the information that we're receiving.
witness_organisation: Australian Skills Quality Authority

agency: Australian Skills Quality Authority
text: Do you have a timeframe that you work towards in terms of responding to those tip-offs?

agency: Australian Skills Quality Authority
text: We don't respond to the tip-offs in the context of—
witness_organisation: Australian Skills Quality Authority

agency: Australian Skills Quality Authority
text: Or addressing the tip-offs?

agency: Australian Skills Quality Authority
text: It's probably important just to clarify that we do certainly acknowledge receipt of all tip-offs that we receive. We have been receiving volumes, so we obviously work through the information received as quickly as possible. We then action appropriately. As a risk based regulator, all of the consideration of those tip-offs are based on risk, so that would mean that if the information, for example, was in relation to a more high risk qualification or industry area or those sorts of things, again, it would be combined with all of the rest of the information that we hold, but then we would take appropriate action based on that.
witness_organisation: Australian Skills Quality Authority

agency: Australian Skills Quality Authority
text: Would you refer to police, for example, if there's something that's unlawful?

agency: Australian Skills Quality Authority
text: Of course
witness_organisation: Australian Skills Quality Authority

agency: Australian Skills Quality Authority
text: Or WorkSafe, if it's a safety sort of matter, or a state regulator—do you do all that?

agency: Australian Skills Quality Authority
text: Yes.
witness_organisation: Australian Skills Quality Authority

agency: Australian Skills Quality Authority
text: Is there a formal protocol in relation to that gate of decision to refer? Or do you just rely on—

agency: Australian Skills Quality Authority
text: To refer to external agencies? We have a number of ongoing engagements with external agencies, so it depends on the nature, if I can put it that way. I'm happy to take any specifics on notice and provide you with further detail, but, as a bit of an example, we are working with state police, other regulators, Commonwealth regulators and the Fraud Fusion Taskforce. We have protocols, information sharing and MOUs all in place as part of all of those operations that we would share information.
witness_organisation: Australian Skills Quality Authority

agency: Australian Skills Quality Authority
text: The person that provides the tip-off, the whistleblower—do they get any feedback?

agency: Australian Skills Quality Authority
text: No. As I say, we acknowledge receipt of the information, but we don't provide ongoing updates on any of the actions that we take—
witness_organisation: Australian Skills Quality Authority

agency: Australian Skills Quality Authority
text: Is there a reason for that?

agency: Australian Skills Quality Authority
text: particularly as we're not a complaints-handling body. Sorry?
witness_organisation: Australian Skills Quality Authority

agency: Australian Skills Quality Authority
text: Is there a reason why you don't?

agency: Australian Skills Quality Authority
text: We certainly don't keep complainants informed of ongoing regulatory activity, but we're not a complaints-handling body, most importantly.
witness_organisation: Australian Skills Quality Authority

agency: Australian Skills Quality Authority
text: I want to go to something specific. The remaining questions I've got here are general, which I'll put on notice. I'm sure you're aware of the reporting in the Age earlier this month detailing a fake qualifications racket operating across Victoria's Big Build. The Age reports that hundreds, possibly thousands, of fraudulent construction certificates have been issued over four years. The article also reports that ASQA was tipped off about this in January 2023 by the training organisation NSTA, but they never got a response. Can ASQA confirm it received a complaint from NSTA in January 2023 about the fraudulent construction qualifications?

agency: Australian Skills Quality Authority
text: I'll give some clarification to the detail of the question there. Yes, we received information from NSTA, but we've received information twice. The first time was on 6 December 2023, and that was in relation to a single, allegedly fraudulent statement of attainment. We opened an investigation into that matter. NSTA, though, was simply acknowledged. We acknowledged receipt of that information at the time. We received a subsequent tip-off from NSTA on 23 January 2024, and that was again regarding a further single, allegedly fraudulent statement of attainment. I believe that was the one referred to in the media, in the Age most recently—that particular tip-off.
witness_organisation: Australian Skills Quality Authority

agency: Australian Skills Quality Authority
text: Yes, I believe that. Can I just confirm that's the same report that identified the suspected issuer to be Mr Jack Younes?

agency: Australian Skills Quality Authority
text: That would have been the tip-off on 23 January 2024.
witness_organisation: Australian Skills Quality Authority

agency: Australian Skills Quality Authority
text: Did anyone at ASQA contact the complainant after the acknowledging receipt?

agency: Australian Skills Quality Authority
text: Contact NSTA?
witness_organisation: Australian Skills Quality Authority

agency: Australian Skills Quality Authority
text: The complainant, yes.

agency: Australian Skills Quality Authority
text: No. We acknowledged receipt of the information.
witness_organisation: Australian Skills Quality Authority

agency: Australian Skills Quality Authority
text: That was the extent of the communication.

agency: Australian Skills Quality Authority
text: That's correct. We did launch, though, as I mentioned, an investigation into the information that was received.
witness_organisation: Australian Skills Quality Authority

agency: Australian Skills Quality Authority
text: Did you refer the complaint that you received to Victoria Police, WorkSafe Victoria or any other agency?

agency: Australian Skills Quality Authority
text:
In the process that we undertook in relation to our investigation, there were two isolated incidents, so we were certainly not aware of any, and nor did the information refer to any, widespread fraudulent activity. It is also probably important to distinguish between bogus qualifications—which are quite literally fraud and criminal activity—and qualifications where, as you know, we have been involved for some time now in having to consider the legitimacy of their issuance, albeit issued through a registered training organisation, and where we've had the authority to cancel those qualifications. They're two very different matters.

From a bogus qualifications perspective, we have some limited powers within our legislation to consider those. The difficulty that we experience is that often, or most often, by definition, the recipient is complicit. Where we seek to engage with the recipient, often the recipient will not engage. From that perspective, we have been continuing to work, for example, with the New South Wales building commission in relation to, I believe, more than 900 licences that the building commission has now cancelled on the basis of bogus qualifications. So we certainly are involved in many fora where we raise these issues.
witness_organisation: Australian Skills Quality Authority

agency: Australian Skills Quality Authority
text: I'm really interested in that, but I've got a minute. Can you provide more information on that on notice. I'm quite interested in understanding that.

agency: Australian Skills Quality Authority
text: Sure.
witness_organisation: Australian Skills Quality Authority

agency: Australian Skills Quality Authority
text: Finally, since January 2023, has ASQA received any other complaints or tip-offs about Mr Younes or any other aliases identified?

agency: Australian Skills Quality Authority
text: I'd clarify that January 2024 was the first information we received in relation to that individual, but I would probably have to take any further detail on notice, also acknowledging that it is relevant to an ongoing police investigation.
